# ItalyInCountry – full text

---
## A minimal payroll input schema for Italian employees
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/minimal-payroll-input-schema-italian-employees.html
Summary: Field-by-field guide to the data an Italian payroll needs from a global EOR or payroll platform, and why each field matters.
Global platforms often ask what an Italian payroll provider needs to run a month. The honest answer is shorter than most expect, but it is stricter than most expect too. Italian payroll is driven by the national collective agreement, the social security position and the individual’s tax situation. If your platform sends clean data for those three areas, the rest is routine.
This article walks through the minimal schema, field by field, and says why each field exists.
Identity and tax identity   Legal name, birth date, birth place, sex. These feed the Italian tax code, the codice fiscale. Italian systems validate the tax code against these fields. A mismatch blocks filings.
Codice fiscale. Send it if the employee already has one. If not, flag it as missing. The payroll provider can usually start the process, but the hire cannot be filed cleanly without it.
Residence address and domicile. Residence drives local tax treatment. Send both if they differ. Do not send a work address in their place.
Citizenship and work authorisation status. Italian filings distinguish between EU and non-EU workers. For non-EU staff, send the permit type and its validity end. The provider needs this to keep the record compliant, not to assess immigration eligibility.
Contract data   Start date and end date, if fixed term. The start date triggers the mandatory employment notification. Late data here creates real exposure, so send it as early as you can.
Contract type. Open-ended, fixed-term, apprenticeship and similar. Use a controlled list, not free text.
Working time. Full-time or part-time, plus the weekly schedule for part-time staff. Italian payroll calculates many items from the agreed schedule, so a vague “part-time” is not enough.
Job title and level. This is the most underestimated field. In Italy the level is not a label. It is a classification inside the collective agreement and it sets minimum pay and many entitlements. Send the level your client believes applies, and expect the provider to confirm it.
Collective agreement (CCNL). Send the name of the agreement that applies to the employer’s sector. If your client does not know, say so. Do not guess. The wrong agreement changes minimum pay, notice periods, leave and sick pay rules.
Pay data   Gross base pay and its period. State whether the figure is monthly or annual, and in which currency. Italian payroll works from gross.
Additional monthly payments. Many agreements provide extra payments beyond the regular months. Do not fold them into an annual total without saying so. The provider needs to know whether your gross figure already includes them or sits on top.
Recurring allowances and benefits. Meal vouchers, company car, housing support, phone. Send each as its own line with a type, an amount and a start date. The tax and contribution treatment depends on the type, so a single “benefits” total is not usable.
Variable pay. Bonuses, commissions and equity. Send the event, the gross amount and the payment month. Equity needs extra detail, so flag it early rather than at the payment month.
Monthly variable inputs   After onboarding, the monthly feed should carry only changes.
Absences. Type (holiday, sick leave, parental leave, unpaid leave), start, end. Sick leave needs the medical certificate reference. Parental and similar leave types carry their own rules, so keep the types separate.
Overtime and supplements. Hours by category, if the agreement pays them.
One-off payments and deductions. Each with a reason code.
Terminations. Last working day, reason, and whether notice is worked or paid. Also send any outstanding leave balance. Italian final settlement includes accrued items that depend on these facts.
Tax and family situation   Dependants and tax allowances. The employee declares these, and they change withholding. Send the declaration as given and the date it was made.
Prior employment in the same year. If the person joined mid-year, the provider needs earlier income and withholding data to calculate correctly.
Regional and municipal tax location. Derived from residence, but worth confirming in the feed.
Payment and delivery   Bank account in IBAN form. Account holder must be the employee.
Payslip language and delivery channel. Italian payslips are in Italian. Decide in advance whether your platform shows a translation or a link.
What not to send   Do not send calculated net pay, estimated contributions or your own tax computation. The Italian provider owns those calculations. Send inputs, receive results, and reconcile.
Practical rules for the feed   Use controlled lists wherever possible. Version every record with an effective date. Send corrections as new records, not overwrites. Return validation errors with a field name and a plain reason. Agree on a cut-off day for monthly changes and keep to it.
A schema this small is enough to run a clean Italian payroll. Most delays come from three fields: the collective agreement, the level and the working schedule. Fix those at onboarding and the monthly cycle becomes predictable.
Partnership teams that want the full field list with formats and validation rules can request our data-exchange specification.

## A missed F24 payment: how to detect it, correct it and tell the client
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/missed-f24-payment-remediation-scenario.html
Summary: A missed F24 payment in Italian payroll, step by step: how to detect it, correct it voluntarily and keep the client informed.
A missed F24 payment is one of the more common operational failures in Italian payroll. It rarely comes from bad intent. A bank file is rejected, an approval stalls, or a funding transfer lands late. What matters is how fast you find it and how cleanly you fix it.
This scenario walks through the three stages: detection, voluntary correction and client communication. It is written for partnership, operations and payroll managers at global EOR and payroll platforms who need to know what happens behind the local entity.
The scenario   A monthly payroll closes on time. Net salaries are paid. The F24 form, which settles withholding tax and social contributions, is prepared. The payment instruction is sent, but the bank rejects it. Nobody notices. The deadline passes.
The employees see nothing wrong. Their payslips are correct and their salaries arrived. The gap exists only between the employer and the tax and social security authorities.
Stage 1: detection   Do not rely on the authorities to tell you. Notices arrive late, and by then the position is worse.
Build detection into the payroll cycle itself:
Reconcile every F24 against bank evidence. Each prepared form needs a matching debit and a receipt. A form without a receipt is an open item. Set a daily exception report after each deadline. It lists forms prepared but not confirmed as paid. Check amounts, not only status. A partial payment looks like success in a status field. Compare the paid total with the calculated liability. Keep a named owner for each open item. An exception report that nobody owns does not help. When the report shows a gap, confirm the facts before you act. Which form is affected? Which tax codes and contribution lines? Which period? Was the money never sent, or sent and returned? Write the answers down. You will need them for the correction and for the client.
Stage 2: voluntary correction   Italian law allows a taxpayer to correct a late or missed payment on their own initiative. This is known as ravvedimento operoso. The employer pays the missing tax, interest for the days of delay and a reduced penalty. The reduction is larger when the correction comes sooner and before any inspection or notice.
The practical rule is simple. Act before the authorities do.
A clean remediation follows a fixed order:
Freeze the facts. Record the original due date, the missing amount and the cause of the failure. Calculate the correction. Work out the tax, the interest and the reduced penalty for the actual date of payment. Have a payroll specialist or the responsible professional check the figures. Pay with the correct codes. The correction is paid through F24 as well, with the specific codes for tax, interest and penalty. Wrong codes create a new problem. File the receipt. Link it to the original open item and close the exception. Check the next cycle. Confirm that the same cause does not repeat. If a bank file was rejected, fix the file path. If an approval stalled, fix the approval route. Speed is the main variable. Every day of delay adds interest and may move the case into a higher penalty band. An EOR that waits for the next monthly close to fix a known gap is choosing a higher cost.
Stage 3: client communication   The client is the foreign company that employs the worker through the EOR. They do not need a tax lecture. They need to know what happened, what it costs, and that it is under control.
Send a short written notice as soon as the facts are confirmed. Keep it plain. It should state:
what was missed and for which period; the cause, in one or two sentences; the corrective action already taken or scheduled; the additional cost, and who bears it under the service agreement; the confirmation that employees are not affected; the preventive change you are making. Do not wait until the correction is complete. Tell the client when you find the gap and again when it is closed. Two short messages are better than one long one sent late.
Be clear about cost allocation. If the failure was caused by the EOR, the EOR absorbs interest and penalties. If it was caused by late or wrong data from the client or the platform, say so and point to the contract terms. Avoid argument in the first message. State the facts and the proposed treatment.
What platforms should ask their EOR partner   If you resell or embed EOR services, you inherit this risk in front of your own customers. Ask your partner:
How do you reconcile every F24 against bank evidence? How quickly does an exception reach a named person? Who calculates and pays the voluntary correction? What do you send to the client, and when? Do you pass remediation status to us in a structured way, so our support team can answer customers without chasing? The last point matters most for platforms. Your customer will contact you first. If your support team cannot see the status, they cannot answer.
Partnership teams can request the data-exchange specification to see how payment exceptions and remediation status are shared.

## Absence data checklist: sick leave, parental leave and permits
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/absence-data-checklist-italy-sick-parental-permits.html
Summary: Which fields your platform must send for each absence type so Italian payroll calculates pay correctly: sick leave, parental leave and permits.
Absence data is where most Italian payroll errors start. A missing field does not cause a rejected file. It causes a wrong payslip, and the fix arrives a month later.
This checklist lists what an EOR or payroll platform should send for each absence type. Use it to review your own payloads before they reach Italian payroll.
Fields every absence needs   Send these for every record, whatever the type.
Employee identifier that matches the payroll master record. Absence type code from an agreed list. Start date and end date, or an open end flag if the end is not known yet. Full-day or partial-day indicator. For partial days, send hours. Record status: new, changed or cancelled. Source and timestamp of the entry. Two rules help here. Never overwrite a record silently. Send a change with a reference to the original. And never reuse one type code for different cases. Pay rules depend on the code.
Sick leave   Sick leave pay depends on the medical certificate, the contract and the collective agreement. The employer and the social security institute each pay part of it, and who pays what changes by case.
Required fields:
Certificate protocol number issued for the electronic certificate. First day of illness and last day of the prognosis. Whether the record is an initial certificate, a continuation or a relapse. Link to the previous episode when it is a continuation. Pay rules treat linked episodes differently from new ones. Hospital stay flag, if applicable. Work accident or occupational disease flag. These follow a different payment route and must never be sent as plain sickness. Collective agreement and employee level, so the correct employer top-up can be applied. Common errors: sending a new episode when it is a continuation, missing the protocol number, and mixing up accident leave and sickness.
Parental leave   This category covers several different entitlements. Maternity and paternity leave are separate from optional parental leave, and each has its own pay logic.
Required fields:
Leave subtype: compulsory maternity, paternity, or optional parental leave. Child’s date of birth, or expected date of birth for leave before the birth. Which parent takes the leave. Whether the leave is taken in full days or in hours. Reference to the application filed with the social security institute, where one is needed. Running total of optional leave already used by this parent for this child, including leave taken with a previous employer if known. Any special circumstance flags, such as a single parent or a child with a disability. Common errors: no child date of birth, which blocks the entitlement check. Another is hourly leave sent without hours. A third is a missing running total, which leads to leave being paid beyond the entitlement.
Permits   Permits are short authorised absences. The pay effect depends on the type.
Required fields:
Permit type: paid permit under the collective agreement, unpaid permit, statutory permit for family reasons, medical visit, study permit, union permit, or accrued time-off bank. Hours or days taken. Which balance to draw from, if the type uses one. Supporting document reference where the rule requires proof. Approval status and approver. For time-off banks, send the opening balance and the movement. Do not send only the new balance. Payroll needs to see the movement to reconcile accruals.
Common errors: a generic “leave” code with no reason, and permits sent as full days when the employee worked part of the day.
Quality checks before you send   Run these checks on your side first.
Does every record have a valid type code from the shared list? Do dates sit inside the employment period? Do overlapping records make sense? A sick leave overlapping a permit usually means one is wrong. Are cancelled records marked as cancelled, not deleted? Is the cut-off for late changes known to both sides? Late changes matter most. If a certificate arrives after the payroll run, payroll needs the change flagged as retroactive so it can adjust the next period correctly.
Why the structure matters   Italian pay for absences depends on the type, the collective agreement and the employee’s history. A free-text note cannot carry that. Structured fields with fixed codes can. Agree the code list once, version it, and treat changes as a controlled process.
This also reduces support work. When a payslip looks wrong, you can trace it to a field instead of reading emails.

## Absorbing a book of Italian employees from an acquired EOR
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/absorbing-italian-employees-acquired-eor.html
Summary: A practical walk through the first weeks of taking over a book of Italian employees from another provider: data, payroll, contracts and communication.
You acquired another provider. Part of the deal is a group of Italian employees you have never run payroll for. The client contracts transfer. The people keep working. Nobody wants a missed payslip.
This is how the first weeks usually go when the work is done well.
Before day one: freeze the facts   Do not start with systems. Start with a single snapshot of what the seller actually holds for each employee.
Ask for the same set of items every time:
The signed employment contract and any later amendments. The applicable national collective agreement and the level assigned to the role. Current gross pay, allowances and benefits, line by line. Leave balances, including accrued holiday and permits. Accrued severance entitlement. Open items: sick leave, parental leave, ongoing disputes, pending expense claims. The social security and tax registrations tied to each employer. If a document is missing, log it. Do not guess. A gap you record on day one is a question. A gap you find at the first payroll is an error.
Early weeks: reconcile, do not migrate   The temptation is to load everything into your platform and move on. Resist it. First reconcile.
Take the last payslips from the seller and rebuild them in your own engine from the contract data. Compare gross to net, line by line. Differences point to one of three causes: a contract term nobody recorded, a calculation rule your engine handles differently, or a past error.
Each difference needs an owner and a decision. Keep a simple register. Record the employee, the difference, the cause, and who approved the fix.
Pay special attention to severance accruals. This is the balance that moves with the employee and that is hardest to rebuild later. Get the seller to confirm the figure in writing.
Employer change and what it triggers   How the employees move matters. If the employer changes, the transfer must respect continuity of service. Seniority, accrued rights and the collective agreement carry over. Your contract templates must not quietly reset them.
Check that registrations with the social security and tax authorities are updated for the new employer. Check that insurance cover against workplace accidents continues without a gap. Confirm who files what, and when, during the handover so that both providers do not file, or neither does.
Communicate early and in plain language   Employees care about three things: will I be paid on time, will my terms change, and who do I call.
Send a short message from the client and from you. Say who the new provider is. Say that pay terms stay the same unless the contract says otherwise. Give one support channel. Write it in Italian and in English.
Do not promise a new portal experience on day one. Promise the payslip and a person who answers.
The first payroll under your name   Treat the first run as a parallel run. Both sides calculate. Both sides compare. Only then do you release.
A short checklist helps:
Input cut-off agreed with the seller and the client. Variable pay and overtime confirmed by the client in writing. Net pay totals compared against the rebuilt payslips. Payment file checked against bank details held on record. Statutory payments scheduled with the right employer identity. If a number does not reconcile, hold that employee and release the rest. A late correction to one person is better than a wrong payment to everyone.
Clean up after the first cycle   Once the first cycle is out, the work changes. You now fix the structural issues the reconciliation exposed.
Standardise contract templates. Align job titles and levels with the collective agreement. Retire spreadsheets the seller used for allowances. Move benefits into your system so they are calculated, not typed.
Then review the client side. Some clients inherit habits from the old provider: late inputs, verbal approvals, special cases. Agree a clear calendar and a single approval route. That protects the next cycle.
What partnership teams should watch   The commercial team often sees the deal as a transfer of revenue. Operations sees it as a transfer of risk. Both are right.
The risk sits in the data. Employees will not forgive a payroll error because the provider changed. Clients will not either. The speed of the handover matters less than the quality of the first payslip.
Set expectations with the client early. Tell them what you need, when, and what happens if it is late. A clean handover depends on their inputs as much as on yours.
A structured data exchange makes all of this easier. When both providers agree on the fields, the formats and the sign-off steps before the transfer, reconciliation becomes a check instead of a rescue.
Partnership teams can request our data-exchange specification.

## Access control and security checklist for ICP integrations
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/icp-integration-access-control-security-checklist.html
Summary: A practical checklist for platform teams connecting to an in-country partner: credentials, logging and least privilege, with what to ask and verify.
An integration with an in-country partner (ICP) moves sensitive data. It carries identity documents, salary details, bank data and tax identifiers. Security for that link is not a one-time review. It is a set of controls you can test, and a set of habits you keep.
This checklist is written for partnership, operations and payroll managers at global EOR and payroll platforms. It focuses on three areas: credentials, logs and least privilege. Use it when you set up an integration with ItalyInCountry, and again at each renewal of the working agreement.
Start with a data map   Before you open any access, list what flows in each direction. For each field, write down who needs it, why, and for how long.
Which fields does the partner need to run onboarding, payroll inputs and statutory filings? Which fields does your platform need back? Which fields are never needed by either side? The last question matters most. Data that is never sent cannot leak. If a field has no named purpose, remove it from the exchange.
Credentials   Most integration incidents start with a credential that lived too long or was shared too widely.
Issue one credential per integration and per environment. Test and production must never share keys. A leaked test key should never open production.
Use service accounts, not personal ones. If an integration runs on a named employee’s login, it breaks when they leave and nobody knows who is acting. A service account has an owner, a purpose and a clear record.
Prefer short-lived tokens. Where the interface supports it, use tokens that expire and refresh automatically. Static keys should be the exception, and each one needs an owner and a rotation routine.
Store secrets in a secrets manager. Never keep them in source code, tickets, chat messages or shared spreadsheets. If a secret was ever pasted somewhere it should not be, treat it as exposed and replace it.
Agree a rotation and revocation process in writing. Both sides should know who can revoke a credential, how fast, and how the other side is told. Test the process before you need it.
Restrict where credentials work. If possible, limit use to known network ranges or to mutually authenticated connections. A stolen key then has less value.
Least privilege   Least privilege means each account can do only what its job requires. In an integration this is easy to say and easy to forget.
Separate read from write. A reporting job that pulls payslip status does not need to create or change employee records.
Scope by function. Onboarding, payroll inputs, document exchange and reporting are different jobs. Give each its own permissions instead of one broad role.
Scope by entity. If you serve many customers, make sure an integration credential cannot see data of customers it does not handle. Ask the partner how tenant separation is enforced and how it is tested.
Limit human access. People on both sides who can see personal data should be few, named and reviewed on a schedule. Support staff should see the minimum needed to resolve a case. Where possible, mask sensitive fields such as bank details and tax identifiers by default.
Review access on a fixed rhythm. Put it in the calendar. At each review, remove accounts that are unused, belong to people who changed role, or were created for a project that has ended.
Remove access at the end of the relationship. Offboarding the partner, or a customer, should include a defined step to revoke credentials and confirm deletion or return of data.
Logs   Logs let you answer a simple question after something goes wrong: who did what, to which record, and when.
Log every access and every change. For each event, record the account, the action, the record affected, the time and the source. Include failed attempts, not only successes.
Keep personal data out of the logs. Log record identifiers, not names, tax identifiers or bank details. A log that holds full payloads becomes a second copy of the data you are trying to protect.
Protect the logs. Limit who can read them, and make them hard to alter. A log that an administrator can quietly edit proves little.
Agree retention and sharing. Decide how long logs are kept and how each side can request an extract during an incident or audit. Decide this before you need it.
Set alerts for unusual behaviour. Examples include bulk exports, access outside normal hours, repeated failures and use of a credential from a new location. An alert nobody reads is noise, so name who receives it.
Incidents   Agree the incident path in advance.
Who is the named contact on each side? How is the other side told, and how quickly? Who decides whether to suspend the integration? Who talks to affected customers and, where needed, to the authorities? Run a short exercise at least once. A rehearsal finds gaps that a document does not.
Questions to ask any ICP   How are credentials issued, stored, rotated and revoked? How do you separate customers from each other? Who inside your company can see our employee data, and how is that access reviewed? What do you log, for how long, and can we get an extract? How do you handle a suspected breach, and how will we hear about it? What happens to our data when the relationship ends? Good partners answer these without hesitation and in writing. Vague answers are information too.
Partnership teams can request the data-exchange specification from ItalyInCountry.

## Accessing INPS and Tax Portals: Helping Employees Self-Serve
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/accessing-inps-tax-portals-employee-self-service.html
Summary: How global EOR and payroll teams can help employees in Italy get digital identity and portal access for INPS and tax services, and why it matters.
Employees in Italy can check their own social security record and tax position online. They can download certificates, view contribution histories and file requests. All of this sits behind a digital identity. For a new hire from abroad, getting that identity is often the hardest part.
This article covers the basics your operations team needs to know. It also covers where you can help without taking on work that belongs to the employee.
Why portal access matters   An employee who cannot log in depends on your support queue for every small request. They ask for a copy of a certificate. They ask whether contributions were paid. They ask what a tax notice means. Each question becomes a ticket.
An employee who can log in answers most of these alone. They see the data at the source. That is faster for them and cheaper for you.
Access also builds trust. People like to check that their employer does what it says. The official portals let them do that without asking you.
The two main portals   The social security institute, INPS, runs a personal area for individuals. There an employee can view their contribution record, download statements and use services linked to their position.
The tax authority, Agenzia delle Entrate, runs its own online services. These cover the personal tax record, returns, communications and certificates.
Both portals use the same family of login methods. Once an employee has a valid digital identity, they can usually reach both.
Digital identity: the basics   There are several ways to authenticate. The ones your employees will meet most often are these.
SPID. This is a public digital identity issued by accredited private providers. The employee registers with a provider, verifies who they are and receives credentials. Those credentials work across many public services. Each provider has its own rules, its own verification methods and its own app.
CIE. This is the electronic identity card. It works as a login method when the holder has the card and a compatible phone or reader. Many foreign nationals do not hold it at the start of employment.
CNS. This is the national services card, a smart card with a certificate. It is less common for new arrivals.
Older portal credentials still exist in some cases, but the direction is clear. Public services are moving toward the unified identity methods. Plan your guidance around SPID and CIE.
What blocks foreign employees   The same problems appear again and again.
No Italian tax code yet. Most identity providers ask for it. The employee needs it before registration can finish. Identity document type. Providers accept certain documents and not others. A foreign passport may work with one provider and need extra steps with another. Phone number and email. Many providers ask for a mobile number and an email address that the person can access. A foreign number may cause problems with some providers. Language. Provider screens and support are mostly in Italian. Some offer English, but not every step. Verification method. Some providers verify in person, some by video call, some with a digital signature or an electronic document. Availability and cost differ by provider, so the employee should check current terms. Residence status. Where the employee is in the process of registering as a resident, some steps may have to wait. None of these is a reason to give up. They are reasons to prepare early.
What your team can do   You should not create identities on behalf of employees. A digital identity is personal. The employee must hold the credentials and control them. Your role is to prepare them and remove friction.
Start before day one. Tell new hires in the onboarding pack that they will need a digital identity. Explain what it is and why. Do not wait for the first payslip question.
Give a checklist. List what they need: the Italian tax code, a valid identity document, a mobile number, an email address and a quiet half hour. Keep it short.
Describe the options. Explain SPID and CIE in plain words. Tell them to compare providers on verification method, language and cost, and to read current terms on the provider site. Do not recommend a provider unless you have a reason you can defend.
Show them what to look for. Once they can log in, tell them which sections matter. For INPS, the contribution record. For the tax authority, the personal record and communications. A short screen guide saves many tickets.
Set expectations on security. Remind them never to share credentials, not even with HR or payroll. No legitimate request will ask for a password or a one-time code.
Offer a support path. Name who they can contact when registration fails. Make sure that person knows the common failure points above.
Where this fits in your platform   Global platforms often show payroll data in one place. Employees in Italy will still want to see the source records. A good flow links to the official portals and explains what each one shows. It does not try to replace them.
It also helps to track onboarding status. Know whether each employee has obtained their tax code. Know whether they report having a working login. That lets your team step in only where someone is stuck.
Keep guidance current   Providers change their steps. Portals change their menus. Treat your guidance as a living document. Review it on a regular schedule and after any reported failure. Link to official pages rather than copying their text.
The practical outcome   Employees who can self-serve ask fewer basic questions. They find errors earlier. They feel in control of their own records. Your team spends its time on real exceptions.
The work is simple. Explain early, give a short checklist, protect their credentials and point them to the source.
Partnership teams that want to connect their onboarding flow to ours can request the data-exchange specification.

## An employee disputes their net pay: triage to resolution in one ticket
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/employee-disputes-net-pay-triage-to-resolution.html
Summary: How a global EOR or payroll platform can take a net pay dispute in Italy from first message to closed ticket, with the right data attached from the start.
A message arrives from an employee in Italy. The net pay is lower than expected. The employee is upset. Your support agent opens a ticket.
What happens next decides whether this is a short exchange or a long chain of emails across time zones.
This article walks through one dispute, step by step. The goal is simple: triage, diagnosis and answer inside a single ticket.
Why these tickets drag on   Most net pay disputes are not errors. They are gaps in understanding. The employee compares the payslip with an offer letter, a colleague’s number or last month’s payment. The platform sees a correct calculation. Neither side has the same view of the data.
The delay comes from missing context. The agent asks for the payslip. The employee sends a photo. The agent asks the local partner. The partner asks for the payroll input. Each handoff adds a wait.
Step 1: Classify before you reply   The first job is to sort the dispute. Do not answer the emotion. Sort the cause.
Most cases fall into a few groups:
The employee expected a gross-to-net figure that was never shown to them in that form. A one-off item changed the month: a bonus, a deduction, an expense refund, an adjustment from a prior period. A change in personal circumstances was not reflected, such as family status or tax details. A real input error: a wrong hours figure, a missed allowance, a late contract change. Only the last group needs a correction. The others need an explanation. Tag the ticket with one of these classes at once. The class decides who works on it.
Step 2: Pull the same data the payroll used   The agent should not rebuild the calculation from memory. The ticket should carry the payroll inputs and the payslip lines together.
That means the agent sees, in one place:
the contract terms on file, the monthly variable inputs, the contributions and tax withholdings applied, the collective agreement the employment is under, the changes since the previous period. If your platform and your Italian partner exchange this as structured data, the ticket fills itself. If they exchange it as attachments, the agent hunts for it. This is the main place where time is won or lost.
Step 3: Compare, line by line   With both periods side by side, the agent compares each line. The difference usually shows up in one or two lines. A deduction that appears only this month. An allowance that stopped. A withholding that adjusted after a change.
Write the finding in plain words. Name the line. State what moved it. State whether it is expected.
Do not paste a statute or a long rule into the reply. The employee needs the reason, not a legal essay. If a source matters for your internal record, attach it as a note for staff.
Step 4: Decide the path   Now the class from Step 1 pays off.
Explained difference. Reply with the line-by-line comparison. Keep the tone calm. Offer a short call if the employee wants one. Close the ticket when they confirm.
Missing information from the employee. Ask for exactly what is needed, once. Do not send a generic form.
Real error. Flag it to payroll with the evidence attached. State the correction route: a supplement in the next run or an off-cycle payment. Tell the employee which one, and what they will see on the next payslip.
Step 5: Close with a record   The ticket is not done when the employee says thanks. It is done when the record is complete.
Store the cause class, the line affected, the action taken and the time to resolve. Over a few months this shows patterns. If many disputes come from the same line, the problem is not support. It is how the payslip is presented, or how a change is communicated before it happens.
That feedback loop is worth more than any single fast answer.
What the platform and the local partner must agree on   A single-ticket flow depends on a few agreements made before any dispute exists:
Who owns the first reply, and in which language. Which data the partner shares with the platform automatically, and in which format. How a correction request is raised and how it is confirmed. What the employee sees, and when. Without these, the ticket bounces. With them, the agent works from one screen.
The short version   Classify first. Attach the payroll data. Compare line by line. Explain in plain words. Correct only what is wrong. Record the cause.
A net pay dispute then becomes a routine event, not an escalation.

## Annual tax return for employees in Italy: the role of the CU and when a CAF is needed
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/employee-tax-return-italy-cu-caf.html
Summary: How EOR and payroll platforms can support employees with the Italian annual tax return: what the CU does, when a CAF helps, and how to split the work.
 Why this matters for your platform   Employees hired through a global EOR or payroll platform often have never filed an Italian tax return. Many come from countries where the employer settles everything and the employee does nothing. In Italy, the employer withholds tax during the year, but the employee may still need to file a return. If your support team cannot explain this clearly, tickets pile up every spring.
This article explains what the CU is, what it does in the return process, and when an employee should use a CAF.
What the CU is   CU stands for Certificazione Unica. It is the annual certificate that an Italian employer issues for each employee. It summarises what happened in the tax year:
employment income paid income tax withheld social security contributions paid certain deductions and credits applied through payroll The employer also sends the same data to the tax authority. This matters because the tax authority uses it to prepare a pre-filled return for the employee.
For 2026, the deadline for employers to deliver the CU to employees was 16 March 2026. Your payroll operations should treat this date as fixed. Late or wrong CUs create problems for the employee and for the employer.
What the CU is not   The CU is not the tax return. It is the input. The employee does not copy numbers from it by hand in most cases. The pre-filled return already contains the CU data. The employee checks it, adds what is missing, and submits.
This is the first thing to explain to foreign employees. They do not need to rebuild their income from payslips. They need to check that the CU is correct and that the pre-filled data matches it.
What your team should do about the CU   A platform can remove most of the confusion with a few simple steps.
Deliver the CU early and in a place the employee can find it. Put it in the employee portal, not only in an email. Add a short plain-English explanation. Name each main box on the CU and say what it means. Do not translate the tax terms word for word. Give the Italian term and a short description. Check the data before issuing. Errors in withholding, contributions or employment dates cause the biggest downstream problems. Reissue fast when needed. If a correction is required, tell the employee what changed and why. Keep records of when each CU was sent and opened. This protects you if there is a dispute. When the employee can manage alone   Some employees have a simple situation. They worked for one employer in Italy for the whole year, have no other income, and have no special deductions to claim. For them, the pre-filled return is often enough. They check the CU against the pre-filled data and submit.
Your role here is information. Tell them where the return is, what to check, and who to ask if something looks wrong.
When a CAF is useful   CAF stands for Centro di Assistenza Fiscale. It is a tax assistance centre that helps individuals with returns and supporting documents. A CAF is worth recommending when the situation is not simple. Typical cases:
The employee changed employer during the year, or had more than one employer. The employee has income from outside Italy, or was tax resident in another country for part of the year. The employee wants to claim deductions that need documents, such as medical costs, housing costs or costs for family members. The employee has dependants and needs to declare them correctly. The employee has other income, such as rent from a property. The employee received a notice from the tax authority and does not understand it. In these cases, the CU still matters. It is the starting point. But the CU alone does not capture the full picture, and a CAF can review the documents and file correctly.
Where the employer stops   Be careful with the line between payroll and personal tax advice. The employer or EOR is responsible for payroll, withholding and a correct CU. The employer is not the employee’s personal tax adviser. Your support team can explain the process and point to a CAF. It should not decide which deductions the employee may claim.
State this clearly in your help pages. It reduces risk and sets the right expectation.
A simple support flow   Here is a flow that works for most platforms.
Before the CU is issued: send a short notice saying when it will arrive and what it is. When the CU is issued: send the document with the plain-English guide. After issue: offer a short checklist. Is this my only employer? Do I have foreign income? Do I have documents for deductions? If the answer to the first is yes and the others are no, the employee can likely proceed alone. Otherwise, suggest a CAF. For questions: route them to a trained agent with a clear script on what can and cannot be answered. Data flow between platforms   If you work with a local partner on Italian payroll, the CU data should move between systems without manual re-entry. Employee identifiers, income totals, withholding, contributions and employment dates must match. A mismatch is the most common cause of corrections.
A clean exchange of this data lets your platform show the employee the same figures the tax authority will use. That reduces tickets and builds trust.
Partnership teams that want to see how this data exchange works are welcome to request the data-exchange specification.

## Choosing the right CCNL for a new Italian hire: the logic an in-country partner uses at quote stage
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/choosing-right-ccnl-new-italian-hire-quote-stage.html
Summary: How an in-country partner proposes a CCNL at quote stage: the inputs, the order of checks, and the data a platform should send with each request.
A quote for an Italian hire depends on one choice more than any other: the collective agreement, the CCNL. It sets minimum pay, job levels, leave, notice, and many employer costs. If the quote assumes the wrong one, the number changes later. Your client notices.
This article describes how an in-country partner (ICP) proposes a CCNL at quote stage. It is written for partnership, operations and payroll managers at global EOR and payroll platforms who want fewer corrections after the quote.
Why the CCNL is not a free choice   In Italy, the CCNL is tied to the activity of the employer, not to the preference of the employee or the platform. A company that works in a given sector normally applies the agreement for that sector. The job title matters, but the business of the hiring entity comes first.
For an EOR model this creates a question. The foreign client has an activity. The EOR is the legal employer. Which activity counts? The ICP has to answer this before proposing anything. The answer should be documented, because it will be asked again at onboarding and at any later review.
The inputs we ask for   At quote stage we need a short, structured set of facts. More is not better. Missing fields are the main cause of wrong proposals.
The client’s main business activity, in plain words and with an industry code if the client has one. The role: title, main duties, and whether the person manages others. The work pattern: full time or part time, fixed term or open ended. The work location in Italy, including remote work from home. Whether the client already has Italian employees or an entity, and under which agreement. Any agreement the client has already signed in another country that it wants to mirror. The last point is often misunderstood. A foreign agreement or policy does not replace the Italian one. It can inform benefits design on top of the CCNL. It cannot lower the floor.
The order of checks   The ICP works through the same sequence each time. This keeps proposals consistent across clients and makes them easy to audit.
First, the activity. Map the client’s business to the sector whose agreement fits. If the activity is clear, this step closes quickly. If the client spans several sectors, ask which one drives the role.
Second, the role inside that agreement. Each CCNL has its own classification of levels. Duties decide the level, not the title. A “manager” title on a person with no team and narrow duties often maps to a lower level than the client expects. A modest title on a person with real autonomy can map higher. Pay and costs follow the level.
Third, the contract type. Open ended, fixed term and part time arrangements each have rules in the agreement. Some agreements are more flexible than others on these points. Check the specific agreement, not general assumptions.
Fourth, the compatibility with the client’s pay offer. Compare the offered salary with the minimum for the proposed level. If the offer is below the minimum, the quote must show the correct figure and flag the gap. Do not adjust the CCNL to fit the budget.
Fifth, the extras. Check supplementary items the agreement may add: additional benefits, welfare provisions, supplementary pension or health funds, and contributions to bilateral bodies. These change the total cost and are easy to miss in a rough quote.
When two agreements look plausible   This happens. A software company hiring a sales person, a consultancy with a technical team, a manufacturer with a pure services office. The ICP does not guess. We present the primary proposal with the reason, and name the alternative with the reason it was set aside. The client or platform can then confirm the facts that decide it.
If the facts are still unclear, we say so in the quote. A clearly marked assumption is better than a confident error.
What the quote should show   A good CCNL proposal inside a quote includes:
the agreement proposed and the sector reasoning; the level proposed and the duties behind it; the minimum pay for that level, set against the client’s offer; the cost items that come from the agreement; the assumptions, listed, so they can be confirmed or corrected. Each item should carry its source and the date it was checked. Agreements are renewed, and minimums change. A quote without a check date cannot be trusted next quarter.
Where platforms can help   Most corrections we see come from data that never reached the ICP. The platform had the client’s activity, but the form did not pass it on. The role description was a title only. The remote work location was left blank.
A fixed data exchange fixes this. The platform sends the same fields on every request, in the same format. The ICP returns the proposal in a matching structure: agreement, level, minimum, cost items, assumptions, sources. Your team can then show the result in your own quote tool without rewriting it, and can see at once when an assumption is open.
This also helps your support team. When a client asks why the figure moved, the answer is in the assumptions, not in an email thread.
A short checklist   Capture the client’s activity, not only the role. Describe duties, not only the title. Treat the CCNL minimum as a floor. State assumptions in the quote. Record the source and check date for every figure. Partnership teams that want to see the fields and the response format can request the data-exchange specification.

## Conguaglio: why December and leaver payslips change
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/conguaglio-year-end-tax-recalculation-italy.html
Summary: Conguaglio is Italy's year-end tax recalculation. Learn why December and leaver payslips shift, and what payroll platforms should expect in their data.
Every payroll team that runs Italian employees meets the same question around the end of the year. Why did net pay change in December? The answer is the conguaglio.
What the conguaglio is   Conguaglio means adjustment or true-up. In Italian payroll it is the recalculation of personal income tax (IRPEF) on the employee’s full-year income. The employer, acting as withholding agent, compares two figures:
the tax withheld month by month during the year; the tax actually due on the total income for the period. The difference is settled in the payslip. If too little was withheld, the employee pays the balance. If too much was withheld, the employee gets a refund through payroll.
Why monthly withholding is only an estimate   IRPEF is an annual tax with progressive brackets. According to the secondary source we use, the brackets are:
up to 28000 EUR a year: 23%; from 28000 to 50000 EUR: 33%; above 50000 EUR: 43%. A monthly payslip cannot know exactly how the year will end. Each month, payroll applies the brackets to a projection of annual income based on what is known at that point. If the projection is right, the year closes with no surprise. In practice it is rarely exact.
Things that move the projection during the year:
a raise or promotion; bonuses and one-off payments; variable pay such as commissions or overtime; unpaid leave or other gaps in pay; changes in the employee’s personal circumstances that affect deductions and tax credits. Each of these makes the earlier monthly estimates a little wrong. The conguaglio is where the error is corrected.
Why December looks different   December is the last payslip of the tax year. At that point all income for the year is known, so payroll runs the full annual calculation and compares it with the tax already withheld.
Three effects show up on the payslip:
The December tax line no longer follows the monthly pattern. It carries the correction for the whole year. Net pay can go up or down. A bonus paid late in the year can push income into a higher bracket and raise the tax due. A year with lower income than projected can produce a refund. Gross pay may look normal while net pay does not. Teams that only reconcile gross figures will miss the cause. For a platform, the practical point is simple. A December variance in net pay is not an error by default. It needs a tax explanation, not a payroll correction.
Why leaver payslips change   The conguaglio does not wait for December when employment ends. When an employee leaves, the employer performs the recalculation on the income paid up to the exit date. The final payslip therefore carries the adjustment.
This catches people off guard. The leaver is not just receiving final pay. The last payslip also closes the tax position for the time spent with that employer. Final settlements, pay for untaken leave and other exit items increase income in the same period, and they are part of the calculation.
A leaver’s final net pay can therefore differ sharply from the previous month, even if the contract terms did not change. Employees often read this as a mistake. Support teams need a clear explanation ready.
What this means for EOR and payroll platforms   A few points worth building into your process:
Flag conguaglio lines. Mark the adjustment as its own item in the data you receive, so your system does not treat it as a normal monthly tax figure. Reconcile tax separately from gross. Compare gross to gross and tax to tax. A net variance alone tells you little. Warn employees early. A short note before December and before an exit prevents most support tickets. Model exits carefully. Forecasts for a leaver should include the recalculation, not just the last month’s pay. Keep the audit trail. Store the annual income used, the tax withheld to date and the balance settled. The brackets above come from a secondary source. Treat them as an explanation of the mechanism, and confirm the current rates against official guidance before you use them in calculations.
The short version   Monthly withholding is a projection. The conguaglio replaces the projection with the real annual figure. It happens in December and again whenever employment ends. If your systems expect a stable net pay in those two cases, they will raise false alarms.
Partnership teams that want to receive conguaglio data in a clean, structured form are invited to request the data-exchange specification.

## Contract checklist for a new Italian ICP agreement
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/contract-checklist-italian-icp-agreement.html
Summary: A practical checklist for EOR and payroll platforms signing an in-country partner in Italy: data, liability, SLA and exit clauses to settle before go-live.
A global EOR or payroll platform that adds an in-country partner (ICP) in Italy is handing over live payroll, employee records and compliance filings. The contract has to describe how that works day to day. Most disputes later come from vague wording, not bad faith.
This checklist covers four areas: data, liability, service levels and exit. Use it before you sign, and again when you renew.
Data   Start with roles. State who is controller and who is processor for each data category. Payroll inputs, payslips, tax and social security filings, and employee contact details may not all sit in the same role. Write it down per category.
Then cover these points:
Scope of processing. List the data fields exchanged, the purpose of each, and the systems that hold them. Format and channel. Define the file or API format, the field names, the encoding and the transfer method. Ambiguity here causes most payroll errors. Location and transfers. Name where data is stored and which sub-processors can touch it. Require notice before any change. Security measures. Reference concrete controls such as access rights, encryption and logging. Avoid the phrase “industry standard” on its own. Breach notification. Set a clear internal deadline for the ICP to tell you, so you can meet your own duties to the authority and to the client. Retention and deletion. Say how long records are kept, who keeps the legal archive, and how deletion is confirmed. Audit rights. Allow reasonable audits or the delivery of independent reports, with a defined process. Also decide who owns the master data. Your platform should remain the system of record for the employee profile. The ICP should hold only what it needs to act.
Liability   Payroll mistakes have a cost that is easy to name: wrong net pay, late filings, interest and penalties. Decide in advance who bears which part.
Split errors into types. An error caused by wrong input from your platform sits with you. An error in calculation, filing or deadline handling by the ICP sits with the ICP. Mixed causes need a rule, not a debate.
Check these clauses:
Indemnity for penalties and interest. The party at fault covers them, including the cost of correcting the filing. Cap on liability. Caps are normal. Make sure the cap does not swallow the cases that matter most, such as data breach, wilful misconduct and gross negligence. Pass-through to the end client. Your client contract will have its own terms. Align the two so you are not left with a gap between what you promise and what the ICP covers. Insurance. Ask for professional indemnity and cyber cover, and request proof of it. Correction duty. The ICP should fix its own errors at its own cost and within a stated time. Do not forget conduct. The ICP deals with authorities and employees on your behalf. Set out what it may and may not say, and who approves communication with institutions.
SLA   An SLA that says “timely” is not an SLA. Tie each service to a measurable target and a consequence.
Cover the full monthly cycle: receipt of inputs, payroll calculation, your approval, payment instructions, payslip delivery and filings. For each step, define the cut-off and the owner.
Include:
Input cut-offs. What happens to late changes from your side. Agree whether they roll into the next cycle or trigger an off-cycle run, and who pays for it. Response and resolution times. Separate urgent payroll issues from routine questions. Onboarding and offboarding. Time to set up a new employee and to process a leaver. Language and support hours. Say which languages and which hours are covered, including cover during holidays. Reporting. Monthly service reports with agreed measures, and a review meeting. Service credits and termination triggers. Repeated failure should lead to credits first, then a right to terminate. Change control. Regulatory updates will arrive. Define how the ICP tells you, how fast it updates its process, and who pays for system changes. Exit   Exit is the clause teams skip and later regret. Write it as if the relationship will end badly.
Ask for:
Termination rights. For convenience with notice, for cause, and on change of control. Transition assistance. The ICP keeps running payroll while you migrate, at agreed rates, until handover is complete. Data return. Full export of employee records, payroll history, filings and open items in a documented format, with confirmation of deletion afterward. Open obligations. Who finishes pending filings, year-end statements and corrections after the exit date. Employee continuity. Employees must see no gap in pay or in contact points during the switch. Non-solicitation and exclusivity. Check that the ICP cannot contact your clients or employees directly, and that you are not locked in against your will. Survival. Confidentiality, liability and audit clauses should continue after the contract ends. Before you sign   Run a short dry test. Send a sample data set through the agreed format, check the output, and log the problems. A contract tells you what should happen. A test shows what will.
Then assign an owner on each side for the data, the SLA and the exit plan. Clauses only protect you if someone reads the reports and acts on them.
Partnership teams that want to align their integration with the contract can request the data-exchange specification from ItalyInCountry.

## Cost-center reporting for multi-client Italian payroll
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/cost-center-reporting-multi-client-italian-payroll.html
Summary: How to allocate Italian payroll costs per client and per employee, so finance teams at EOR and payroll platforms can reconcile and invoice with confidence.
Italian payroll is rarely a single number. For a platform that serves many clients, the real question is simple: which client owes which cost, and for which employee? If the payroll output cannot answer that, finance teams rebuild it by hand every month.
This article sets out how to structure cost-center reporting so allocation per client and per employee is a by-product of the payroll run, not a separate project.
Why the default payroll output falls short   Most Italian payroll outputs are built for compliance. They support the payslip, the social security filings and the tax filings. They are not built for client invoicing.
That creates three common problems:
Totals are grouped by filing, not by client. Employer costs appear in several documents with different names. Accruals are shown at company level, not per employee. A partnership or operations manager then has to map each line to a client in a spreadsheet. That works for a few clients. It breaks as the book grows.
Start with a stable allocation key   Every cost line needs two keys: a client identifier and an employee identifier. Both must stay the same across payroll runs, amendments and corrections.
A third key helps: the cost center inside the client. Many clients want their cost split by team, project or legal entity. If the platform stores this at hire, the report can follow without extra mapping.
Keep these rules:
One client identifier per employment relationship. One employee identifier that never gets reused. Cost center codes set by the client, validated by the platform. Changes tracked with an effective date, not overwritten. Separate the cost components   An allocation report is only useful if each component is visible. A single “total employer cost” column hides what finance needs to check.
We suggest these groups, reported per employee and rolled up per client:
Gross pay, including recurring and one-off elements. Employer social security contributions. Insurance contributions for work accidents and occupational illness. Severance accrual (TFR) set aside during the period. Accruals for leave and additional monthly payments. Pass-through items, such as benefits or expense reimbursements. Platform fees, kept apart from payroll cost. Keeping platform fees apart matters. The client should see what is payroll cost and what is service charge. Mixing them makes disputes harder to resolve.
Cash cost versus accrued cost   Italian employment has costs that build up before they are paid. Severance accrual is the clearest case. Leave and additional monthly payments behave in a similar way.
Two views are needed:
Cash view: what was paid in the period, and what the platform must collect from the client. Accrual view: what the period actually cost, including amounts set aside. Finance teams at the client need the accrual view for their books. The platform needs the cash view for funding and collection. If you only report one, someone will ask for the other.
Handle corrections without breaking history   Payroll gets corrected. A late bonus, a changed contract level or a back-dated adjustment will change figures for a closed period.
Do not overwrite the old report. Post the difference as a correction line, linked to the original period and employee. This gives three benefits:
The client sees both the original cost and the change. Reconciliation to earlier invoices stays possible. Audit questions have a clear trail. Make the data machine-readable   PDF reports do not scale. Platforms with many clients need structured data that feeds their own ledger and billing tools.
A useful export has these traits:
One row per employee, per cost component, per period. Client, cost center and employee keys on every row. A clear flag for cash, accrual and correction lines. Stable field names and documented codes. Delivery on a predictable schedule after each payroll run. With this, your finance team can load the file, match it to the client, and invoice. No manual re-keying.
Check the report before it leaves payroll   Build simple controls into the process:
The sum of employee lines must equal the client total. The sum of client totals must equal the payroll run total. Every line must carry a valid client and cost center. New or changed employees must be flagged for review. These checks catch most errors before the client sees them. They also make month-end shorter for both sides.
What this means for your operations   A platform that gets cost allocation right gains time and trust. Invoices match payroll. Client finance teams stop asking for breakdowns. Your operations team spends less time on exceptions.
The design work is small compared to the manual effort it removes. Agree the keys, split the components, separate cash from accrual, and handle corrections as new lines. Then deliver it all as structured data.
Partnership teams: request the data-exchange specification to see the full field list and delivery format.

## Daily contribution minimum: part-time payroll FAQ
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/daily-contribution-minimum-part-time-payroll-faq.html
Summary: What the Italian daily contribution minimum is, how it is derived, and how it affects part-time payroll. A short FAQ for EOR and payroll platform teams.
Part-time contracts raise the same questions again and again in Italian payroll. One of them is the daily contribution minimum. This FAQ answers the questions that operations and payroll teams ask most often.
What is the daily contribution minimum?   It is the lowest daily amount of pay on which social security contributions are calculated. The figure we use is EUR 58.13 per day. It is expressed as 9.5% of a reference amount of EUR 611.85.
The figure comes from a secondary source, a specialist tax publication. Treat it as a working value. Confirm it against the official INPS circular before you load it into a production payroll engine.
How is the figure derived?   The calculation is simple. Take 9.5% of 611.85. The result is 58.13.
This matters for your data model. Do not store only the final daily amount. Store the reference amount and the percentage as well. When the reference amount changes, you can recompute the minimum and keep an audit trail.
Why does the minimum exist?   Contributions must be paid on a pay base that is at least the minimum. If the contractual pay is lower than the minimum, the minimum is used for the contribution calculation. The employee’s social security record is protected, and the contribution base never falls below a floor.
For a platform, this means the contribution base is not always the gross pay. A payroll run needs a comparison step. It checks actual pay against the minimum and uses the higher value.
Why is it expressed per day?   The rule is built around days worked, not around monthly salary. This is the key point for part-time work. The minimum is tied to the working days in the period, so the number of days drives the result.
A monthly view hides this. Two employees can have the same monthly pay and a different number of working days. The check against the minimum can then give different results.
How does part-time change the calculation?   There are two effects to keep in mind.
Fewer working days. A part-time employee who works fewer days in the month has fewer daily minimums to compare against. The floor for the month is lower than for a full-time employee.
Lower pay per day. A part-time employee who works every day but fewer hours earns less per day. Their daily pay can come close to the minimum, or fall below it. When it falls below, the minimum replaces the actual pay as the contribution base for that day.
The second case is the one that surprises teams. The employer pays contributions on more than the actual pay. The cost per euro of salary is higher than in a full-time contract.
What should a platform check on a part-time contract?   Run these checks at onboarding and at every payroll cycle:
Is the contract’s working pattern recorded as days, hours, or both? Is the daily pay above or below the minimum? Does the number of working days match the days used in the calculation? Is the minimum used by the engine the current value, with a source and a date? If the engine cannot answer these, the cost estimate you show to the client may be wrong.
How does this affect cost quotes?   A quote for a part-time hire often uses a simple ratio. The full-time cost is scaled down by the part-time share. This is not always correct. When daily pay is near the minimum, the contribution cost does not scale down in the same way.
Give clients a cost estimate that includes the minimum check. A flat ratio is acceptable only when daily pay is clearly above the floor.
What about changes over time?   The reference amount is updated periodically. When it changes, the daily minimum changes with it. Every stored value should carry a source and a date. A payroll engine that uses a hard-coded number will drift out of date without anyone noticing.
Plan for a small, versioned table of reference values. Each row holds the amount, the percentage, the derived daily minimum, the source, and the date it was checked. Payroll reads the row that applies to the period.
What are the common errors?   Using monthly pay to test against a daily floor. Counting calendar days instead of working days. Applying the full-time minimum to a part-time contract without checking the pattern. Rounding the percentage early. Compute from the reference amount and round only the final value. Keeping the figure without its source. What should you do next?   Start with the data. List the contracts in your portfolio that are part-time. For each one, record the working pattern and compare the daily pay with the minimum. The contracts near the floor are the ones where your cost estimates are most likely to be off.
Then check the process. Make sure the engine stores the reference amount, the percentage and the source. Make sure it compares pay with the minimum on every run.
Partnership teams that want to exchange these values in a structured way can request the data-exchange specification.

## Document retention for Italian payroll: what to keep and who keeps it
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/italian-payroll-document-retention-faq.html
Summary: FAQ for EOR and payroll platforms: which Italian payroll documents to keep, who is responsible for each, and how to split duties with a local partner.
Retention is a shared job in Italian payroll. A global platform, a local partner and the employer each hold part of the record. Problems start when nobody knows which part is theirs.
This FAQ covers what to keep and who keeps it. It does not state retention periods. Periods depend on the document type and on the authority asking. Confirm them with your local payroll provider and put them in writing.
What documents make up the payroll file?   Think in groups.
Hiring records. Employment contract, the notice of hiring sent to the authorities, identity and tax code details, and any signed policies. Pay records. Payslips, the monthly calculation, adjustments, bonuses, expense reimbursements and final settlement. Contribution and tax records. Social security filings, withholding calculations, payment receipts and year-end certifications. Time records. Attendance, leave, sick leave notices, overtime and any collective agreement rules that drive them. Compliance records. Health and safety training, medical fitness certificates where required, and data protection consents or notices. Termination records. Resignation or dismissal letters, final pay calculation and exit paperwork. Who keeps the legal payroll record?   In Italy the employer carries the legal duty to keep the mandatory employment record. In an Employer of Record model, the EOR is the legal employer. So the EOR, or its local payroll provider acting for it, holds the official record.
Your platform may be the contract holder with the end client. That does not move the legal duty. You can hold copies. You are not the system of record unless the contract says so.
What should the platform keep?   Keep what you need to run the service and answer your customers.
Copies of payslips and summaries for display in your portal. The inputs you sent to the local provider and the date you sent them. Approval trails: who approved a change, when, and on what basis. The data-exchange logs between your systems and the partner’s. Customer contracts and the scope of service for each worker. These copies support disputes and audits on your side. They do not replace the original record.
What should the local partner keep?   The local payroll provider usually holds the working file.
The full set of payslips and calculations. Filings made to social security and tax authorities, with proof of submission. Payment confirmations. The reasoning behind any manual correction. The collective agreement version applied to each worker. Ask for this to be listed in your service agreement. A vague promise to keep records is not enough.
What should the end client keep?   The client does not hold the legal record, but it holds facts the payroll depends on. These include worker schedules, approved leave, overtime instructions and workplace safety records for the site where the worker operates. If the client does not keep these, your payroll inputs have no source.
Write this into the client contract. Say what the client must keep, and that it must hand it over on request.
Can records be kept only in electronic form?   Often yes, but do not assume it. Some documents need a proper signature or a certified format to be reliable as evidence. Ask your local provider which documents are safe to hold as digital files only, and which need a specific format or storage method. Record the answer.
How should access work?   Set access by role. Payroll staff see pay data. Customer success staff see status and summaries. Partnership teams see aggregate and process data, not individual salaries unless needed.
Personal data in a payroll file is sensitive in practice and regulated by data protection law. Keep access logs. Review them on a schedule you can defend.
What happens when a partner relationship ends?   This is where records get lost. Before you sign, agree on three points.
The partner returns the full file in a usable format. The partner keeps its own copy for as long as the law requires it to. Both sides know who answers an authority request after the handover. Test the return process before you need it. Ask for a sample export during onboarding.
What should the data exchange include?   A clean exchange makes retention easier. Each record should carry a worker reference, a document type, an issue date, a version and a source system. Corrections should be new versions, not overwrites. That gives you a history that matches what the partner holds.
A short checklist   List each document type and name the keeper. Put retention periods in the contract, confirmed by the local provider. Define what the client must keep and hand over. Agree on format, access and deletion rules. Plan the return of records at exit. Test the export before go-live. Partnership teams that want to align on a shared record model can request the data-exchange specification.

## Due diligence checklist for selecting an Italian in-country partner
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/due-diligence-checklist-italian-in-country-partner.html
Summary: A practical set of questions global EOR vendor managers should ask before signing an Italian in-country partner, grouped by risk area.
Choosing an Italian in-country partner (ICP) is a vendor decision with long consequences. Your customers will see the partner’s errors as yours. Payroll mistakes, late filings and slow responses all land on your brand.
This checklist is built for partnership, operations and payroll managers. The questions are grouped by risk area. Ask them in writing. Keep the answers in your vendor file.
Entity and accountability   Start with who you are actually contracting with.
Which legal entity will sign the agreement, and which entity will employ the workers? Who are the directors and who is the named person responsible for compliance? Which insurance covers errors and omissions, and what does it exclude? What happens to your employees and data if the partner is sold or stops trading? Which subcontractors touch your workers’ data or payroll, and are they named in the contract? A partner who cannot answer these plainly is a partner you cannot audit.
Employment and payroll accuracy   Italian payroll depends on the national collective agreement that applies to each role. Errors here are common and expensive.
How do you choose the collective agreement for a new hire, and who signs off on that choice? How do you track changes to collective agreements and contribution rates? Can you show the source and the date for every rate in your payroll engine? Who reviews payslips before release, and what is the error rate you measure? How are corrections handled when a mistake is found after payment? How do you manage leave, severance accruals and year-end items so that they reconcile with your customer’s ledger? Ask for a sample payslip and a sample reconciliation file. Do not accept a description in place of a document.
Social security and tax representation   Who files with the social security and tax authorities on behalf of the employer, and under whose credentials? How do you evidence that each filing was made and accepted? What is your process when an authority sends a notice or opens a query? Who pays penalties if a filing is late because of the partner’s delay? The last question matters most. Many contracts leave it vague. Make the answer explicit.
Immigration and relocation   If your customers hire non-EU talent, this section decides whether a start date holds.
Do you handle work and residence permits in house or through a third party? How do you report case status, and how often? What do you do when an application is delayed or refused? Who supports the employee on arrival: registration, tax code, housing paperwork? Ask for anonymised case timelines. They tell you more than a service brochure.
Data, integration and security   Will you exchange data through an API, files or manual email, and in which formats? Can you send payroll inputs and outputs in a structured, versioned specification? Where is data stored, and who can access it? How do you handle personal data requests and breach notification under EU rules? Which security certifications or independent audits can you share? How do you test changes before they reach production payroll? Manual data exchange is the most common source of silent errors. A partner that offers a clean specification saves your team hours every cycle.
Service and commercial terms   Who is my named contact, and who covers when they are absent? What response times do you commit to, and what happens when you miss them? How is pricing structured, and which events trigger extra fees? How do you handle exits, including transfer of records and employee data? Can I speak with another global platform that uses you today? How to score the answers   Do not rely on a gut feeling. Score each area as clear, partial or missing. A clear answer comes with a document, a named owner and a process. A partial answer has only some of these. A missing answer has none.
Treat missing answers in entity, social security representation or data security as blockers. Treat missing answers elsewhere as items to fix in the contract.
Run a pilot before you commit volume. Pick a small set of real employees. Check the first payroll cycle line by line. Review how the partner handles the first correction. Their behaviour under a small problem predicts their behaviour under a large one.
Finally, ask what the partner will not do. Good partners have limits and state them. A supplier that says yes to everything has not understood the work.
Partnership teams that want to see how structured data exchange works with an Italian partner can request the data-exchange specification.
