## Employee welcome pack for Italian EOR hires: what every new hire should receive
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/employee-welcome-pack-italian-eor-hires.html
Summary: What a new hire in Italy should receive from an EOR on day one: contract, payslip guide, benefits, tax and social security basics, and who to contact.
A new hire in Italy judges your platform in the first days. The contract is signed, but the questions start right after. What is my CCNL? When do I get paid? What is this line on my payslip? A good welcome pack answers these before they are asked.
This article lists what every new hire should receive. It is written for partnership, operations and payroll teams at global EOR and payroll platforms who work with an Italian provider.
Why the pack matters   Italian employment looks different from what most foreign hires expect. Pay is often described in gross annual terms, but the contract follows a national collective agreement (CCNL). Benefits, notice rules and leave come from that agreement, not only from the individual contract. A hire who does not know this will open a support ticket. A hire who has the pack will not.
The pack also protects your partner relationship. Fewer tickets mean fewer escalations to your team and ours.
What to include   Signed contract and CCNL summary   Send the signed employment contract and a plain-language summary of the CCNL that applies. The summary should name the agreement, the job level assigned to the hire, and the rules that matter most: working hours, leave, notice and sick pay. Keep it to a page. Link to the full text for those who want it.
Who is the employer   Explain the structure in simple words. The EOR is the legal employer in Italy. The client company directs the daily work. The hire should know who handles pay, who handles HR questions and who handles work tasks. Put names and contact channels in the pack.
Payroll calendar and payslip guide   Give the pay date for every month and the cut-off for changes such as expenses or hours. Add an annotated sample payslip. Mark gross pay, income tax withholding, employee social security contributions, regional and municipal tax items, and net pay. Italian payslips are dense. A single annotated example saves many questions.
Explain that the severance fund (TFR) builds up over time and is not paid monthly. New hires from other countries are often surprised by this.
Benefits and welfare   List every benefit the hire is entitled to, split into two groups. The first group comes from the CCNL. The second group comes from the client or the EOR package.
Meal vouchers are a common example. The source we use reports a figure of 10 EUR per day for electronic meal vouchers. Treat this as a reference point and confirm it against the hire’s contract and current rules before you publish it in a pack. Say clearly whether the hire receives vouchers, in which form, and how to activate them.
Tax and social security basics   Explain what the employer withholds and what the hire does not need to file. Many hires fear a separate tax return. Tell them whether one is needed in their case. If the hire moved from abroad, add a short note on tax residence and point to the right contact. Do not give personal tax advice in the pack. State the limits of what the EOR can answer.
Time off, sickness and absence   Show how to request leave, how to report sickness and what proof is required. Sickness reporting in Italy follows a set procedure with medical certification. Describe each step in order and name who the hire must inform. Include public holidays that apply to the work location.
Equipment, data and policies   Confirm who supplies equipment and who owns it. Add the data protection notice and any remote work terms. Keep policies short and link to the full documents.
Visa and relocation status   For hires who need a work permit or are relocating, add a checklist of steps, owners and current status. Update it as things move. Hires who relocate are anxious until the paperwork is done, and a visible status page lowers that anxiety.
Support map   End with a single table: question type, who answers, channel, expected response time. Payroll, benefits, contract changes, expenses and immigration should each have a named owner.
Format and delivery   Send the pack before the start date, not after. Use the hire’s language where possible, with the Italian terms kept in brackets, because payslips and official letters will be in Italian. Use one page per topic. Avoid long PDFs that nobody opens.
Make the pack data-driven. If contract data, payroll dates and benefit rules sit in structured fields, the pack can be generated for each hire and kept current when rules change. Static documents go stale.
What partners can expect   A platform partner should receive the same pack content as structured data, so it can show it inside its own product. That means the hire sees one experience, and the partner keeps its brand. Source and date should travel with each rule, so your team can see what a statement is based on.
A short checklist   Signed contract and CCNL summary Employer roles explained Payroll calendar and annotated payslip Benefits list with conditions Tax and social security basics Leave and sickness procedure Equipment, data and policy notes Visa and relocation status Support map with owners If every hire gets these items before day one, onboarding tickets drop and trust rises.
Partnership teams: request the data-exchange specification and we will send it.

## Employer contribution stack in Italy: IVS and INAIL for cost modelling
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/italy-employer-contributions-ivs-inail-cost-modelling.html
Summary: How employer IVS and INAIL fit into an Italian cost model: what is a fixed rate, what depends on the risk class, and what to flag as unverified.
Employer contributions are the part of Italian employment cost that most often breaks a pricing model. The gross salary is easy. The stack on top of it is not. This note covers two blocks: employer IVS and INAIL. It shows how each should sit in a cost model and where the inputs need care.
Two blocks, two different behaviours   IVS is the pension contribution for invalidity, old age and survivors. It is paid to INPS. The employer share is a fixed share of taxable pay.
INAIL is the insurance against workplace accidents and occupational disease. It does not work like a flat rate. The premium depends on the tariff, which in turn depends on the nature of the work performed.
For modelling, treat them as different object types:
IVS is a parameter. You multiply it by a base. INAIL is a lookup. You first need to know the classification of the role, then apply the tariff. If both sit in one “employer on-cost %” field, the model will be wrong for every role that is not average.
Employer IVS   The employer IVS share is 23.81% of the taxable base (0.2381 as a decimal). In a model, this is the largest single line you will build from a fixed rate.
Practical points:
Apply it to the taxable contribution base, not to total employer cost. The base is defined by the contribution rules, and it is not always the same as gross salary as shown in a contract. Keep the rate as a named parameter with an effective date. Do not hard-code it in formulas. Store the source next to the value. The figure above comes from a secondary source, a payroll reference site covering INPS contributions in the payslip. Your team should confirm it against the primary INPS publication before it reaches a customer quote. The IVS line is also not the whole employer INPS cost. It is one component. Other employer contributions exist, and this article does not give figures for them. Do not read the IVS rate as a total on-cost.
INAIL   INAIL needs more care, because the rules around it have moved recently.
The tariffs in force are the ones set by DI 27/02/2019. On top of that, the way those tariffs are applied was modified by DM 02/04/2026, published on 03/06/2026. This status is also taken from a secondary source, so the same rule applies: verify against INAIL before use.
What this means for a cost model:
The tariff table and the application rules are separate inputs. Version them separately. A change in application rules can change the premium without any change in the tariff table. A model that only tracks the table will miss it. The premium is tied to risk classification. Two employees with the same salary can carry different INAIL costs. Because the modified application rules were published on 03/06/2026, any model built before that date should be reviewed. Quotes issued on the old logic may need a check. This note does not give an INAIL rate. The facts we hold confirm which tariff set applies and which act changed its application. They do not give a single percentage, and a single percentage would be misleading anyway.
How to structure the inputs   A clean structure for the employer stack has these fields for each component:
Component name (IVS, INAIL) Calculation type (fixed rate, or tariff lookup) Value or reference to the tariff set Base to which it applies Effective date and the act it derives from Source URL and source status (primary or secondary) Last verified date The source status field matters. Both inputs discussed here are marked as secondary. A model that shows this flag lets an operations manager see at a glance which numbers still need a primary check. It also gives a sales team an honest basis for saying “estimate” instead of “quote”.
Common errors   One blended percentage. It hides the INAIL variation by role and breaks as soon as the hiring mix changes. Wrong base. Applying the IVS share to a figure that is not the contribution base. Stale INAIL logic. Using the tariff table correctly but missing the change in how it is applied. No audit trail. A rate with no source and no date cannot be defended when a customer questions an invoice. Treating a secondary source as final. Fine for a first model. Not fine for a signed commercial offer. What to do with this   For a platform that prices Italian employment for clients abroad, the stack should be built as data, not as constants in code. IVS goes in as a dated rate on a defined base. INAIL goes in as a tariff reference plus application rules, both versioned. Each carries its source and its verification status.
This lets you update a single record when a rule changes. It also lets you show a customer where each euro of on-cost comes from.
Partnership teams that want to receive these parameters in a structured form can request the data-exchange specification.

## English-only vs bilingual support for Italian employees: what changes in resolution time and satisfaction
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/english-only-vs-bilingual-support-italian-employees.html
Summary: Why English-only support slows resolution and lowers satisfaction for Italian employees on global EOR and payroll platforms, and what bilingual support changes.
Most global EOR and payroll platforms run support in English. It is efficient for the platform. For an employee in Italy, it often is not.
This article looks at how the language of support affects two measures your team already tracks: time to resolution and employee satisfaction. It makes no claims about specific percentages. It describes the mechanisms, so you can test them against your own ticket data.
Where English-only support breaks down   An Italian employee writes to support about a payslip. The question is rarely simple. It may concern a deduction, a contribution line, a leave balance or a bonus treated under the national collective agreement. These topics come with Italian terms that have no clean English equivalent.
The employee has two options. They can write in English and risk describing the problem imprecisely. Or they can write in Italian and wait for someone to translate it.
Both options add friction. The first produces vague tickets. The agent replies with a clarifying question. The employee replies. The agent asks again. Each round trip adds delay.
The second option adds a translation step before anyone starts work. The ticket may sit in a queue until someone with the right language skills picks it up.
Why resolution time suffers   Resolution time is not only about how fast an agent replies. It is about how many exchanges the case needs.
In a payroll case, a precise question saves time. When an employee can name the exact line on a payslip in the language it was printed, the agent can find it at once. When the employee has to paraphrase it in a second language, the agent must guess which line is meant.
Three patterns tend to show up in English-only support for Italian staff:
More clarifying questions per ticket. More reopened tickets, because the first answer addressed a slightly different question. More escalations to a local expert who can read the original document. Each of these lengthens the case. None of them shows up as a language problem in the dashboard. They show up as complexity, or as agent performance. This hides the real cause.
Why satisfaction suffers   Satisfaction scores reflect more than the outcome. They reflect how the employee felt during the exchange.
An employee who needs to ask about their pay is already under some stress. Being asked to explain a technical matter in a foreign language adds to it. Even confident English speakers often prefer their own language for matters involving money, contracts and legal rights.
There is also a trust effect. When a reply uses the wrong term for an Italian concept, the employee notices. They may not know whether the answer is correct. Doubt about the answer becomes doubt about the employer of record, and by extension about the company that hired through it.
For your client, this matters. The employee does not separate your platform from their employer. A poor support experience reflects on both.
What bilingual support changes   Bilingual support means the employee can write in Italian and get an answer in Italian, from someone who knows the Italian rules. That last part matters. A translation layer alone does not fix the problem, because the agent still needs to understand the subject.
When both conditions are met, the effects are practical:
Tickets arrive with the right terms, so fewer clarifying questions are needed. Answers cite the correct contract and payslip terminology, so fewer tickets are reopened. Fewer cases need escalation, because the first agent can read the source document. The employee feels understood, which lifts satisfaction even when the answer is not the one they hoped for. What this means for partnership and operations teams   You do not need to rebuild your support team to test this. Start with your own data.
Split Italian tickets from the rest. Compare the number of exchanges per case, the reopen rate and the satisfaction score. If Italian cases show more back and forth, language is a likely contributor.
Then look at the ticket categories. Payslip queries, contribution questions and leave balances are the most language-sensitive. These are the ones to route to Italian-speaking support first.
A full bilingual desk is one option. Another is a partner who handles Italian-language first-line support and feeds structured case data back to your platform. This keeps your own tooling in place. It also keeps your reporting complete, since the partner’s cases appear in your system.
The key design point is the data exchange. If the partner works outside your ticketing system, you lose visibility. If the partner works through a defined exchange of case data, you keep it.
A practical way to start   Pick one ticket category. Route it to Italian-language support for a limited period. Compare the exchanges per case and the satisfaction score against the same category before the change. Keep the test small enough to reverse.
The result will tell you whether language is a real driver in your Italian caseload, or whether the delay lies elsewhere.
Partnership teams can request the data-exchange specification to see how Italian-language support can plug into their existing ticketing and reporting.

## Escalation matrix template for Italian payroll issues
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/escalation-matrix-template-italian-payroll-issues.html
Summary: A practical escalation matrix for Italian payroll issues: named levels, clear owners and timeboxes that global EOR and payroll platforms can adapt to their SLAs.
Italian payroll issues rarely stay small. A wrong contribution code, a late collective agreement update or a rejected filing can reach the employee’s payslip fast. Without a clear path, the ticket bounces between your support team, your local partner and the authorities’ portals.
An escalation matrix fixes this. It tells everyone who owns the issue, who steps in next and how long each step may take. This article gives a template you can adapt.
Design rules   Keep the matrix short. Long matrices are not read.
Name levels by role, not by number. Names survive reorganisations. Give every level a single owner. Shared ownership means no ownership. Give every level a timebox. When the timebox ends, the issue moves up automatically. Separate severity from level. Severity says how bad it is. Level says who handles it. Severity classes   Use three classes.
Blocking. Net pay cannot be paid on time, or a statutory filing will miss its deadline.
Degrading. Pay is correct but a document, report or filing contains an error that needs correction.
Informational. A question about a rule, a calculation or a process. No money or deadline is at risk.
Agree these definitions with your partner before the first payroll cycle. Disputes about severity waste more time than the issues themselves.
The levels   Triage   Owner: your platform’s payroll support agent.
Job: confirm the issue, collect the employee and entity identifiers, attach the payslip or filing in question and classify severity.
Timebox: set by severity. Blocking issues are acknowledged immediately. Degrading issues are acknowledged the same business day. Informational issues are acknowledged within the standard queue time.
Exit rule: if the agent can answer from the knowledge base, close it. If not, hand over with a complete case file.
Specialist   Owner: the Italian payroll specialist at your local partner.
Job: reproduce the calculation, check the applicable collective agreement, contribution rules and tax treatment, and propose a fix.
Timebox: a fixed window per severity. Write it into the partner agreement. Blocking issues get the shortest window and are worked in parallel with the next level.
Exit rule: the specialist either resolves the case or states in writing why it needs a decision from above.
Payroll lead   Owner: the head of payroll operations at the local partner, paired with your operations manager.
Job: decide on exceptions, approve off-cycle payments or corrections, and coordinate with the social security and tax channels where a filing is involved.
Timebox: same business day for blocking issues. Next business day for degrading issues.
Exit rule: a documented decision and a customer-facing message.
Partnership owner   Owner: your partnership manager and the partner’s account director.
Job: handle repeat failures, contract questions, service credits and root-cause reviews. This level does not fix payslips. It fixes the process that produced the error.
Timebox: review within the next operating review, or sooner if the same cause appears again.
Executive   Owner: a named senior sponsor on each side.
Job: step in only when the lower levels have failed to resolve a blocking issue within its window, or when the customer relationship is at risk.
Rules that make it work   One case file. Every level reads and writes the same record. No side emails. The file holds the identifiers, the calculation, the source rule and the decision.
Automatic promotion. When a timebox ends, the case moves up without anyone asking. The owner of the next level is notified at the same moment.
Holiday and cut-off cover. Name a deputy for every owner. Mark the payroll cut-off days in a shared calendar. Most blocking issues cluster around them.
Customer messaging. The platform owns the customer message. The partner owns the technical content. Agree a standard template for each severity so nobody improvises under pressure.
Evidence for every fix. Each resolution cites the rule applied and the date it was checked. This builds trust and makes audits easier.
What to measure   Track a short list.
Time to acknowledge, by severity. Time to resolve, by severity. Share of cases that moved up a level because a timebox ended. Repeat causes per quarter. The third metric is the most useful. A high share means the timeboxes are unrealistic or the lower levels lack information. Fix the cause, not the number.
Putting it in the contract   Attach the matrix as an annex to the service agreement. Include the severity definitions, the owners by role, the timeboxes and the promotion rules. Review it after each payroll cycle during onboarding, then on a regular schedule.
A matrix that exists only in a slide deck will not hold under pressure. A matrix that sits in the contract, the ticketing tool and the shared calendar will.
Partnership teams: request the data-exchange specification to see how case files, identifiers and status updates can be shared between your platform and ours.

## Final pay in Italy: what goes into the last payslip
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/final-pay-italy-last-payslip-components.html
Summary: What an Italian leaver payslip contains: accrued pay, unused leave, severance accrual (TFR), notice items and deductions. A guide for EOR and payroll teams.
A leaver in Italy does not get a simple final salary. The last payslip closes several accruals at once. Each one follows the national collective agreement (CCNL) that applies to the employee, plus the individual contract. If your platform exports a single “final pay” line, local payroll will have to rebuild the detail. This article lists the components so partnership and operations teams can map them.
Why the leaver payslip is different   In most countries, final pay is the last salary plus unused holiday. In Italy there are more moving parts. Some are paid out. Some are settled through other channels. Some depend on the CCNL, the job level and how the employment ended.
The payslip itself is only the output. The inputs sit in time records, leave balances, the contract and the CCNL tables. Missing data at any of these points delays the payment.
The components   1. Salary for the period worked   This is the pay from the start of the last payroll period up to the last working day. If the employee leaves mid-period, the salary is prorated. The proration method depends on how the CCNL defines the daily rate. Do not assume calendar days. Some agreements use a different divisor.
Variable pay for the period belongs here too. That includes overtime, shift allowances and any commission already earned.
2. Unused leave and paid time off   Accrued holiday that was not taken is normally settled in the final pay. The same applies to other paid time off banks where the CCNL or company policy provides for payment of the balance.
Two points cause most errors. First, the balance must be reconciled against the leave actually taken, not against the figure in a foreign HR system. Second, leave accrued in a prior year may be treated differently from leave accrued in the current year. Ask local payroll for the split.
3. Additional monthly salary installments   Many CCNLs provide extra salary installments paid on top of the regular monthly pay, often at set times of the year. When employment ends, the portion accrued since the last payment is paid out in the final payslip. The accrual is proportional to the time worked in the reference period.
The number of installments and the payment calendar are set by the CCNL. Do not hard-code them in your platform. Read them from the agreement that applies.
4. Severance accrual (TFR)   TFR (trattamento di fine rapporto) is the statutory severance accrual. It builds up during the whole employment. At termination it is paid to the employee as a lump sum.
It is usually not paid as part of the regular salary line. It appears in the final payslip as its own item and is taxed under a separate regime. Teams that treat it as a bonus will get the tax treatment wrong.
If the employee chose to move TFR to a supplementary pension fund, part or all of it may not sit with the employer. In that case the payslip shows less than the full historical accrual. The employee should be told this in advance. Otherwise they will ask why the figure is lower than expected.
5. Notice period items   If the employer ends the contract and does not require the notice to be worked, an indemnity in lieu of notice may be due. If the employee resigns and leaves without serving notice, the employer may be entitled to withhold the equivalent amount.
The notice length depends on the CCNL, the job level and seniority. Your platform should pass the termination type and the last working day. Payroll then applies the right rule.
6. Other indemnities and agreed payments   This line is a catch-all, and it needs care. It may include:
an agreed exit payment a pro-rata bonus under a company plan expense reimbursements still outstanding allowances tied to a role that ends with the contract Each item needs a legal basis and a tax treatment. A negotiated exit payment is not handled like salary. Flag it early so payroll can classify it.
7. Deductions and offsets   The payslip also shows what is taken out. That covers social security contributions, income tax withholding and local surcharges. It can also cover the recovery of advances, unreturned equipment value where the contract allows it, and balances from salary loans.
Recoveries are limited by law and by the agreement. Payroll cannot simply net everything against the final amount. Check what is permitted before you promise an employee a figure.
What payroll needs from you   To produce the final payslip on time, local payroll needs a short, structured set of inputs:
the termination type and who initiated it the last working day confirmation of whether notice is worked or paid the leave balance, with accrual dates any variable pay not yet processed any agreed exit payment, with its description the employee’s TFR election open advances or recoveries Send these as fields, not as an email thread. Late or unstructured data is the main reason leaver payslips are delayed or corrected after issue.
Common mistakes   Treating TFR as ordinary salary. Using the home-country holiday balance instead of the Italian one. Ignoring the additional salary installments accrued since the last payment. Applying a notice rule from the wrong CCNL level. Netting recoveries that the law does not allow. Each of these creates a payslip that has to be reissued. That costs time on both sides and frustrates the employee at the worst moment.
Summary   The leaver payslip in Italy is a set of separate calculations: salary, leave, extra installments, TFR, notice items, other payments and deductions. Each has its own rule. Map them one by one in your integration, and pass the inputs as structured data.
Partnership teams that want to align their offboarding flow with Italian payroll can request the data-exchange specification.

## Fixed-fee vs per-ticket support models for ICP services
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/fixed-fee-vs-per-ticket-support-icp-services.html
Summary: How fixed-fee and per-ticket pricing change the incentives of an in-country support partner, and what that means for service quality on EOR and payroll platforms.
Every EOR and payroll platform that works with a local partner has to decide how to pay for support. The choice looks like a pricing detail. It is really a choice about behavior. The model you pick shapes what the partner does when a case is hard, when a case is boring, and when a case could have been avoided.
This article compares fixed-fee and per-ticket models for ICP services in Italy. It looks at incentives first, then at quality outcomes. It gives no price points. Those depend on your scope and volume.
What each model pays for   A per-ticket model pays for activity. Each request that reaches the partner creates revenue. A payslip query, a social security question, a document request: each is a unit.
A fixed-fee model pays for availability. The partner is paid to keep a defined service running. The number of requests does not change the fee.
That difference sounds small. It is not. Each model rewards a different kind of work.
Incentives under per-ticket pricing   Per-ticket pricing is easy to explain and easy to audit. You pay for what you use. Finance teams like it because cost tracks volume.
The weakness is that the partner earns more when you have more problems. A partner that fixes a root cause reduces its own revenue. A partner that answers each repeat question one at a time keeps it. Few partners act in bad faith. But incentives work without anyone intending them to. Over time, the process drifts toward handling tickets, not removing them.
There are other side effects:
Ticket definitions become a negotiation. Is a follow-up a new ticket or part of the old one? Is a bundled question one ticket or several? Your own team learns to hold questions back to save cost, or to split them to get faster answers. Both distort your data. Complex cases are the most expensive per ticket, and the ones where you most need the partner to spend time. Pricing by count does not reflect effort well. Quiet periods leave the partner with little revenue. That makes it hard to keep experienced people assigned to your account. Incentives under fixed-fee pricing   Fixed fees reverse the pressure. The partner now benefits from fewer, cleaner requests. Every avoidable question costs them time and brings no extra income. So they have a reason to fix templates, correct data at the source, and write clear guidance for your operations team.
That is the good case. The bad case is also real. A partner paid the same amount whether they do much or little may do the minimum. Slow responses, thin answers and unclear ownership are the typical symptoms. The fee can also be set too high or too low at the start, and then nobody wants to reopen it.
Fixed fees need the service to be defined well. Without a clear scope, response targets and reporting, you are buying a promise, not a service.
Quality outcomes compared   The two models tend to produce different quality profiles.
Responsiveness. Per-ticket partners often respond fast, because each response is billable. Fixed-fee partners need response targets in the contract to hold the same line.
Depth of answers. Fixed-fee partners can afford to spend time on a hard case. Per-ticket partners may close it quickly and wait for the follow-up.
Prevention. Fixed-fee models favor prevention. Per-ticket models favor resolution. If your pain is recurring errors, prevention matters more.
Predictability. Fixed fees make budgeting simple for the platform. Per-ticket costs rise exactly when you onboard many new employees or hit a regulatory change, which is when you want the least friction.
Data quality. In a per-ticket model, ticket counts become the main metric. They measure workload, not outcomes. In a fixed-fee model, you are forced to define outcome measures: errors found, time to resolution, repeat issues.
A hybrid that works   Most platforms end up between the extremes. A common structure is a fixed base fee for a defined scope, plus a per-case charge only for work outside that scope, such as a special project or an unusual request. The base fee covers routine support and prevention. The variable part covers real exceptions.
For this to work, three things must be in place.
A written scope that names what counts as routine. Service targets tied to outcomes, not just to response time. Shared reporting, so both sides see the same categories of request and the same trends. Without the third point, the other two decay. Disputes about what a ticket is, or what is in scope, usually come from each side keeping its own records.
How to decide   Use these questions.
Is your request volume stable or spiky? Stable volume suits fixed fees. Spiky volume may need a variable element. Do you want the partner to improve your processes or only to answer? If improve, avoid pure per-ticket. Can you measure outcomes today? If not, a fixed fee is risky until you can. How mature is your scope? A new market with unknown demand may start per-ticket and move to a fixed base once patterns are clear. The common mistake is to treat the model as a procurement choice made once. It is better treated as a setting you review. Volumes change, scope changes, and the incentive that worked at launch can work against you later.
What this means for operations   Whichever model you choose, the operational test is the same. Look at what your partner does with a repeated question. If they answer it again, your model rewards repetition. If they come back with a fix, it rewards improvement. Pay for the behavior you want to see.
Partnership teams that want to compare models on real data need a shared structure for requests, categories and outcomes. We have defined one for ICP services in Italy. Partnership teams are welcome to request the data-exchange specification.

## Four-eyes review in Italian payroll: what it catches
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/four-eyes-review-italian-payroll-gross-to-net.html
Summary: How maker-checker controls work on Italian gross-to-net, which errors a second reviewer catches, and what EOR and payroll platforms should expect from a provider.
Payroll errors rarely come from bad intent. They come from a wrong input, a stale rate or a rule applied to the wrong person. A maker-checker control is built for exactly this. The person who prepares the gross-to-net is not the person who approves it.
This article explains what that control looks like in Italian payroll and what it tends to catch. It is written for partnership, operations and payroll managers at global EOR and payroll platforms who rely on a local provider.
What maker-checker means here   The maker prepares the payroll run. They load the inputs, apply the contract rules and produce the gross-to-net for each employee.
The checker reviews the result before it is released. The checker must be a different person, with their own login and their own sign-off. The system should block approval by the same user who prepared the run.
This is often called four-eyes review. The name is simple. The discipline behind it is not. A checker who only looks at totals is not a control. The review has to test the logic.
Why Italian gross-to-net needs it   Italian payroll has many moving parts. The national collective agreement sets minimum pay, job levels and additional payments. Social contributions depend on the employer’s classification and on the employee’s situation. Income tax withholding depends on personal data, deductions and local surcharges. Year-end settlements and deferred pay items add more rules.
Each part is manageable alone. The risk sits in how they combine. A small input error can pass through several steps and reach the payslip looking plausible.
What a good checker catches   Wrong collective agreement or level. A new hire is mapped to the wrong agreement or job level. Minimum pay and extra payments then follow the wrong table. The net looks reasonable, so only a review against the contract exposes it.
Stale rates and tables. Contribution rates and tax parameters change. A run that reuses last period’s table produces a clean but incorrect result. The checker compares the table version used with the current one.
Input mistakes. A misplaced decimal in a bonus. A start date entered in the wrong month. Overtime loaded twice. These are the most common errors. A checker who sees the variance against the previous period spots them quickly.
Missing or duplicated items. An employee is left out of a run. Another is paid twice. A leaver still appears after the final payment. Headcount reconciliation against the HR record catches these.
Tax situation errors. Family deductions or other personal data are not updated. The withholding is then wrong in a way that only appears later, at year-end adjustment. Reviewing changes in personal data alongside the run helps.
Treatment of special items. Benefits in kind, expense reimbursements and relocation payments follow different rules from regular pay. The checker confirms each item is classified correctly and taxed as intended.
What the control does not do   Four-eyes review does not fix bad source data. If the HR record is wrong, both people may approve a wrong result. The control also fails when the checker is rushed or rubber-stamps the work.
Three practices keep it honest.
Give the checker a defined checklist, not a general instruction to review. Show variances against the previous period, line by line, so changes stand out. Record who prepared, who approved and when, and keep that log. What it means for your platform   You carry the client relationship. When an Italian payslip is wrong, your client does not blame the local provider. They blame you.
So ask your provider concrete questions.
Is the checker always a different person from the maker? Does the system enforce this, or is it only policy? What is on the checker’s list? How are rate and table updates verified before they go live? Can you see the approval log for a given run? Good answers are specific. Vague answers about experienced staff are not evidence of a control.
It also helps to agree on the data you exchange. Clean, structured inputs reduce the errors the checker has to find. They also make the review faster, because variances are easier to explain when the data arrives in a consistent format.
Summary   Maker-checker review is a basic control that works when it is enforced and tested against real logic. It catches mapping errors, stale tables, input slips and omissions before they reach an employee. It does not replace good source data.
Partnership teams can request the data-exchange specification from us.

## Fringe benefits in Italy: tracking the annual cap and handling over-cap taxation
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/fringe-benefits-annual-cap-tracking-over-cap-taxation.html
Summary: How EOR and payroll platforms can track Italian fringe benefits against the annual cap and flag over-cap amounts before payroll closes.
Fringe benefits look simple in Italy. There is an annual cap per employee. Stay under it and the benefits are not taxed as income. Go over it and the treatment changes. For a platform that runs payroll across many countries, the hard part is not the rule. It is tracking the running total correctly and early enough to act.
This article covers how to structure that tracking and how to deal with the over-cap case.
The cap   The figures we use come from a press review of the current rules. They are:
EUR 1000 per year as the general threshold. EUR 2000 per year for employees with dependent children. These are annual amounts per employee. The higher threshold depends on the employee’s family situation, so your data model needs that status as an input, not an assumption.
One caution. The source is a secondary one. Before you hard-code these values into a production rule, check them against the primary legislative text and keep the check date on record. Thresholds in this area have changed between years and can change again.
What to track   A single running total is not enough. For each employee and each tax year, store:
The applicable threshold, and the reason for it (general or dependent children). Each benefit item with its date, type and taxable value. The cumulative value after each item. The remaining headroom under the cap. The source and verification date of the threshold in force. The last point matters for audits. If a client asks why a benefit was taxed in March, you need to show which threshold applied and when it was last verified.
Dependent children status   The status that moves an employee from the lower to the higher threshold can change during the year. A birth, or a change in who the child is dependent on, alters the situation. Decide in advance how your platform handles this.
The safest design is to treat the status as a dated attribute. Each benefit is evaluated against the threshold valid at the moment it is granted. Where a client wants to apply the status for the whole year, record that as an explicit setting, with the supporting declaration from the employee on file.
Check before you grant   The most useful control sits before payroll, not inside it. When a client or an HR admin proposes a benefit, the platform should return three things at once:
The value of the proposed benefit. The current cumulative total. The headroom left, and whether the new item fits. If the item fits, it proceeds. If it does not, the admin sees the shortfall and can reduce the item, split it, or accept the over-cap outcome knowingly. This turns a payroll surprise into a decision made at the right time.
Over-cap taxation   When the cumulative value passes the threshold, the benefits no longer sit inside the exemption. The over-cap case must be handled as a defined payroll event, not as a manual correction.
Two points to settle with your payroll engine and your tax advisers:
Which part of the value becomes taxable once the cap is passed: only the excess, or the whole amount. Do not infer this from another country’s logic. Confirm it against the primary rule and encode it as a documented decision. Which contributions and withholdings follow. The taxable portion flows into the normal payroll calculation, so the interaction with social contributions must be tested, not assumed. Whatever you decide, the output should be explicit. The payslip line, the employer cost and the net effect for the employee should all be visible and explainable. Employees notice when a benefit they expected to be tax-free reduces their net pay.
Year-end and corrections   Benefits can be reversed, corrected or granted late. Build for that.
Keep the ledger append-only. A correction is a new entry, not an edit. Recalculate the cumulative total from the ledger every time, so the result is reproducible. Re-run the cap check when an earlier item is changed, since it can move later items across the threshold. Run a final reconciliation before the last payroll of the year, and list every employee close to or over the cap. Multi-client and multi-entity setups   Platforms often serve several client entities. Keep the cap check scoped to the employee and the employer relationship that applies. If an employee changes employer during the year, decide how benefits already received elsewhere are declared and counted. This usually relies on a declaration from the employee, so the data flow needs a place to capture it.
Data exchange   Tracking only works if benefit data arrives in a consistent format. A workable exchange carries the employee identifier, the tax year, the benefit type, the taxable value, the grant date, the family status flag and a reference to the source document. In return, the platform sends the cumulative total, the headroom and the over-cap indicator for each item.
With that loop in place, partnership teams can offer fringe benefit administration as a controlled service, not a year-end clean-up.
Partnership teams can request the data-exchange specification.

## Funding Italian payroll in EUR from a non-EUR platform
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/eur-funding-italian-payroll-non-eur-platforms.html
Summary: How non-EUR EOR and payroll platforms can fund Italian payroll in euros: who bears FX risk, where to convert, and what to agree with a local partner.
Italian payroll is paid in euros. Net salaries, social contributions and withholding taxes are all due in euros. If your platform holds client money in another currency, you carry an FX step between the client invoice and the Italian bank account. How you handle that step decides your margin, your cash timing and how often finance asks you questions.
This article covers the practical choices. It does not give rates or fees, because those depend on your banks and your volumes.
Where FX risk actually sits   There are three moments where currency matters.
The client is quoted a price. The payroll is calculated in euros. The funds arrive in the Italian account and are paid out.
Between these moments the exchange rate moves. Someone has to own that movement. If nobody owns it on paper, you will own it by default.
The cleanest rule is simple. The euro payroll amount is fixed when the payroll is approved. Everything after that is a conversion problem, not a payroll problem. Do not let a rate change reopen a payroll that has already been approved.
Three funding models   Pre-fund in euros. You convert ahead of time and hold a euro balance with your partner or in your own euro account. Payroll runs never wait for a transfer. The cost is that you tie up cash and take rate risk on the balance you hold.
Fund per run. You convert and send funds for each payroll after approval. You hold less cash and take less rate risk. The cost is timing. A late transfer becomes a late salary, and a late salary is the one failure your clients and employees will not forgive.
Client funds in euros. You invoice the client in euros, or the client pays into a euro account directly. The FX risk moves to the client. This is the simplest for you. It is also the hardest sell to clients who want one invoice in their home currency.
Most platforms end up with a mix. Large, steady clients get per-run funding. Small or new clients get an invoice in euros, or a deposit held in euros.
Decisions to make before the first payroll   Choose the quote currency and the rate source. If you quote in the client currency, state which rate you use and when it is fixed. Name the source. A vague rule such as the rate on the day causes disputes later.
Set a buffer. Rates move between approval and settlement. A small buffer in your pricing absorbs this. Decide whether it is built into the price or shown as a separate line.
Agree who pays conversion costs. Bank fees and spreads add up. Write down whether they sit in your margin or pass through to the client.
Define the cut-off. Payroll approval, funding and payment each need a clear time limit. Share these with your Italian partner and keep them in the run calendar.
Plan for corrections. Retroactive changes, bonuses and final settlements create extra euro amounts after the main run. Decide how these are funded and at what rate.
Reconciliation is where most pain appears   A euro payroll gives you euro totals. Your ledger may be in another currency. If the two do not tie out, finance spends days hunting small differences.
Keep three figures for every run. The euro amount approved. The amount received in the euro account. The amount in your home currency that you converted. Link them with a single run reference. Do this from the first run, not after the first audit.
Also keep the rate and the date it was applied. You will need both when a client asks why an invoice differs from a quote.
Failure cases to plan for   A transfer that arrives short because of intermediary fees. A transfer that arrives late because of a bank holiday on either side. A rate spike between approval and settlement. A client who disputes the rate after the fact.
For each, decide in advance who covers the gap and how fast. A small standing euro float on the Italian side removes most of the stress. It lets payroll go out on time while you sort out the cause.
What your Italian partner needs from you   Your partner needs a clear funding instruction for each run. That means the euro amount, the funding deadline, the reference and the account details. It also needs to tell you when funds have landed and when salaries have left.
This works best as structured data, not email. A machine-readable payroll summary and a machine-readable funding status let both sides reconcile automatically. They also give your finance team an audit trail without extra work.
A short checklist   Fix the euro amount at payroll approval. Pick a funding model per client type. Name the rate source and the fixing time. Keep a euro float on the Italian side. Tie every run to one reference across all systems. Agree in writing who pays for gaps and fees. Partnership teams can request the data-exchange specification to see how payroll summaries, funding instructions and status updates are structured.

## GDPR and payroll data with Italian ICPs: FAQ on roles, transfers and retention
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/gdpr-payroll-data-italian-icps-faq.html
Summary: Plain answers for EOR and payroll platforms on controller and processor roles, data transfers and retention when working with an Italian in-country partner.
Global EOR and payroll platforms that work with an Italian in-country partner (ICP) share employee data across borders every month. Partnership and operations teams ask the same questions again and again. This FAQ answers them in plain terms.
It is not legal advice. It sets out how the roles usually work, so your teams can ask better questions during due diligence.
Roles   Who is the controller and who is the processor?   It depends on who decides why and how the data is used. Do not assume one answer for the whole relationship.
In many EOR setups, your platform is the employer of record or the contracting party with the client. It decides which data it needs and why. In that case it is a controller for the employee data it collects.
The Italian ICP often runs payroll calculation, filings and social security reporting on your instructions. For that work it usually acts as a processor.
The ICP may also be a controller in its own right. It has its own legal duties in Italy. It must keep certain records and file certain declarations with Italian bodies. For those duties it decides the purpose, because the law does. That makes it a controller for that part.
So the honest answer is often a mix. Write it down per processing activity, not per contract.
Do we need a data processing agreement?   Yes, wherever the ICP acts as a processor. The agreement must set out the subject matter, the type of data, the instructions, confidentiality, security measures, sub-processor rules, assistance with data subject requests, and deletion or return at the end.
Where the ICP is an independent controller for its legal duties, a processor agreement is the wrong tool. Use a clear allocation of responsibilities instead, and say so in the contract.
Are we joint controllers?   Rarely, but it happens. If both sides jointly decide the purposes and means for the same processing, the joint controller rules apply. Then you must agree who handles transparency and data subject requests. Check this when you build shared portals or shared employee records.
Transfers   Does data moving between us and the ICP count as a transfer?   It depends on where each party sits.
If your platform and the ICP are both inside the EU or EEA, the data stays within the area where GDPR applies directly. No special transfer tool is needed for the movement itself.
If your platform is outside the EU, data sent from Italy to you is a restricted transfer. You need a valid transfer basis. That can be an adequacy decision for your country, or standard contractual clauses with a transfer assessment, or another tool the regulation allows.
Data flowing from you to the ICP is also covered by GDPR when the ICP processes it in Italy for Italian employees.
What about your sub-processors?   Map them. Hosting providers, payroll engines, support tools and analytics vendors all count. For each one, record the country where data is stored and the countries from which it can be accessed. Remote access from a third country is a transfer too.
The ICP will ask for this list. Have it ready, and agree how you will notify each other of changes.
Which data is sensitive in payroll?   Payroll files carry more than names and salaries. They can hold health information through sick leave, union membership through deductions, family data through allowances, and tax identifiers. Treat these as high risk. Share the minimum, use encrypted channels, and restrict access by role.
Retention   How long must payroll data be kept?   Italian law sets minimum retention periods for payroll, tax and social security records. These are different from the GDPR principle that data should not be kept longer than needed. The two fit together: keep the data for the legal period, then delete it or anonymise it.
We do not state specific periods here. Ask the ICP to confirm the current periods per record type in writing. Build those into your retention schedule.
Who deletes what when the engagement ends?   Agree this before you start. A workable pattern is:
The ICP returns or deletes data held as a processor, as you instruct. The ICP keeps what Italian law requires it to keep as its own obligation, and says so. Both sides document the deletion and confirm it. What about data subject requests?   An employee may ask either party for access, correction or deletion. Set one intake route and a clear handover. Whoever receives the request forwards it fast. Deletion requests must be weighed against legal retention duties, and the answer to the employee should explain that.
What about breaches?   Agree who notifies whom, and how fast. A processor must tell its controller without undue delay. A controller may have to notify the supervisory authority within the legal time limit. Put contact names and a channel in the contract, and test them.
A short checklist   Map each processing activity and name the role of each party. Sign the right agreement for each role. List sub-processors and data locations. Pick a transfer tool for any flow leaving the EU or EEA. Get retention rules per record type from the ICP. Define return, deletion and request handling. Define breach contacts. Partnership teams that want to see how we structure these points in practice can request the data-exchange specification from ItalyInCountry.

## Gross-to-net in Italy: the calculation order for payroll operators
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/gross-to-net-italy-payroll-operators.html
Summary: A fixed order of steps for Italian gross-to-net: employee pension contribution, taxable base, IRPEF brackets, employment deduction. Built for platform payroll teams.
Most gross-to-net errors in Italy come from order, not from rates. If your platform runs the steps in the wrong sequence, the net pay is wrong even when every rate is correct. This article sets out the sequence and the inputs each step needs. It covers the core employee-side chain only.
The figures below come from secondary sources. Check them against the primary source before you put them into production. Store the source and the check date next to each parameter.
Step one: fix the gross and the period   Start with the gross amount for the pay period. Decide early whether you calculate monthly or annualise. The IRPEF brackets and the employment deduction are defined on an annual basis. A monthly engine has to either annualise the income or prorate the annual parameters. Pick one method and apply it everywhere.
Also record the contract type at this point. Fixed-term contracts change the minimum employment deduction, so the flag must exist before step five.
Step two: employee pension contribution   The employee share of the main pension contribution (IVS) is 9.19% of the contributory base. Calculate it first. Everything after it depends on it.
Other employee-side contributions can apply depending on the contract and sector. They are outside the verified set used here. Add them as separate lines in the same step, each with its own rate, base and source.
Step three: taxable income   Taxable income for IRPEF is gross pay minus the employee contributions from step two. Call this R.
The common mistake is to apply the tax brackets to gross pay. Do not do that. The contribution comes out before the tax base is set.
Step four: gross IRPEF by brackets   Apply the three annual brackets to R, in slices:
Up to 28,000: 23%. From 28,000 to 50,000: 33%. Above 50,000: 43%. The rates apply only to the part of income inside each bracket. Compute each slice, then add them. Do not apply the top rate that fits R to the whole amount.
Step five: employment income deduction   The deduction for employees depends on R. It is a function, so implement it as one. The structure is:
R up to 15,000: a fixed 1,955, with a minimum of 690. For fixed-term contracts the minimum is 1,380. R from 15,000 to 28,000: 1,910 plus 1,190 times (28,000 minus R) divided by 13,000. R from 28,000 to 50,000: 1,910 times (50,000 minus R) divided by 22,000. An extra 65 applies when R is between 25,000 and 35,000. Above 50,000: zero. Two points matter for testing. First, the deduction falls smoothly across the upper bands, so test values just either side of 28,000 and 50,000. Second, the extra 65 is an add-on, not a separate band. It stacks on whatever the formula returns.
The deduction cannot make tax negative. Subtract it from gross IRPEF and floor the result at zero.
Step six: net IRPEF and local surcharges   Net IRPEF is gross IRPEF from step four minus the deduction from step five, floored at zero.
Regional and municipal surcharges come after this. They vary by location and are not part of the verified set here. Model them as a lookup keyed on the employee’s tax residence, with its own source and validity date. Do not hard-code them into the bracket logic.
Step seven: net pay   Net pay is gross pay minus employee contributions minus net IRPEF minus surcharges. Then add or subtract any items that sit outside the chain, such as benefits or reimbursements, each with its own tax treatment.
Keep the intermediate values. Store gross, each contribution, R, gross IRPEF, deduction, net IRPEF and net pay as separate fields. When a payslip is disputed, you can show which step moved.
Implementation notes for platform teams   Keep parameters in data, not in code. Rates, thresholds and formula coefficients should carry a source, a status and a validity date. Test the boundaries. Run cases at each threshold: 15,000, 25,000, 28,000, 35,000 and 50,000. Version the calculation. When a parameter changes, old periods must still reproduce the old result. Reconcile against a trusted reference. Run a sample of payslips through both your engine and a second calculation before go-live. Separate the employee chain from employer cost. The steps above give the net pay. Employer-side contributions are a different calculation with a different base. The order is the part to get right: gross, employee contribution, taxable income, bracketed tax, deduction, surcharges, net. Once the order is fixed, the rest is parameter maintenance.
Partnership teams that want to align their payroll data flow with this sequence can request the data-exchange specification.

## Hidden costs in Italian ICP contracts: fees to watch
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/hidden-costs-italian-icp-contracts.html
Summary: Which one-off and recurring fees tend to hide in Italian in-country partner contracts, and how EOR and payroll platforms can spot them before signing.
Most contracts with an Italian in-country partner (ICP) look simple on the first page. A set-up fee, a monthly fee per employee, done. The surprises sit further down, in schedules, definitions and side letters. This article lists where they usually are.
The goal is not to avoid fees. Partners need to be paid for real work. The goal is to know what you are paying for and to price it correctly in your own customer contracts.
One-off fees to check   Onboarding and set-up. Ask what the fee covers. Some partners include social security registration, the employment contract and the first payroll setup. Others charge each step separately. Get a list of deliverables, not just a price.
Contract drafting and changes. A standard employment contract may be included. A contract that needs a bespoke clause, a different working time model or a sector-specific variation may be billed as legal work. Check who decides what counts as non-standard.
Visa and work permit support. If your clients hire non-EU talent, this is where costs grow. Look for separate fees for the application, for document legalisation, for translations and for appointments. Ask whether a refused or delayed application is billed again.
Relocation services. Housing search, tax code, residence registration and bank access are often sold as packages. Confirm whether they are optional and whether the partner subcontracts them. A subcontracted service often carries an extra handling charge.
Termination. Ending an employment relationship in Italy needs care. Partners may charge a fixed exit fee, an hourly rate for the procedure, or both. Ask what happens when a dismissal is challenged. Legal defence costs and settlement amounts are rarely covered by the base fee.
Offboarding administration. Final payslip, final settlement calculation, notices to the authorities. Some partners fold this into the termination fee. Others bill it on its own.
Recurring fees to check   Monthly per-employee fee. Check the definition of an active employee. Is a person on unpaid leave, long sickness or parental leave still billable? A partner who counts every person on the payroll register will bill more than one who counts only those paid in the month.
Minimum billing. Many contracts set a floor on monthly invoicing, or a minimum number of employees. This hurts platforms with a small and uneven Italian headcount.
Payroll processing extras. Italian payroll has features that foreign teams do not expect. Additional monthly payments, severance provisions and sector agreement rules all affect the calculation. Ask whether off-cycle runs, corrections and retroactive adjustments are included or charged per run.
Benefits administration. Meal vouchers, supplementary pension funds, health funds and company cars each need setup and ongoing handling. Some partners charge a flat fee per benefit, others per employee. Ask for both models in writing.
Reporting and data access. Standard reports may be free. Custom exports, API access and data feeds into your own system are often priced as extras. For a platform, this matters more than almost any other line, because you need clean data every month.
Indexation. Look for a clause that lets the partner raise fees each year. Check whether it ties to a published index or to the partner’s own judgement.
Pass-through costs   The contract should separate the partner’s service fee from costs paid to third parties. Social contributions, insurance premiums, statutory payments and authority fees belong to the second group. Three questions help:
Is each pass-through item listed by name? Do you receive the supporting document? Does the partner add a handling charge on top, and if so, where is it stated? If a clause says “other costs as incurred”, ask for a closed list.
Timing and currency   Payment terms can hide cost too. Early funding requirements tie up your cash. Currency conversion margins add a silent charge when you are invoiced in one currency and the partner pays in euro. Late payment interest and suspension rights deserve a read. A short suspension right can stop payroll, which is not a risk you want to carry.
Exit and transfer   Check what it costs to leave. Some contracts charge for transferring employee records, for a handover period or for early termination of the agreement. If you may later move employees to your own Italian entity or to another partner, the transfer terms matter on day one.
A practical checklist   Request a full fee schedule with every line named. Ask for the definition of billable employee. Separate service fees from pass-through costs. Ask what is included in termination and in visa support. Check indexation, minimums and payment terms. Confirm what data you receive, in which format, and at what price. Read the exit clauses before the commercial ones. A partner who answers these questions clearly is usually a partner who runs clean operations. A partner who avoids them is giving you information too.
Partnership teams can request the data-exchange specification to see how fees, pass-through costs and payroll data are reported line by line.

## How ICP pricing for Italy is built
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/how-icp-pricing-italy-is-built.html
Summary: What sits behind a per-employee partner rate for Italy: pass-through costs, service fees, and the variables that move the total for EOR and payroll platforms.
A per-employee rate looks simple on a price sheet. Behind it sit several separate cost layers. Partnership and operations teams at global EOR and payroll platforms need to see them apart. Otherwise it is hard to compare partners, forecast margin, or explain a quote to a customer.
This article explains how an ICP rate for Italy is built, layer by layer. It does not quote figures. Exact values depend on the contract, the role and the data you send us.
Layer one: employee gross pay   Everything starts with gross pay. In Italy this is rarely a single number. It is set by the applicable national collective agreement (CCNL), which defines minimum pay by job level, additional salary instalments, paid leave, notice periods and allowances.
The CCNL is the main variable in the whole build. Two employees with the same job title can sit under different agreements and cost different amounts. For this reason we price from the agreement and level, not from the title.
Layer two: employer contributions and mandatory charges   On top of gross pay, the employer pays social security contributions, workplace injury insurance and other statutory charges. Rates depend on the sector, the company profile and the contract type.
These are pass-through costs. They are not our margin and they are not negotiable. We show them as a separate line, with the source and the date of the rate used, so your finance team can check them against the regulation.
Layer three: deferred and accrued items   Italian employment carries accruals that are easy to miss in a quick estimate. Severance accrues during employment and is paid at exit. Unused leave and extra salary instalments also build up over time.
A good rate states how these are treated. They can be invoiced as they accrue, or reserved and settled at the end. Either way, the cash cost reaches you. The only question is when. We agree this with each partner up front, so there is no surprise at termination.
Layer four: the service fee   This is the part we actually charge for. It covers the work of running Italian payroll and employer administration for your customer’s worker:
contract drafting and employment registration monthly payroll processing and payslips filings with social security and tax authorities handling of leave, sickness and changes in the employment relationship support for your team when a case needs an answer The service fee is the only layer where scope changes the price. A partner that wants us to handle all employee queries directly will pay differently from one that keeps first-line support in house.
Layer five: optional services   Some services are not part of the base rate because not every employee needs them. Visa and work permit support for non-EU hires is one. Relocation help is another. Representation before social security bodies in specific cases is a third.
We price these as separate items. Mixing them into the base rate makes every hire look more expensive and hides what the partner is paying for.
What moves the total   When a quote differs from a previous one, the cause is almost always one of these:
a different CCNL or job level a different contract type, such as fixed term or open ended a different company profile for contribution purposes a change in statutory rates between quotes a change in service scope optional services added or removed This is why we ask for structured inputs before we quote. A job title and a salary are not enough. We need the agreement, the level, the contract type and the work location.
Why we separate pass-through from fees   We split every rate into regulated costs and our own fee. There are three reasons.
First, it keeps the comparison honest. You can compare our fee with another partner’s fee, and our pass-through lines with the regulation.
Second, it protects your margin model. If statutory rates change, only the pass-through layer moves. Your service fee stays stable.
Third, it shortens customer conversations. When your sales team can show a clean breakdown, the customer sees where each part comes from.
What we need from you   To build a rate for your platform, we work from a small set of data points per role: the agreement, the level, the contract type, the location, and any services beyond standard payroll. For volume, we also need to know how you want accruals handled and how you want invoices structured.
For each regulated value, we document the source and the date it was checked. If a rate changes, you see it in the next statement, with the reason.
A per-employee rate is only useful if you can explain every part of it. That is the standard we build to.
Partnership teams can request the data-exchange specification to see exactly which fields we need and return.

## How TFR accrual works and how to report it to partners
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/tfr-accrual-reporting-partners.html
Summary: How monthly TFR accrual, annual revaluation and fund choices work in Italy, and how to structure the data you send to your EOR partner.
TFR is the Italian end-of-service allowance. It is not a bonus and it is not a severance payment triggered by dismissal. Every employee builds it up during employment, and it is paid when the employment ends, whatever the reason. For a global payroll platform, it is a liability that grows on every payslip and has to be visible in your reports.
This article explains how the accrual works, how it is revalued, where it can sit, and what your Italian partner should send you each month.
Monthly accrual   TFR accrues from pay. Each year, a share of the employee’s eligible annual remuneration is set aside. The payroll calculates this share month by month, so the amount appears in every pay cycle even though nobody is paid anything at that moment.
Three points matter for reporting.
The base is not the same as gross pay. Collective agreements and the law decide which pay elements count. Some items are excluded. Others are included even when they are paid irregularly. Unpaid absences can change the accrual. Some absences reduce it. Others, such as statutory leave, keep it running. Your partner should flag these months. Accrual is a cost for the employer in the month it arises, even if the cash stays in the company or goes to a fund. If your platform shows total employment cost, TFR must be in it. A common error is to treat TFR as a leaving cost and book it only at termination. That understates cost during the whole employment and creates a large surprise at the end.
Revaluation   The balance already accrued is revalued every year. The revaluation has a fixed part and a variable part linked to the national consumer price index. The result is added to the balance. A substitute tax applies to the revaluation, and it reduces the net amount added.
For reporting, keep these items apart:
opening balance for the period new accrual from payroll revaluation gross substitute tax on the revaluation closing balance Partners often send a single closing balance. That is not enough for audit. You cannot reconcile a balance you cannot rebuild. Ask for the movements, not only the total.
Revaluation is calculated on a year basis, so a mid-year exit gets a pro-rata treatment. Your partner should state the method in the exit report.
Where the TFR sits: fund options   The employee decides where future accrual goes. There are two main routes.
Stay with the employer. The amount accrues on the company books. Depending on the size of the employer, it either stays in the company or is transferred monthly to a public treasury fund managed by the social security institute. In both cases the employee keeps the right to the amount. Only the place where the liability sits changes.
Move to a pension fund. The employee can direct the accrual to a supplementary pension scheme. This can be a negotiated fund linked to the collective agreement, an open fund, or an individual pension plan. The employer then pays the accrual to the fund on a regular schedule, and the balance is no longer a company liability.
If the employee makes no choice within the legal window after hire, the law treats this as a tacit choice. The accrual then goes to the pension fund set by the applicable agreement or, failing that, to a default option. This is the point where onboarding errors happen. A missed election form can send contributions to the wrong place for months.
For your platform this means each employee record needs a TFR destination field with a valid status, a start date for the election, and the name of the fund where relevant. When the destination changes, the history must remain readable.
What to ask your partner to report   A workable monthly data set is short. For each employee and each pay period:
TFR base for the month accrual amount destination: company, treasury fund, or named pension fund amount paid to the fund in the period, if any advances paid to the employee against the balance Once a year, add the revaluation and tax breakdown listed above, plus the closing balance reconciled to the ledger.
At exit, ask for a final statement. It should show the full balance, any advances already paid, the tax treatment applied, and the amount paid out. Termination payments are the moment when gaps in earlier reporting show up, so this statement is where your finance team will test the whole chain.
Advances   Employees can ask for an advance on their TFR in defined cases, such as buying a first home or covering medical costs. An advance reduces the balance. If your partner does not report advances, your balance will drift from theirs. Treat advances as their own movement type, with a date and a reason code.
Practical checks   A few controls prevent most disputes.
Reconcile the closing balance to opening balance plus movements every year. Compare accrual to the base each month. A sudden drop usually means an absence code or a contract change. Check that every employee has a recorded destination before the first payroll. Keep the applicable collective agreement on each record, since it affects both the base and the default fund. TFR is predictable once the data is structured. The problems come from totals without movements and from missing election records.
Partnership teams that want a field-level layout for these reports can request the data-exchange specification.
