## Meal vouchers in Italian payroll: electronic vs paper daily limits
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/meal-vouchers-italy-payroll-electronic-vs-paper-limits.html
Summary: How Italian meal voucher daily exemption limits differ for electronic and paper vouchers, and how payroll teams should model them in a platform.
Meal vouchers look simple. An employee gets a benefit, and payroll treats part of it as exempt. In Italy the detail sits in the daily limit, and that limit depends on the format of the voucher.
This article is for partnership, operations and payroll managers at global EOR and payroll platforms. It covers how the daily exemption works, where the two formats differ, and what your payroll logic needs to hold.
Two formats, two daily limits   Italian meal vouchers come in two forms: electronic and paper. Each has its own daily exemption threshold.
Electronic meal vouchers: EUR 10 per day. Paper meal vouchers: EUR 4 per day. The gap is large. An electronic voucher can carry more than twice the exempt value of a paper one for the same working day. That is a policy choice, and it pushes employers toward electronic formats.
Both figures come from a secondary source, a specialist tax publication that summarises the recent budget law changes. Treat them as working values. Confirm them against the primary legal text before you hard-code them into production rules.
What “daily exemption” means in payroll   The threshold is a daily amount. It is not a monthly pot that the employee can spend freely. Payroll has to compare the face value of the voucher for each day with the threshold for that format.
There are two outcomes for each voucher day.
The face value is at or below the threshold. The benefit stays within the exemption. The face value is above the threshold. The excess does not benefit from the exemption and must be treated as ordinary taxable remuneration. The excess is the part that creates errors. A platform that stores only a monthly voucher total cannot see it. It needs the daily face value and the number of days the voucher applies to.
Why the format changes the calculation   The same face value can give different payroll results depending on the format.
Take a voucher worth EUR 7 per day. As an electronic voucher, it sits under the EUR 10 limit and is fully within the exemption. As a paper voucher, it is above the EUR 4 limit. The part over the limit is not exempt.
So the format is not a cosmetic field. It is an input to the tax and contribution treatment. If your data model drops it, you cannot compute the result correctly.
What your payroll data model needs   For each employee and each pay period, a platform should hold at least the following.
The voucher format: electronic or paper. The daily face value. The number of days for which vouchers were granted. The applicable daily threshold for that format. The source and the verification status of that threshold. The last point matters. When a limit changes, you want to know which pay periods used the old value and which used the new one. Store the threshold with its source, not as a constant buried in code.
Common operational mistakes   Applying one limit to both formats. A single flat threshold is the most common shortcut. It will be wrong for one of the two formats.
Mixing formats inside a company. Some employers move to electronic vouchers gradually. Employees on the same payroll can hold different formats. Your logic must work per employee, not per client.
Ignoring the excess. If the face value is above the threshold, the excess must flow into taxable pay. A silent cap that drops the excess understates remuneration.
Treating a secondary source as final. The figures here come from a secondary source. Build a review step so that a payroll specialist confirms the limit against the primary text before it goes live.
What this means for EOR platforms   An EOR platform that hires in Italy carries the payroll risk for its clients. A wrong voucher treatment is not a client problem alone. It becomes a compliance problem for the platform.
The practical steps are short.
Add the voucher format as a required field in the benefits record. Keep the daily thresholds in a versioned reference table with source and date of verification. Calculate the excess per day, then aggregate for the period. Show the exempt and taxable parts separately on the payslip preview, so clients and employees can see the split. Flag any benefit configuration where the face value exceeds the threshold, before payroll closes. Keeping the rules current   Daily thresholds are the kind of value that changes with budget laws. A platform that relies on manual updates will fall behind. A reference table with a clear source, a verification status and a change history lets your team update one record instead of hunting through code.
The current figures are EUR 10 per day for electronic vouchers and EUR 4 per day for paper vouchers. Both are marked as secondary until checked against the primary text.
Summary   The voucher format decides the daily exemption. Electronic vouchers are exempt up to EUR 10 per day. Paper vouchers are exempt up to EUR 4 per day. Payroll must compare the daily face value to the right threshold and treat any excess as taxable. Store the format, the daily value, the days granted and the source of the threshold.
Partnership teams that want to exchange this data with us in a structured way can request the data-exchange specification.

## Mid-month changes in Italian payroll: what an in-country partner can and cannot absorb
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/mid-month-changes-italian-payroll-icp.html
Summary: Which changes arriving after cut-off can still land in the current Italian payroll month, and which must move to the next cycle. A guide for EOR ops teams.
Every payroll team knows the moment. The cut-off has passed. The run is being prepared. Then a change arrives from the client: a raise, a new hire, a resignation, an allowance, a correction.
For a global EOR or payroll platform, the question is simple. Can the in-country partner (ICP) in Italy still put this in the current month, or does it wait?
This article gives a practical way to sort those changes. It does not replace the rules agreed in your contract with the ICP. It helps you ask the right questions before you promise anything to your own client.
Why the answer is rarely a plain yes or no   Italian payroll is not a single calculation. A change after cut-off touches several things at once:
the gross-to-net calculation for the employee the payslip that must be issued the contribution and tax figures reported to the authorities the payment file that goes to the bank A change can be easy for the calculation and still be blocked by one of the later steps. A change can also be hard to calculate and still fit, because the data was already complete. So the useful test is not “how big is the change”. The useful test is “how many downstream steps does it disturb”.
Changes an ICP can usually absorb   These are changes that alter inputs but not the structure of the run.
Variable pay amounts. A bonus, an overtime figure or an expense reimbursement that is already approved. The employee exists in the run. The pay element exists in the setup. Only the amount changes.
Corrections to attendance data. Absence or leave entries that were wrong or missing, where the employee is already in the run and the payroll codes already exist.
Bank detail updates, if flagged early enough. The risk here is not the calculation. It is the payment file. If the file has not been released, the change is often possible. If it has, it is not.
Data fixes that do not affect pay. Address, contact and similar fields can usually be updated at any time.
For all of these, the condition is the same. The ICP must still have time to recalculate, review and approve before the run is closed.
Changes an ICP can absorb only with conditions   These need a conversation, not an assumption.
Terminations. The calculation of final pay is more complex than a normal month. Whether it fits depends on how complete the data is: the end date, the reason, the leave balance and any notice position. If any of these is open, expect the final settlement to move.
Changes to salary or contract terms. A raise is easy to calculate. But if the contract amendment is not signed or the effective date is unclear, the ICP should not process it. Payroll follows the signed document, not the email.
Retroactive changes. A change that reaches back into earlier months creates adjustments across several periods. Some ICPs can do it in the current run. Many prefer to do it in the next cycle with a clear reconciliation.
Changes that should move to the next cycle   New hires with incomplete onboarding. An employee cannot be paid correctly without the required registration and personal data. If these are missing at cut-off, the first payment is at risk, whatever the start date says.
Anything that needs a new payroll element or a new tax or social security treatment. If the setup does not exist, someone has to build it and check it. That is not a late change. It is a new configuration.
Changes that arrive after the payment file is released. At that point the right answer is usually an off-cycle payment or a correction next month. Do not ask the ICP to reopen a closed run unless both sides have agreed it as an exception.
A simple triage you can apply   When a late change arrives, ask four questions in this order:
Is the employee already in the current run? Does the pay element already exist in the setup? Is the supporting document signed and complete? Has the payment file been released? If the answers are yes, yes, yes, no, the change is likely to fit. If any answer differs, tell your client early that it will probably move.
Set the expectation before the problem   Most late-change disputes come from unclear promises, not from the rules themselves. Three habits help.
Publish a clear cut-off to your own clients and state which change types are exceptions. Agree with the ICP a short list of changes they will always try to absorb, and a short list they will not. Log every late change with a timestamp, so that both sides can see where a delay started.
A platform that explains the limits in advance loses fewer clients than one that promises everything and then misses.
What to ask your ICP   Which change types do they treat as standard late changes? What is the last point at which a run can be reopened? How do they handle corrections: in the current run, off-cycle, or the next month? What data must be complete for a termination or a new hire to be processed? Written answers to these questions turn most late-change arguments into a routine decision.

## Modello 770: what it is and why partners should care
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/modello-770-partner-view.html
Summary: The Modello 770 is Italy's annual withholding return. See what it means for EOR and payroll platforms, and which data a partner must supply to file it on time.
The Modello 770 is the annual withholding tax return filed in Italy by the party that withholds tax on payments. In Italian this party is the sostituto d’imposta. For an employee on Italian payroll, that is the employer.
If your platform places people in Italy through an Employer of Record (EOR), the 770 is part of your supply chain. You will not file it. But the quality of what you send decides whether it is filed correctly.
What the 770 does   During the year, the employer withholds income tax from salary and pays it over to the tax authority. It also issues each worker a yearly certificate of income and withholdings, the Certificazione Unica.
The 770 is the summary at the other end. It reports, for the whole year, the withholdings the employer made and the amounts it paid over. The tax authority can then compare what was withheld, what was certified to workers and what was actually paid.
It is a reconciliation document. It does not calculate anything new. It confirms that the year’s payroll, the certificates and the payments tell the same story.
The date to know   For 2026, the deadline for the Modello 770 is 31 October 2026. That day falls on a Saturday, so it moves to 2 November 2026. This date comes from a secondary source, a press summary of the 2026 tax calendar. Your Italian payroll provider should confirm it before you plan around it.
The point for partners is simple. The filing happens after the payroll year closes. Problems found at this stage are problems from months earlier.
Why a platform should care   Most platforms look at Italy through the monthly payslip. The 770 shows the year as the tax authority sees it. That view differs from yours in a few ways.
Your records and the filing must match. If your system shows a payment that the payroll record does not, someone has to explain it. The 770 is where such gaps become visible.
Corrections are slow. A wrong figure found in the return is hard to fix quietly. It often means changes to certificates already given to workers.
Workers notice. The certificate feeds the worker’s own personal tax return. An error there reaches your customer’s employee, and then your customer, and then you.
Customers ask. Finance teams at your clients want to know their Italian tax position is closed for the year. A clean filing is the evidence.
Where platforms cause problems   The EOR files. The platform supplies inputs. Most filing errors trace back to inputs that arrived late, in the wrong shape or with no explanation.
Common causes:
Bonuses or equity-linked payments decided on the platform side and reported to the EOR after the payroll run. Changes of start or end date that are not passed on in time. Benefits paid outside payroll that still count as taxable income. Different worker identifiers in the platform and in payroll, which makes matching slow. Corrections to earlier months sent as free text, not as structured data. None of these is exotic. Each one is easy to prevent when the data flows in a fixed format on a fixed schedule.
What good looks like   A platform that handles the 770 well tends to do the same few things.
It sends variable pay data before each payroll cut-off, not after. It uses one worker identifier on both sides. It treats corrections as new records with a reason, not as edits. It keeps a year-end checklist with its EOR, started well before the filing date. It asks for a reconciliation view from the EOR before the return is submitted. This is an operations habit, not a legal project. It costs little and removes most of the year-end surprises.
Questions to ask your Italian partner   Who files the 770 for your workers, and who signs it? When do you receive the year-end reconciliation, and in what format? How are late changes handled after certificates are issued? Which of our data fields feed the filing directly? What happens if the filing date moves? If the answers are vague, treat that as a risk to your service, not a detail for the back office.
The practical takeaway   The 770 is not a product feature and your customers will never ask for it by name. But it is the moment when the Italian year is checked end to end. Platforms that send clean, timely data get a quiet filing. Platforms that do not get questions in the autumn about events from the spring.
Treat it as a data-quality test that runs once a year. The cheapest time to pass it is during the months before it.
Partnership teams: request the data-exchange specification to see which fields and timings support a clean 770.

## Monthly F24 payment checklist for payroll in Italy
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/monthly-f24-payment-checklist.html
Summary: What a monthly F24 run covers, who confirms the amounts, and which evidence to keep, written for EOR and payroll platform operations teams.
The F24 is the form Italian employers use to pay payroll taxes and social contributions in a single transfer. For a global EOR or payroll platform, it is the step where a correct payslip becomes a compliant payment. If it is late or wrong, the employer faces penalties and the employee’s record is affected.
This checklist sets out what gets paid, by when, and with what evidence. Use it as a control sheet for each payroll cycle.
What gets paid   The F24 normally groups several lines. Confirm each one against the closed payroll.
Withholding tax on employee income, taken from the gross pay. Regional and municipal surcharges on income tax, where they apply to the employee. Social security contributions owed to the national institute, split between the employer share and the employee share. Other contributions that depend on the contract and the collective agreement applied. Each line carries a tax code and a reference period. The code tells the authority what the money is for. The period tells it which month the money covers. A correct amount with the wrong code or period is a common cause of misallocated payments.
By when   The due date is set by law for each type of payment. Do not hard-code a date from memory. Take it from a verified source and store it with the date you checked it. Calendars shift when a due date falls on a weekend or holiday, so build the date from a rule, not from last year’s spreadsheet.
Work backwards from the due date. Payroll must be closed early enough to leave time for review, funding and submission. Your internal cut-off should sit well before the legal deadline, so that one late input does not push the payment past it.
Pre-payment checklist   Run these checks before any money moves.
Payroll is closed and no further changes are open for the period. Totals on the F24 match the payroll register line by line. Tax codes and reference periods are correct for every line. Employer and employee contribution shares reconcile to the gross pay. Any credits or offsets are documented and approved before they are applied. The paying entity and its tax identifier are correct. Funds are available in the paying account. A second person has reviewed the form. The second review matters. The person who prepared the form tends to see what they expect to see.
Payment and submission   F24 forms are submitted through channels the authority accepts, usually online banking or the tax authority’s own services. Submission is not the same as settlement. Check that the payment was accepted and that the debit actually cleared.
If you pay on behalf of a client entity, make sure the entity’s own identifiers are on the form. Paying under the wrong identifier creates a reconciliation problem that can take weeks to untangle.
Evidence to keep   An auditor, a client or the authority may ask you to prove the payment. Keep these items together for each period.
The final F24 as submitted. The receipt issued by the bank or the authority’s service. The bank statement line showing the debit. The payroll register the amounts were drawn from. A reconciliation note linking the register totals to the form totals. The name of the preparer and the reviewer, with the time of each sign-off. The source and check date for the due date rule you applied. Store the evidence under the employer, the period and the payment type. A folder per month with clear names is enough. The test is simple: could someone who was not involved find the proof in a few minutes?
After payment   Close the loop. Compare the amount paid with the amount due. Record any difference and its cause. If a correction is needed, file it through the proper procedure and keep the new receipt next to the original.
Also feed the result back into payroll. Employee records should show that contributions for the period were paid. A gap between payroll status and payment status is an early sign of a process fault.
Common failure points   Wrong tax code or reference period on an otherwise correct amount. Payroll changed after the form was prepared. Due date taken from an outdated calendar. Credits applied without documentation. Receipt saved in a personal inbox instead of the shared record. Payment made under the wrong entity. Most of these are process faults, not knowledge faults. They are fixed by a fixed sequence, a second reviewer and a shared evidence folder.
For platform operations teams   If your platform runs payroll across countries, treat the F24 as a defined event with inputs, an owner, a due date and an evidence pack. Expose its status to your own customers. They want to know that the payment was made, not only that the payslip was issued.
Partnership teams that want to connect payment status and evidence to their own systems can request the data-exchange specification.

## Monthly ICP Performance Scorecard for Italy: A KPI Set for Vendor Reviews
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/monthly-icp-performance-scorecard-italy.html
Summary: A ready-to-use monthly scorecard for reviewing your in-country partner in Italy: payroll, onboarding, compliance, support and data quality KPIs.
A vendor review is only as good as the data behind it. Many global EOR and payroll platforms review their Italian in-country partner (ICP) with anecdotes. A support escalation here, a late payslip there. That does not scale, and it does not give you leverage in a commercial conversation.
This article gives you a scorecard you can use as it is. It covers the areas that matter in Italy: payroll accuracy, onboarding, compliance, support and data quality. Each KPI has a definition, a source and a reason to track it. Set your own targets with your partner. We deliberately do not publish thresholds here, because they depend on your contract, your volume and your client mix.
How to use the scorecard   Run it every month. Use the same definitions each time. Ask the ICP to send the raw data, not a summary. Keep one owner on your side, usually the partnership or operations manager, and review trends rather than single months.
Three rules keep it honest:
Every KPI has a written definition that both sides have signed off. Every KPI has a named data source, such as the payroll system, the ticketing tool or the filing log. Every miss gets a root cause and an owner, not just a red cell. 1. Payroll quality   Payroll is the part your clients feel first. Italian payroll has many moving parts: collective agreement rules, contribution calculations, allowances and year-end items. Errors are visible and costly.
Payroll accuracy rate. Share of employee payslips issued with no correction needed after release. Source: payroll system and correction log. On-time payroll delivery. Share of payroll runs delivered to you by the agreed cut-off. Source: delivery timestamps. Correction cycle time. Time from a reported error to a corrected payslip. Source: ticketing tool. Input rejection rate. Share of your payroll inputs sent back by the ICP as incomplete or unclear. This one points at your own process as much as theirs. 2. Onboarding and offboarding   Slow onboarding costs you deals. Slow offboarding creates risk.
Time to contract-ready. Time from a complete hire request to a contract ready for signature. Time to first payroll-ready. Time from signed contract to a complete employee record in payroll. Right-first-time rate. Share of onboardings completed without a request for missing documents after the ICP has accepted the file. Offboarding completeness. Share of terminations closed with final pay, filings and records completed as agreed. Track the median and the slowest cases. The median shows normal performance. The slow tail shows where clients complain.
3. Compliance and filings   This is where the ICP carries the local obligations on your behalf. You need proof, not assurance.
Filing timeliness. Share of statutory filings and payments submitted by their deadline. Source: filing log with submission evidence. Filing evidence completeness. Share of filings for which a receipt or confirmation is stored and available to you on request. Notices from authorities. Count of notices or queries received from authorities, with status and time to resolve. Rule update response. Time from a change in collective agreement terms or contribution rules to the change being applied in payroll. Ask the ICP to name the source for each change. For any rule-based KPI, insist on a stated source and an effective date. If the ICP cannot say where a rate or a rule comes from, treat that as a finding.
4. Support and responsiveness   Support data tells you how the ICP behaves when something goes wrong.
First response time. Time from ticket creation to a substantive reply, not an automatic acknowledgement. Resolution time. Time from ticket creation to confirmed closure. Reopen rate. Share of tickets reopened after closure. A high rate means fixes are cosmetic. Escalation count. Number of tickets that needed escalation, grouped by cause. Language coverage. Whether replies reach your team in the agreed language without delay. 5. Data quality and exchange   Most scorecard disputes come from data, not from service. Fix this layer and the rest becomes easier.
Data completeness. Share of required fields populated in the monthly data file. Delivery timeliness. Whether the file arrives on the agreed day. Reconciliation variance. Difference between the ICP’s reported totals and your own ledger, with explained items listed. Format stability. Number of unannounced changes to the file structure. 6. Commercial and relationship health   Keep a short section for the points that never fit in a dashboard.
Open improvement actions and their owners. Clients that raised a complaint naming the ICP. Capacity: can the ICP absorb your forecast volume next quarter? Open commercial questions, such as pricing for new services. Running the monthly review   Send the data request early in the month. Hold a short review call with the same attendees each time. Walk through exceptions only. Agree actions, owners and dates in writing. Revisit open actions at the next review before looking at new data.
After a few cycles you will see patterns. Some KPIs will be stable and can move to a quarterly check. Others will keep moving and deserve a closer look. Use the history in contract renewals and in any discussion about service credits or volume allocation.
What good looks like   A good ICP does not fear the scorecard. It sends the data on time, explains misses and proposes fixes. A weak ICP argues about definitions, delays files or offers summaries instead of records. Both outcomes tell you something useful.
Partnership teams that want to make this operational should agree the data fields up front, so the scorecard fills itself from a structured monthly file instead of manual chasing.
Partnership teams: request the data-exchange specification to run this scorecard with your Italian partner.

## Moving an employee from a client entity to your EOR in Italy: handing over balances and history
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/transfer-employee-client-entity-to-eor-italy-balances-history.html
Summary: How partnership and payroll teams hand over leave, severance accruals, tax and contribution history when an Italian employee moves to an EOR.
A client already employs someone in Italy through its own entity. Now it wants that person on your EOR platform. The contract is easy to draft. The hard part is the history that travels with the employee.
This article covers what must be handed over, who owns each item, and where transfers usually go wrong.
Why the handover matters   In Italy, an employee’s rights build up over time. Severance accrual, paid leave, seniority and contribution records all belong to the person, not to the employer. If the new employer starts from zero, the employee loses something real. Payroll then has to fix it later, and the fix is rarely clean.
So the transfer is not a new hire with a copy of the old contract. It is a continuation of a record. Your platform needs that record in a form it can load without retyping.
What to collect from the client entity   Ask for these items before the transfer is agreed, not after.
Severance accrual (TFR). The balance to date, the revaluation applied, and whether the employee chose a pension fund or left it with the employer. This item carries real money and needs a clear owner. Leave balances. Paid leave accrued and not taken, plus the separate hour-based permits that many national contracts grant. Ask for both, in hours and in days. Extra monthly payments. Where the national contract provides year-end or summer payments, the accrued portion that is not yet paid. Seniority. The original start date and any earlier service the employer recognised. This drives notice periods and some contract rights. Contract data. National contract applied, job level, working hours, and any individual agreements on top of it. Tax and contribution data. Year-to-date earnings, withholdings, contributions paid, and any adjustments pending at year end. Absence history. Sickness, maternity or parental leave, and any ongoing case with the social security institute. Benefits and deductions. Company car, meal vouchers, loans, salary garnishments, supplementary health cover. Who is responsible for what   Decide this in writing. We see the same gaps again and again.
The client entity is responsible for the accuracy of what it supplies up to the transfer date. It also settles anything it chooses to pay out at exit, such as untaken leave, if that is the agreed route.
The EOR is responsible for loading the data correctly, running payroll from the transfer date, and keeping the record continuous afterwards.
The employee should receive a statement of the balances carried over. Silence here is how disputes start months later.
Two routes, different data needs   There are broadly two ways to move the person. Which one applies is a legal decision for the client and its advisers, and your platform should support both.
In the first route, the employment continues and the balances move with the contract. The EOR needs the full list above, because it inherits everything.
In the second route, the old employment ends and a new one begins, with the old balances settled at exit. The EOR needs less historic data, but it still needs seniority and year-to-date tax figures, and it must check that the settlement matches the carried-over statement.
In both cases the cut-off date must be exact. A payroll cycle that straddles the transfer is where double payments and missing payments appear.
Where transfers break   Balances in the wrong unit. Leave in days from one system and hours from another gives a silent error. Severance accrual without its history. A single figure with no revaluation trail cannot be audited. Year-to-date tax split badly. If the two employers report different parts of the year, the employee’s annual statement must still add up. Seniority reset by default. Many payroll tools set it to the system start date. Override it at load. No sign-off. Nobody confirms the opening balances, so the first payslip becomes the first review. A practical sequence   First, agree the route and the cut-off date. Second, request the data set in a fixed structure, with units stated. Third, load it into a staging record and compare it to the client’s last payslip. Fourth, send the opening-balance statement to the client and the employee for confirmation. Fifth, run the first payroll from the confirmed figures only.
Keep the source documents with the record. When a question comes up a year later, you can answer from the file instead of asking the client to search for it.
What this means for platform teams   If you resell or white-label EOR coverage in Italy, the handover is part of your product, not a one-off task. Partners who define the data structure up front onboard transferring employees faster and with fewer corrections. The structure is the same each time, which means it can be automated.
Partnership teams: request the data-exchange specification.

## Notice periods under Italian CCNLs: how notice is set and paid in lieu
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/notice-periods-italian-ccnl-pay-in-lieu.html
Summary: How Italian CCNLs set notice periods, who must give notice, and how pay in lieu works. A guide for EOR and payroll platform partnership and operations teams.
Notice is one of the first questions a global payroll platform asks when it works with Italy. The answer is not in one statute with a single table. It sits mostly in the national collective agreement, the CCNL, that applies to the employee. This article explains how notice is set and how pay in lieu works, so your teams know what data they need before they quote or process a termination.
Where the rule comes from   Italian law sets the principle. A party who ends an open-ended contract must give notice. The length of that notice is left largely to collective agreements, custom and, where they exist, individual terms that are not worse for the employee.
In practice, the CCNL is the working source. It states the notice period and how it is calculated. You cannot read the notice period from the country alone. You need the agreement.
Which CCNL applies   The sector and the employer’s activity usually decide which CCNL applies. The contract of employment normally names it. Payslips and the employer’s registrations also point to it.
Two employees in the same city can have different notice rules because they sit under different agreements. For a platform with many clients, this means notice cannot be a country-level default. It has to be a field linked to the agreement and the employee’s classification.
What drives the length of notice   Most CCNLs build notice from the same few inputs:
The employee’s classification level (inquadramento). Higher levels usually carry longer notice. Length of service with the employer. Notice usually grows as seniority grows. Agreements often use bands of service. Who ends the contract. Many agreements set a different period for resignation than for dismissal by the employer. The employee’s period is often shorter. The type of role. Managers (dirigenti) follow their own agreements, with their own rules and often their own protections. The agreement states these in tables or articles. Your system should store the table, not a summary. Summaries lose the bands and the exceptions.
How notice is counted   The CCNL also says when notice starts and how the period is measured. Some agreements count in calendar units and start the period from a fixed point, such as the start of the next month or the next half-month. Others count from the day after the written notice is received. The difference changes the last working day.
Notice must be in writing. For resignation, Italy also has a digital procedure for validating the employee’s resignation. Operations teams should treat the date of valid communication as the key date and record it with evidence.
Working the notice period   By default, the employee keeps working during notice. The employment relationship continues in full. Salary, contributions and accrual of leave and other rights go on as normal. Holiday cannot be freely used by the employer to shorten notice unless the parties agree.
Pay in lieu of notice   If the party ending the contract does not want the notice to be worked, or cannot give it, the law and the CCNL provide for an indemnity in place of notice (indennità sostitutiva del preavviso).
Points that matter for payroll:
The indemnity is owed by the party who fails to give or work the notice. An employer who ends the contract with immediate effect owes it to the employee. An employee who leaves without working notice can owe it to the employer, and the employer can deduct it where the rules allow. The amount is based on the pay the employee would have received during the missing notice. The CCNL defines which pay elements count. This often includes more than base salary, such as regular additional pay items. Check the agreement for the exact list. The period used is the notice period the agreement would have required. That is why the length rules above must be correct first. The indemnity is generally treated as remuneration for contribution and tax purposes. It also affects the calculation of the end-of-service payment (TFR) and related items in the way the rules and the CCNL provide. Do not assume it is a flat, untaxed sum. A dismissal for just cause is a separate case. Where the cause is so serious that the relationship cannot continue, notice is not due. The label used in the termination letter and the facts behind it matter, and an error can turn into a dispute.
Final settlement items   On exit, the final payslip normally brings together several items: pay up to the last day, unused leave, accrued additional monthly pay, TFR and any indemnity in lieu. Notice is only one line, but it often sets the last day that all other lines depend on. A wrong notice date moves everything.
What platforms should collect   To calculate notice and pay in lieu without manual research, a platform needs structured data per employee:
The applicable CCNL and its version Classification level Start date and service history, including any recognised prior service Who ends the contract and the reason Date of valid written communication The pay elements the CCNL includes in the indemnity base Any individual terms more favourable than the CCNL With these fields, notice becomes a lookup and a calculation. Without them, it becomes a case-by-case legal question each time.
Practical advice   Keep the CCNL tables as versioned data with the source and the date checked. Agreements are renewed, and notice terms can change at renewal. Show the user which version produced a figure.
Flag edge cases for review rather than guessing. These include managers, mixed pay structures, long service and disputes over cause.
Partnership teams that want to exchange this data with us in a structured way can request the data-exchange specification.

## Offboarding Italian Employees: Final Pay, TFR, Documents and System Closure
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/offboarding-checklist-italian-employees.html
Summary: A practical offboarding checklist for Italian employees: final pay, TFR, documents and system closure, for EOR and payroll platform operations teams.
Offboarding in Italy is not a single event. It is a chain of payroll, social security and document steps. If one link is late or wrong, the former employee notices, and your client notices too.
This checklist is for operations, payroll and partnership managers at global EOR and payroll platforms. It follows the order in which the work usually happens.
Start with the exit facts   Before any calculation, confirm the basics in your system of record.
The reason for the end of employment: resignation, dismissal, mutual agreement, end of a fixed term, or retirement. The last working day and the termination date, if they differ. Whether notice is worked or paid in lieu. The applicable national collective agreement and the employee’s level. The reason for exit drives notice rules, possible indemnities and the tone of every later document. Do not let the calculation start until these facts are agreed in writing.
Final pay   Final pay in Italy is more than the last salary. Build it line by line and keep a worksheet that someone else can audit.
Salary up to the last working day, prorated where needed. Accrued but unused holiday and leave entitlements. Any notice indemnity, if notice is not worked. Prorated additional monthly payments that the collective agreement provides for, often called thirteenth and fourteenth month pay. Variable pay, bonuses and expense reimbursements that are already earned. Deductions: tax, employee social contributions, and any agreed recovery of advances. Check the collective agreement for each item. Rules on accruals and indemnities differ by sector. Do not reuse a worksheet from a different agreement.
TFR   TFR is the end-of-service severance fund that builds up during employment. It is paid when the contract ends, whatever the reason.
For offboarding, three questions matter.
Where has the TFR been held? Some employees chose a pension fund, and in that case the fund holds the accrued amount. Others left it with the employer. Has the employee taken any advance during employment? An advance reduces what is due now. Is the final amount reconciled with the annual revaluation records? Treat TFR as its own calculation, separate from the final payslip, with its own supporting schedule. Taxation of TFR differs from ordinary pay, so show it as a separate line. Employees often ask about it first, so explain the figure in plain terms when you send it.
Documents   Prepare the document pack before the last day, not after it.
Final payslip with a clear breakdown of every component. TFR statement and the calculation behind it. The termination or resignation record, filed correctly. The mandatory notification of the end of employment to the relevant authorities, within the deadline that applies to the case. Year-to-date tax and contribution summary, so the employee can file their own return. A signed settlement document, if the parties agree one. Return of company property, with a signed receipt. Keep the originals in the employee’s file. Send the employee a copy in their language and in Italian. Both versions should carry the same numbers.
Social security and tax closure   After the final payroll run, close the books with the authorities.
Make sure the last contribution reports are filed and paid. Confirm the employee record is closed with the social security institute. Issue the annual tax certificate for the period worked, and plan for the following filing cycle. If the employee had a work permit tied to the employer, record the end of that link and tell the client what follows for the permit. Mistakes here rarely show up at once. They show up months later, as a letter to the former employee or an inspection query to the client.
System closure   Internal systems need a clear order of operations.
Disable access to email, collaboration tools, HR portals and expense tools on the last working day. Keep payroll and document records in line with retention rules. Do not delete them. Remove benefits, such as supplementary health cover or meal vouchers, from the provider’s active list. Stop recurring payments and update any open headcount reports. Close the case in your ticketing system only when every item above is confirmed. On a platform, each of these steps should create a status that partners can read. A closed case with open tasks is the most common source of disputes.
What partners should expect   For a platform that relies on a local provider, the useful question is not whether the provider can pay the final salary. It is whether the provider sends structured data back: the final pay breakdown, the TFR amount, the filing confirmations and the closure status for each system. Without that, your team ends up chasing emails.
Agree the fields, the timing and the owner of each step before the first exit, not during it.
Partnership teams that want to see how this data can flow between systems can request the data-exchange specification.

## Own entity vs ICP for Italy: the operations view for EOR platforms
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/own-entity-vs-icp-italy-operations-view-eor-platforms.html
Summary: Own Italian entity or in-country partner? A comparison of headcount thresholds, staffing and control, seen from the EOR platform's P&L rather than the client's.
Most comparisons of an own entity and an in-country partner (ICP) are written for the client. They ask which route is cheaper for the employer. This article asks a different question. Which route is better for your platform’s P&L, and for the team that has to run Italy every month?
The decision is about your margin, not the client’s   An own entity gives you the full gross margin on every Italian employee. It also gives you the full fixed cost of being present. An ICP turns much of that fixed cost into a variable one. You pay for what you use, and you share the margin.
So the real question is volume. Below some headcount, fixed costs of an entity are not absorbed. Above it, the partner’s share of margin costs you more than a local team would. Where that crossover sits is specific to your platform. We do not give a figure here, because it depends on your pricing, your mix of roles and your cost of local staff.
What you can do is model it. Take your expected Italian headcount over the coming planning period. Add the fixed costs of the entity: registrations, local accounting, legal cover, insurance, a responsible person, audit and filing. Compare that with the partner’s fee and revenue share at the same headcount. The line where the two cross is your threshold.
Headcount thresholds in practice   There are usually three zones.
Low volume. Few employees, uncertain pipeline. An ICP is almost always the better choice. You avoid fixed cost and you can stop without winding anything down. Your risk is concentration in the partner, not in the entity.
Middle volume. This is where most platforms get stuck. The entity looks attractive on paper, but the team you need to run it is under-used. Payroll runs, authority correspondence, onboarding and terminations each need a trained person. If volume is uneven, those people sit idle in some months and overloaded in others.
High volume. The partner’s margin share becomes visible in your reporting. At this point an own entity, or a hybrid, often wins on cost. It also gives you the control that large accounts ask for in their procurement questionnaires.
Do not set the threshold only on current headcount. Use committed pipeline, and apply a realistic conversion rate to it. Platforms often build an entity for a pipeline that never fully closes.
Staffing: who actually does the work   An own entity means you hire for Italy. You need people who know Italian payroll, collective agreements, social security filings and the habits of local authorities. They need to work in Italian with advisers, unions and employees. Few platforms can cover that from an existing team abroad.
With an ICP, the partner carries that staffing. Your own team shrinks to a governance role. It checks outputs, manages escalations and owns the client relationship. That is a smaller team, and a cheaper one, but it needs different skills. Vendor management and data quality matter more than payroll depth.
There is also a continuity point. Italian expertise is not easy to replace at short notice. If one person holds the knowledge of your Italian setup, you carry a key-person risk. A partner with a bench reduces that risk. An own entity with a thin team increases it.
Control: where each model gives and takes   Own entity:
You set the service levels and the payroll calendar. You hold the data and the bank flows. You decide how to handle exceptions and corrections. You also own every error, every late filing and every dispute. ICP:
You depend on the partner’s calendar, cut-off times and tooling. Your visibility depends on the data you receive and how fast. Liability allocation sits in the contract, so the contract needs care. You can change partner, but migration of live employees is real work. Control is not only a risk topic. It affects your product. If you want a single employee experience across countries, you need structured data from Italy in a format your system can read. Under an ICP this is a contract and integration question. Under an own entity it is an internal build.
What to check in the ICP model   If you lean toward a partner, test these points before you sign.
How does the partner exchange data with your platform? Files, API, or email? How are payroll inputs cut off, and what happens to late changes? Who answers employee questions, in which language, and in what time? How are errors reported, corrected and costed? What are the exit terms, and how is employee data returned? Can the commercial model scale down as well as up? A partner that cannot answer these clearly will cost you more in operations than the fee suggests.
A hybrid path   Many platforms start with an ICP and keep the option to move to an own entity later. This works if you plan for it from the start. Keep your employee data in your own system. Keep contract terms that allow transfer. Track your Italian cost per employee from day one, so the switch decision rests on your numbers and not on opinion.
The reverse also happens. A platform opens an entity, finds volume lower than planned, and moves part of the load to a partner. That is harder, because fixed costs are already in your P&L.
Summary   Choose an ICP when volume is uncertain, when you lack Italian staff, or when speed matters. Choose an own entity when volume is proven, when margin share is material, and when you can staff the team properly. In between, use a hybrid and measure.
The decision should come from your own cost model, not from a general rule. The data you exchange with the partner is what makes that model reliable.
Partnership teams are invited to request the data-exchange specification.

## Parental leave in Italy: a support guide for platform teams
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/parental-leave-italy-support-guide-platform-teams.html
Summary: What platform support teams should tell employees about parental leave in Italy, and which data payroll needs to process it correctly.
Parental leave questions reach your support desk at a bad moment. The employee is often stressed and short on time. They want to know what they can take, what they will be paid and what to send. If your team answers vaguely, the question comes back as a ticket, then as an escalation, then as a payroll correction.
This guide sets out what to tell employees and what data payroll needs. It does not give legal limits or amounts. Those depend on the employee’s situation and must come from a verified source for each case. Your job is to collect the right inputs and set the right expectations.
Why Italy needs a clear process   In Italy, leave around childbirth and childcare is not a single product. There are several types of leave, and they follow different rules. Some are mandatory. Some are optional. Some are available to either parent. Each type can affect pay, contributions and the employee’s record in a different way.
The result is a common mistake. Support agents say “parental leave” when the employee means something narrower or broader. Payroll then receives a request that cannot be processed because the leave type is missing.
Fix this at intake. Ask which type of leave the employee is requesting before you ask anything else.
What to tell employees   Keep the message short and honest.
Say what is certain. Leave exists, it is protected, and the employee should not worry about asking. Make it clear that requesting leave is a normal process.
Say what depends on the case. The duration, the share of pay and the way the benefit is paid depend on the leave type and the employee’s circumstances. Do not guess. Do not quote an amount from memory or from another country.
Say who does what. Explain the roles. The employee provides the request and the supporting documents. The platform checks the request and passes it to payroll. Payroll applies it. The relevant authorities and the employer may each have a part in payment, depending on the leave type.
Say what happens to the pay slip. Tell the employee that the pay slip may look different during leave. Net pay may drop, change in structure or arrive in separate payments. Warn them before it happens, not after.
Say what you need from them. Give a clear list of documents and details. Tell them the request cannot move forward until it is complete.
Avoid promises. Do not say “you will receive the full salary” or “it will be quick.” Say that you will confirm the exact treatment once the leave type and documents are checked.
What payroll needs   Payroll cannot work from a message that says “employee is going on leave.” It needs structured data. Collect the following for each request.
Employee identifier as it appears in the payroll system, not just the name. Leave type, chosen from a fixed list, not free text. Start date and expected end date. If the end date is not known, mark it as open and record when it will be confirmed. Child details needed to support the claim, such as the date of birth or expected date of birth. Supporting documents as received, with the date each was received. Employee’s relationship to the child, because eligibility can differ between parents. Whether the leave is continuous or split. Split leave means several short periods. Each period needs its own dates. Whether the other parent has taken or plans to take leave, where this affects entitlement. Contact for follow-up, in case payroll needs a correction. Add two internal fields. The first is the name of the person who checked the request. The second is the status: received, checked, sent to payroll, applied, or closed. These make it possible to answer “where is my request?” without asking payroll.
Common failure points   Missing leave type. The most frequent cause of delay. Use a fixed list in your intake form.
Dates that change. Employees extend, shorten or split leave. Treat every change as a new event with its own timestamp, not as an edit to the old record.
Late documents. Do not let a request sit while you wait. Send a reminder and show the employee what is outstanding.
Unclear ownership. If the platform, the local provider and the client each assume another party will contact the employee, nobody does. Name one owner for each request.
Mixed messages between channels. If chat says one thing and email says another, the employee loses trust. Use approved wording for the main questions and store it in one place.
Escalation rules   Set clear triggers for sending a case to the local payroll or legal specialist. Examples: the employee asks about a leave type outside your list, the dates conflict with another absence, or the documents do not match the request. Support agents should not interpret these cases.
A short checklist for your team   Confirm the leave type first. Collect dates, child details and documents in one request. Tell the employee what depends on the case and do not quote amounts. Warn them that the pay slip will change. Record each change as a dated event. Name one owner and one status for each request. Escalate anything that does not fit the list. A good process does not need your agents to be experts in Italian labour rules. It needs them to ask for the right data, set honest expectations and pass clean requests to payroll.
Partnership teams that want to connect their intake and payroll flows can request the data-exchange specification.

## Payment proof: reading an F24 receipt
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/payment-proof-reading-f24-receipt.html
Summary: What an F24 receipt proves for Italian payroll payments, what it leaves open, and how platforms can reconcile it with their own records.
Every month, a payroll platform asks the same question about Italy. Were the taxes and social contributions actually paid? The usual answer is a PDF called the F24 receipt. It looks final. It is useful. But it proves less than most teams assume.
This article explains what the receipt shows, what it does not show, and how to build a reliable check around it.
What the F24 is   The F24 is the Italian unified payment form. One form can carry many different charges. Withholding tax, social contributions and regional or local taxes can all sit on the same payment. Each line carries a code that tells the authorities what the money is for, plus the period it refers to.
That structure matters. A single receipt is rarely a single payment obligation. It is a bundle.
What the receipt proves   A proper receipt, issued after the payment is processed, proves a limited set of facts.
A payment was submitted and accepted through a bank or an online channel. A named taxpayer, identified by tax code, was the payer. The total amount was debited. Specific lines were paid, each with its own code, period and amount. The payment happened on a recorded date. This is real evidence. If a client asks whether the money left the account, the receipt answers it. If an auditor asks which codes were used, the receipt answers that too.
What the receipt does not prove   This is where teams get into trouble.
It does not prove the right amount was paid. The receipt shows what was paid. It does not show what was due. If the payroll calculation was wrong, the receipt will faithfully record a wrong payment.
It does not prove the right people were covered. The form does not list employees. A payment for a whole payroll run looks the same whether it covers every worker or only some of them. The link between the money and the individual payslips lives in your payroll data, not on the receipt.
It does not prove the right entity paid. The payer is whoever is named on the form. In a multi-entity setup, a payment made under the wrong tax code can look perfectly valid and still fail to settle the obligation you care about.
It does not prove the period is correct. The period reference is typed in by whoever prepared the form. A typo or a wrong reference can send a valid payment to the wrong month. The receipt will not flag it.
It does not prove the authorities have allocated the money as intended. Acceptance of a payment and correct allocation to the right position are separate steps. Problems can surface later, through notices or mismatches in the taxpayer’s account.
It does not prove compliance on its own. Paying is one part of the obligation. Filing and reporting are others. A receipt covers only the payment.
Common failure patterns   In practice, the gaps above show up in a few repeatable ways.
A receipt is attached to the wrong month. The file name says one period, the codes inside say another.
A payment is split across several forms, and only one receipt reaches the client. The total looks short.
A correction is paid on a new form. Now two receipts relate to the same period, and nobody has linked them.
A scanned or screenshot copy replaces the original. Fields are cut off, and the reviewer cannot read the codes.
How to read a receipt in a review   A short routine catches most problems.
Confirm the payer identity matches the entity that employs the workers. Read the line codes, not just the total. Match each code to an expected obligation. Check the period reference on every line. Compare the line amounts to the figures in the payroll run, line by line. Confirm the payment date and status come from a processed receipt, not from a request or a draft. Store the original file and a structured copy of the fields. The last step is the one most teams skip. A PDF is evidence for a human. A structured record is evidence for a system.
From PDF to data   For a global EOR or payroll platform, the receipt should not live as an attachment in a ticket. It should become a record that your systems can test.
A useful record carries the payer, the line codes, the periods, the amounts, the payment date and a reference to the payroll run it is meant to settle. With that, you can automate the checks that people now do by eye. You can flag a missing line. You can flag a period mismatch. You can show an account manager that a client’s month is fully paid, or exactly where it is not.
This also changes the client conversation. Instead of sending a PDF and saying it is paid, you can show the receipt, the match to the payroll run, and any open differences. That is a stronger statement, and it holds up better when someone asks a hard question later.
The practical rule   Treat the receipt as proof of payment, and nothing more. Proof of correctness comes from matching it against the calculation behind it. Proof of coverage comes from linking it to the workers and the period. Do both, and the receipt becomes a reliable part of your audit trail instead of a comfortable assumption.
Partnership teams that want to connect receipt data to their own reconciliation flows can request the data-exchange specification.

## Payroll cut-off and pay-date design for Italian employees
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/payroll-cut-off-pay-date-design-italy.html
Summary: How a clear cut-off window protects payroll quality and keeps pay-date promises to Italian employees on global EOR and payroll platforms.
A pay date is a promise. Employees plan rent, loans and family costs around it. When a platform misses it, the cost lands on the employee first and on your support team second.
The cut-off is what makes that promise possible. It is the point after which the payroll data for a period is frozen. Everything that arrives before it goes into the run. Everything that arrives after it waits for the next run, or goes through a defined exception path.
This article explains how to design that cut-off for Italian employees, and why it matters more here than many partners expect.
Why Italian payroll needs a firm cut-off   Italian payroll is not a simple gross-to-net calculation. The result depends on the national collective agreement that applies to the role, on contribution rules, on tax withholding and on the employee’s personal situation. Each of these inputs can change from period to period.
Variable data makes it harder. Overtime, absences, leave, allowances, expense reimbursements and benefit changes all feed the calculation. If any of them arrives late, the run has to be redone or the employee is paid wrongly.
A firm cut-off limits that risk. It gives the payroll team a stable data set, enough time to check it, and enough time to correct problems before money moves.
What a good cut-off protects   Accuracy. Checks only work on frozen data. If inputs keep changing, reviewers compare against a moving target. Errors slip through.
The pay date. Payment files must reach the bank in time. Banks have their own processing windows. The cut-off is the first domino. If it moves, every later step moves with it.
Filings and reporting. Payroll output feeds social security and tax obligations. Late or changed data creates reconciliation work later.
The employee relationship. An employee who is paid late or wrongly does not blame the payroll engine. They blame the employer, and through the employer, your platform.
Design the cut-off backwards from the pay date   Do not set the cut-off first and hope the pay date works. Start with the date the employee must have the money. Then work backwards.
Fix the date funds must be available to the employee. Subtract the time the bank needs to process the payment file. Subtract the time for approval of the net pay figures by the client. Subtract the time for payroll review and correction. Subtract the time to calculate the run. What remains is the latest moment the input data can arrive. That moment is your cut-off. If the client cannot live with it, the answer is not to shrink the review time. The answer is to move the pay date or to agree a different input process.
Separate the cut-off for each type of input   Not all data deserves the same deadline. Treat inputs in groups.
Structural data. New hires, terminations, salary changes and contract changes. These have the strictest cut-off because they affect the whole calculation.
Variable data. Overtime, absences, allowances. These can often have a slightly later cut-off if the process is automated and validated on entry.
Corrections. Late changes after the cut-off. Define them up front. Most should roll into the next period as adjustments, not trigger a rerun.
Write this down in the service agreement. Partners and clients should be able to see which input falls into which group.
Plan for the exception path   Some late changes cannot wait. A wrongly stated salary or a missing termination can create real harm if left for the next period.
Define a narrow exception route. State who can approve it, what evidence is needed, and what it costs in time. Keep it rare. If exceptions become routine, the cut-off is not real, and quality drops.
Track every exception. A pattern tells you where the upstream process is broken. Often the fix is a better data feed, not a looser deadline.
Make the cut-off visible   A cut-off that only the payroll team knows will be missed. Publish the calendar for the full year ahead. Send reminders before each deadline. Show the cut-off in the partner portal or the integration status, not only in a PDF.
Automate where you can. A clean data feed with validation at entry catches errors while the sender can still fix them. This also means fewer manual touches inside the cut-off window.
What this means for partnership and operations teams   When you pass Italian employees to a local provider, ask for the cut-off design, not just the price. Check four things:
Is the cut-off tied to the pay date, with the logic written out? Are inputs grouped by type with clear deadlines? Is there a defined exception path with approval rules? Is the calendar shared in advance and kept up to date? A provider that answers these clearly is managing risk. A provider that answers with “we are flexible” is shifting the risk to you.
A firm cut-off can feel strict. In practice it is what lets a payroll team keep its promise to every employee, every period.
Partnership teams: request the data-exchange specification to see how cut-off windows, input types and corrections are handled.

## Per-employee fee vs percentage of payroll for Italy: what it does to platform margins
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/per-employee-fee-vs-percentage-of-payroll-italy.html
Summary: Flat per-employee fee or percentage of payroll in Italy? The pros and cons for global EOR and payroll platforms, and what each model does to margin.
Every global EOR and payroll platform has to decide how to price an Italian partner. The choice is usually between a flat fee per employee and a percentage of payroll. Both work. They protect different things.
This article looks at the choice from the platform side. The question is what each model does to your margin, your forecasting and your relationship with the local partner.
Why Italy makes the choice harder   Italian payroll is not a single number. Cost depends on the collective agreement that applies, the employee’s level, the mix of fixed and variable pay, and a set of contributions and allowances that differ by case. Two employees with the same gross salary can produce different workloads and different totals.
That matters for pricing. A percentage tracks the size of the payroll. A flat fee tracks the number of people. Neither tracks the effort of running the case.
Flat fee per employee   Pros for the platform
Easy to quote. Your sales team can put a single line in a proposal and the customer understands it. Predictable cost of goods. If you pay the partner per head, your cost and your price move together. Stable margin per seat. A large raise for one employee does not change what you pay or what you charge. Simple invoicing and reconciliation. Headcount is easier to audit than payroll totals. Cons for the platform
Weak link to complexity. A simple case and a hard case cost the same. If the partner treats them equally, you carry the risk of unusual cases. Pressure on high-salary roles. Senior hires pay the same fee as junior ones, so you leave revenue on the table. Customers with senior teams will also compare you with cheaper options. Exposure to mix shifts. If your Italian base moves toward lower-cost roles, margin per seat can look fine while total revenue stays flat. Hard to price extras. Visas, relocation and benefits changes tend to end up as add-ons, which makes the quote less clean. Percentage of payroll   Pros for the platform
Revenue grows with the customer. Raises, bonuses and promotions lift your income without a new conversation. Better fit for senior and variable pay. Higher earners usually bring more complexity, and the fee follows. Easy to bundle. One rate can cover a range of services, which keeps the proposal short. Natural alignment with large accounts. Big payrolls pay more, which matches the support they ask for. Cons for the platform
Margin depends on the partner’s pricing structure. If your partner charges per head and you charge a percentage, your margin swings with salary levels you do not control. Forecasting is harder. Payroll totals change with bonuses, end-of-year items and one-off payments. Monthly revenue becomes noisier. Customers push back. Buyers see a percentage fee on a large salary as paying more for the same work. Expect discount requests on bigger accounts. Reconciliation is heavier. You need clean payroll data to bill correctly, and disputes about the base are common. Is it gross pay, total employer cost, or something narrower? Every definition needs to be written down. Match the model to the partner agreement   The most important rule is simple. Your customer price and your partner cost should use the same unit.
If you buy per head and sell per head, margin is stable. If you buy as a percentage and sell as a percentage, margin is stable. Mixing the two creates a margin that moves with the customer’s salary mix. Sometimes that is a deliberate bet. Most of the time it is an accident.
If your market requires a different unit on the sales side, consider a hybrid. A flat base fee per employee covers the fixed work of running a case. A smaller percentage component covers the variable part. This keeps a floor under margin and still lets revenue grow with larger payrolls.
What to check before you choose   Define the base for any percentage. Write down which pay elements are included. Decide how variable pay, one-off payments and corrections are treated. Decide how off-cycle runs and retroactive changes are billed. Set rules for minimum fees on very small payrolls. Agree how terminations and short-term assignments are priced. Make sure your reporting can show margin per employee and margin per payroll euro. You need both views to see where the model leaks. A practical way to decide   Look at your existing Italian or similar European base. Group employees by salary band and by case complexity. Then compare cost to serve against revenue under both models.
If most of your base sits in a narrow salary band, a flat fee is usually safer and easier to run. If your base is spread wide, with many senior roles and variable pay, a percentage or a hybrid captures value better.
The data you need is mostly operational: headcount, pay components, case types and support effort. Getting it in a consistent format from your Italian partner is what makes any of these models workable.
Partnership teams that want to see how that data can be exchanged can request the data-exchange specification.

## Pre-cut-off data validation checklist for Italian payroll
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/pre-cut-off-data-validation-checklist-italian-payroll.html
Summary: A practical checklist of input validations for Italian payroll, run before cut-off, so most data errors are caught before the run and not after it.
Most Italian payroll corrections do not start in the payroll engine. They start in the input file. A wrong tax code, a missing contract level or a late absence record travels through the whole run and comes back as a rework ticket.
The cheapest fix is a short set of checks, run before cut-off. They are mechanical. They need no judgment. They catch the bulk of input errors before anyone opens a payslip.
This checklist is written for partnership, operations and payroll managers at global EOR and payroll platforms who send data to an Italian payroll provider.
1. Identity and registry data   Start with the person. Errors here block everything else.
Tax code (codice fiscale). Check the format and the control character. Check that it matches name, surname, date of birth and place of birth. Foreign workers often have a code issued after arrival, so do not accept a placeholder. Names. Match the spelling to the identity document. Reject truncated names and special characters your system cannot export cleanly. Residence and domicile. Both must be present and complete. Tax and local surcharges depend on them. Bank details. Validate the IBAN structure and country. Confirm the account holder name matches the employee. Duplicates. Look for the same person under two employee IDs. This happens after rehires and entity transfers. 2. Contract and employment data   The contract record drives pay, contributions and leave. Check it field by field.
Start and end dates. The start date cannot be after the end date. Fixed-term contracts must have an end date. Open-ended contracts must not. National collective agreement (CCNL). Every employee needs one assigned. Reject blanks and free-text labels. Use a controlled list. Job level and category. The level must exist in the assigned agreement. A level from another agreement is a common silent error. Working time. Full-time or part-time must be explicit. If part-time, the schedule must be stated. Base pay. It must be at or above the minimum set by the agreement for that level. Flag anything below it for review. Probation and notice. Make sure the fields are filled when the contract requires them. 3. Variable pay and period movements   This is where most late changes appear. Treat every movement as new data that needs its own check.
Period. Every variable item must carry the payroll period it belongs to. Reject items with no period. Item codes. Each code must exist in the provider’s code list. Unknown codes should fail at import, not during the run. Overtime and allowances. Check that the agreement allows the item for that level. Bonuses and one-off payments. Require a clear gross or net flag. Mixing the two is a frequent cause of wrong payslips. Retroactive changes. Mark them as such. A raise applied late must show the original effective date. Expense reimbursements. Keep them separate from taxable pay, with the supporting category. 4. Absences and leave   Absence data is often the last to arrive and the least structured.
Type. Holiday, sickness, maternity, parental and unpaid leave follow different rules. Do not accept a generic “absence” type. Dates. No overlaps between absences. No absence outside the contract dates. Sickness. The medical certificate reference must be present. Without it, the provider cannot report correctly. Balances. Check that leave taken does not exceed what the system shows as accrued, unless an advance is approved. 5. Leavers and joiners   Starts and exits carry deadlines and extra calculations.
Joiners. Confirm the registry and contract data are complete before cut-off, not after. Late joiners create off-cycle work. Leavers. Require the last working day, the reason for termination and any unused leave. Check the notice period against the agreement. Final pay items. Make sure severance-related items and leave payouts are listed as separate lines. 6. Cross-file consistency   The last layer compares the current file with the previous one.
Headcount. New, changed and removed employees should reconcile with the HR system. Unexpected changes. Flag any change in base pay, bank account or agreement that has no matching change request. Missing people. An employee present last period and absent now, without a leaver record, needs an explanation. Entity mapping. Each employee must map to a valid legal entity or client account. How to run it   Run the checks automatically at import. Group failures by severity. Registry and contract errors block the file. Variable pay warnings go to a review list. Send the full result back to the sender the same day, so corrections arrive before cut-off.
Keep the rules versioned. When an agreement or a code list changes, the checklist changes with it. A rule nobody updates becomes a source of false alarms, and teams stop reading the report.
The goal is simple. Fewer surprises on payroll day, fewer corrections after it, and a clear record of who fixed what.
Partnership teams that want to align their exports with these checks can request the data-exchange specification.
