## Pre-funding vs actuals for Italian payroll: what each does to your cash flow
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/pre-funding-vs-actuals-italian-payroll-cash-flow.html
Summary: How pre-funding and actuals funding models change cash exposure, reconciliation and risk for global EOR and payroll platforms running payroll in Italy.
Every platform that runs payroll in Italy has to decide when the money moves. The choice sounds like a finance detail. It is not. It shapes your working capital, your exposure to client credit risk and the amount of reconciliation work your operations team carries each month.
This article compares the main funding models and what each means for platform cash flow.
The models in plain terms   Pre-funding. The client sends the full payroll cost to the local provider before payment runs. Net pay, social contributions and withholding taxes are covered by cash already in the account. The provider pays employees and authorities from those funds.
Actuals. The provider pays employees and authorities first, using its own liquidity or the platform’s. It then invoices the client for what was actually paid. The client reimburses after the fact.
Most real arrangements sit somewhere between these. Some platforms pre-fund net pay only and settle contributions and taxes on actuals. Others pre-fund for new or higher-risk clients and move trusted clients to actuals.
What pre-funding does for cash flow   Pre-funding removes the gap between paying out and getting paid. The platform does not finance the client’s payroll. Cash arrives before it leaves.
The benefits are clear:
No working capital tied up in client payroll. No credit exposure if a client stops paying. Simple risk story for finance and audit teams. The costs are less visible:
Clients feel the cash drag. They must fund earlier than they would with their own payroll. Late client transfers delay pay runs, so cut-off discipline becomes a client-facing issue. Estimates must be right. If the funded amount is short, someone has to chase a top-up before the run. Excess funds must be tracked and returned or credited, which adds a reconciliation step. What actuals does for cash flow   Actuals feels easier for the client. They pay for what happened, after it happened. Variances such as late hires, unpaid leave and corrections flow through naturally, because the invoice follows the real payroll.
The platform pays for that convenience:
Someone must fund the payroll in advance. That is usually the provider or the platform. Credit risk sits with the platform. A client that disputes an invoice or goes insolvent leaves a hole. Employee pay and statutory payments cannot wait for a slow client, so the platform carries the timing gap in full. Growth makes it worse. More clients means more cash tied up, at the same time. For a platform with a thin balance sheet, actuals at scale is a financing problem disguised as a payroll product.
Where Italy adds friction   Italian payroll has several moving parts that each follow their own timing. Net pay, social contributions, withholding taxes and other periodic items do not all settle on the same day. A funding model has to cover each stream, not only net salary.
This matters for the hybrid designs. If you pre-fund net pay but run contributions on actuals, you still carry a timing gap on the statutory side. Define which items are covered by which model, and write it down in the contract and in the data flow.
Corrections also matter. Retroactive changes, adjustments and late data change the real cost after the run. Under pre-funding they create a true-up. Under actuals they create a supplementary invoice. Both need a clear owner.
How to choose   Use these questions to decide per client segment:
Who carries credit risk? If you cannot absorb a client default, do not offer actuals without security or limits. How predictable is the payroll? Stable headcount suits pre-funding with small true-ups. Volatile headcount creates frequent shortfalls and refunds. How strong is your liquidity? Actuals needs a funding line or reserves sized to your growth plan, not to today’s client count. What does the client expect? Enterprise buyers often push for actuals. Smaller companies usually accept pre-funding if the cut-off is clear. A practical pattern is pre-funding by default, with actuals as a earned status. Move a client only after a track record of on-time payment, and keep the right to revert.
Operations that make either model work   The model matters less than the data behind it. Three things keep cash flow predictable:
A fixed cut-off calendar. Funding deadlines, data deadlines and payment dates should be agreed per client and shared with everyone. Early cost estimates. Send the expected total before the run, so the client can fund the right amount the first time. Clean reconciliation. Match every payment to a payroll line, every refund to a funding event and every adjustment to its cause. When these are in place, the choice between pre-funding and actuals becomes a risk and pricing decision. When they are missing, both models produce disputes.
What this means for partnership teams   If you are adding Italy to your platform, agree the funding model before you agree the integration. The model decides what data you need to exchange, how often and in which format. It also decides who sees a shortfall first and who has to fix it.
Partnership teams that settle this early avoid the common failure: a technically live integration with an unresolved cash question.
Partnership teams can request the data-exchange specification to see how funding, cut-off and reconciliation data are structured.

## Preparing for a client's year-end audit request on Italian payroll
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/client-year-end-audit-request-italy-payroll.html
Summary: A client's auditor asks for Italian payroll evidence. What to produce, in what order, and how fast, with the filing dates that frame the request.
A client’s auditor sends a request list for the Italian entity. It lands on your desk in the busiest weeks of the year. The auditor wants evidence, not explanations. This article covers what to produce and how fast.
The scenario   Your platform employs people in Italy on behalf of a foreign client. The client’s group auditors are closing the year. They ask for proof that Italian payroll, withholding and social contributions are correct and filed. The request usually comes through the client’s finance lead, who is not an Italian payroll expert and needs answers they can forward unchanged.
The partnership manager owns the relationship. The operations manager owns the evidence. Payroll owns the numbers. The audit goes well when those three agree on who sends what before the first reply goes out.
Reply fast, deliver in stages   Send a short acknowledgment the same day. Confirm that you received the list, name one contact, and say which items you can deliver immediately and which need preparation. Do not wait until everything is ready to say anything.
Then deliver in stages. Auditors prefer a steady flow they can start testing over a late complete package. Put the items that exist as ready documents first. Put the items that need reconciliation last.
Stage one: documents that already exist   These should be retrievable without new work:
Employment contracts and any amendments for each employee in scope. The national collective agreement applied to each role, with the level and the date it was assigned. Payslips for the audit period. The payroll register for each period. The Certificazione Unica issued to each employee. Per a secondary source, the deadline for employee CUs in 2026 was 2026-03-16. Send the filing receipt together with the document, so the auditor sees both that it was issued and that it was filed on time. If any of these cannot be pulled quickly, that is a process gap. Note it and fix it after the audit.
Stage two: payments and filings   This is where auditors spend their time. They want to see that what was withheld and accrued was actually paid and reported.
Proof of payment of withholding tax and social contributions, matched to the payroll periods they cover. Filing receipts for the periodic contribution declarations. The status of the annual withholding-agent declaration, the Modello 770. Per a secondary source, the deadline falls on 2026-10-31. That date is a Saturday, so the due date moves to 2026-11-02. If the audit request arrives close to that date, say clearly whether the filing is done, in preparation or scheduled. A plain status line with a date is better than silence. These dates come from a secondary source. Check them against the official calendar before you quote them to a client in writing.
Stage three: reconciliations   This is the part that takes preparation. Auditors compare payroll to the general ledger. They want to see that gross pay, employer contributions, withholdings and net pay in your records tie to the amounts the client booked.
Produce a reconciliation by period with these columns:
Gross pay per payroll register. Employer contributions accrued. Withholdings accrued. Net pay disbursed. Amount invoiced to the client. Differences, each with a one-line reason. Unexplained differences are what cause follow-up questions. Explain every one, even the small ones. A rounding note costs you a sentence. A missing explanation costs you a week.
Stage four: leave and variable pay   Expect questions on accrued leave, end-of-service entitlements, bonuses and benefits. Provide the balance per employee at period end, the rule used to calculate it, and the source document. These are liabilities on the client’s balance sheet, so the auditor will test them.
How to keep the answers usable   Auditors forward your files to colleagues in other countries. Make each file stand alone.
Name files by employee reference, period and document type. Never use personal data in file names. Add a cover note to each package that says what it contains, the period, and the source system. Write in plain English. Give the Italian term once, with its meaning, then use it consistently. Keep one index that lists every request item, its status and where the evidence sits. Protect personal data. Share only what the request requires, through the secure channel the client has agreed to, and log what was sent and when.
What good looks like   The best response needs very little of your time during the audit itself. The documents are already organized by employee and period. Filing receipts are stored with the filings. Reconciliations are produced as part of each close, not rebuilt on request.
If you must assemble all of this by hand each year, the cost shows up as delay and as exposure. Build the evidence trail into the monthly cycle and an audit request becomes a retrieval task.
Before the next request   Run a dry run. Take one employee and one period, and try to produce the full evidence set, from contract to filing receipt to ledger tie-out. Time it. Whatever slows you down is what will slow you down in a real audit.
Partnership teams that want to align on how this evidence is exchanged with their platform can request the data-exchange specification.

## Probation Periods in Italian Contracts: An Ops FAQ
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/probation-periods-italian-contracts-ops-faq.html
Summary: How probation length depends on the CCNL and job level in Italy, and how payroll and partnership ops teams can track end dates without missing them.
Probation in Italy looks simple until you run it at scale. The length is not a global default. It depends on the collective agreement (CCNL) that applies to the employee, and often on the job level inside that agreement. This FAQ covers what ops teams ask most.
Who sets the probation length?   The applicable CCNL sets the maximum. The individual contract then states the actual period. The contract value can be shorter than the CCNL maximum. It cannot be longer.
The period must be agreed in writing before the employee starts work. If it is missing from the signed contract, there is no probation. This is the most common gap we see in contracts that arrive from foreign templates.
Why do durations differ by CCNL?   Each CCNL was negotiated by a different sector and a different set of parties. Commerce, metalworking, IT services and hospitality each define their own scale. Within one CCNL, the period usually grows with seniority. A junior role gets a shorter period. A manager gets a longer one.
So you cannot store a single country-level value. You need a lookup keyed on at least two fields: the CCNL and the job level. Some agreements also distinguish between categories of staff, so keep that field open.
What data do we need to compute the end date?   Keep these fields for every employee:
CCNL name and version in force Job level as written in the contract Start date Probation length stated in the contract Unit of the length (days, weeks or months) Whether the CCNL counts calendar days or working days The last two fields cause most errors. A period in months and a period in working days give different end dates. Store the unit with the value, never a bare number.
How do we calculate the end date?   Take the start date and add the contractual period in the unit the CCNL uses. If the CCNL counts working days, you need an Italian holiday calendar and a rule for weekends. Check how the agreement treats public holidays and days of absence before you automate anything.
Write the rule per CCNL, not per employee. Then test it against a sample of real contracts that your Italian payroll team has already confirmed by hand.
Does sickness or leave pause probation?   It can. Some agreements suspend or extend the period when the employee is absent for certain reasons. Others do not. This is a CCNL-level rule and it must be in your lookup table as a flag, with a note on the source clause.
If your system only stores a fixed end date, an absence will silently make that date wrong. Store the original end date and a recalculated end date as two separate fields. Show both to ops.
What happens at the end of probation?   During probation, either side can usually end the contract with much lighter notice rules than normal. After it ends without a decision, the employment continues as a standard contract and the employee keeps the time already served for seniority.
This matters for your calendar. A decision to confirm or end the role has to be taken before the end date, not after. Waiting for the date to pass is a decision, and a costly one.
How early should alerts fire?   Set more than one alert. A first alert gives the client time to run a review. A second alert is a final reminder to the account owner and the payroll lead. Choose the lead time per client, since review cycles differ. Send alerts to a shared queue, not to one person’s inbox.
What should partnership teams ask us?   When you integrate with an Italian EOR, ask for these items in writing:
The CCNL and level for every employee, as structured fields The contractual probation length and unit The computed end date and the rule used A flag for any suspension or extension event A change log when the end date moves If a provider can only send a PDF of the contract, your team will re-key dates by hand. That is where mistakes start.
What are the common failure points?   Using a default length when the CCNL was not captured Mixing calendar days and working days Treating the contract template as proof of probation, when the signed copy has no clause Ignoring absences that move the end date Alerting after the date instead of before it Updating a CCNL table without versioning, so old contracts are recalculated under new rules Each of these is a data problem, not a legal puzzle. Clean fields and versioned rules remove most of them.
A practical setup   Build one table of CCNL, level, maximum period, unit, counting rule and suspension rule. Add a source reference and a review date to every row. Link each employee record to a row by key, not by free text. Recalculate on any change and keep the history.
Then reconcile monthly. Compare your computed end dates with the ones the Italian payroll team holds. Investigate every mismatch. After a few cycles the mismatches should be rare, and the ones left will point to real gaps in the contract data.
Partnership teams that want to exchange these fields automatically can request the data-exchange specification from us.

## Productivity bonuses in Italian payroll: how the 1% substitute tax works
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/productivity-bonus-substitute-tax-italy-payroll.html
Summary: How the 1% substitute tax on Italian productivity bonuses works in payroll: rate, EUR 5,000 cap, income limit and the data a platform must capture.
Italian productivity bonuses can be taxed at a flat substitute rate instead of the normal progressive rate. For a payroll platform this is a calculation rule, an eligibility check and a data-exchange problem. This article covers the mechanics.
The verified parameters   The figures below come from one secondary source. Treat them as the working baseline and re-check before you hard-code anything.
Substitute tax rate: 1% (0.01 in the data). Cap on the bonus amount that receives the flat treatment: EUR 5,000. Income limit for the employee: EUR 80,000. The income limit is a 2025 figure. We did not find a confirmation for 2026. Your rules engine should hold this value as a configurable parameter with an effective date, not as a constant in code.
What the rule does   When the conditions are met, the bonus is not added to ordinary taxable pay. It is taxed separately at the flat rate. The result is a net amount that differs from what the normal progressive calculation would give.
The cap limits the amount that benefits. Anything above the cap goes back to ordinary taxation. Your engine needs to split the bonus into two parts: the portion inside the cap and the portion outside it.
Eligibility checks   There are two checks that a payroll system can automate and one that it cannot.
Income check. The employee must be under the income limit. The limit refers to the employee’s own income, so the platform needs a reliable income figure from the right period. For employees who joined mid-year, or who had other employers, the platform may not hold the full picture. Ask the employee for a declaration where needed and store it.
Cap check. Track how much flat-taxed bonus has already been paid in the period. A second or third payment can push the total past the cap. The engine must apply the cap cumulatively, not per payment.
Bonus qualification. Whether a given payment counts as a productivity bonus depends on how it is defined and agreed. This is a business and documentation question. Payroll can store the evidence, but it cannot decide it. Make the qualification a flagged input on the payment record, set by a named person, with a reference to the supporting document.
Payroll mechanics   Separate pay element. Create a distinct earnings code for the flat-taxed bonus. Do not mix it with ordinary bonuses. This keeps reporting clean and makes audits simpler. Split at the cap. If the payment exceeds the remaining cap, the engine posts two lines: one flat-taxed up to the cap, one taxed normally. Exclude from the progressive base. The flat-taxed part must not enter the base used for the progressive calculation. Check that your gross-to-net sequence does this in the right order. Cumulative tracker. Keep a running total per employee per tax year for the flat-taxed amount. Reset it at year start. Payslip line. Show the bonus, the rate applied and the amount of tax withheld on its own line. Employees ask about this, and support teams need to see it. Reporting. The flat-taxed amount needs to be identifiable in year-end reporting. If the earnings code is separate, this is a simple extract. Where platforms usually go wrong   Stale parameters. The income limit is not confirmed for the current year in our source. If a platform assumes it carries over without checking, it may apply the flat rate to people who no longer qualify, or deny it to people who do. Per-payment caps. Applying the cap to each payment separately lets the total exceed the limit. No audit trail. Without a record of who qualified the payment and why, a correction later is slow and expensive. Mid-year joiners. Income from a previous employer may be missing. A declaration step avoids guesswork. Corrections. If a payment was wrongly flat-taxed, the engine must be able to reverse the split and recompute the tracker. Build the reversal path before you need it. Data the partner platform should send   For a clean handoff between a global platform and local payroll, the minimum set is:
Employee identifier and tax year. Bonus amount and payment date. Qualification flag and a reference to the supporting document. Employee income declaration, where the platform holds it. Flat-taxed amount already paid in the year, if the employee had payments through another channel. With these fields, the local side can apply the rate, enforce the cap and return the withheld amount and net pay in a format the global platform can reconcile.
Practical advice   Store the rate, the cap and the income limit as dated parameters. Log the source for each. When a value changes or a confirmation arrives, update the parameter and keep the history. Run a test set that includes a bonus below the cap, one exactly at the cap, one above it, and an employee above the income limit.
Partnership teams that want to connect their platform to Italian payroll for this and similar items can request the data-exchange specification.

## Public holidays and payroll timing in Italy: how national and local dates move your deadlines
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/public-holidays-payroll-timing-italy.html
Summary: National and local holidays in Italy shift payroll cut-offs, bank transfers and filings. Here is how ops teams can plan for them and keep payments on time.
Payroll in Italy runs on a calendar. Pay dates, contribution payments and filings all depend on working days. When a holiday lands on or near a deadline, the deadline moves, or the bank does not process the payment, or both. Global EOR and payroll platforms feel this most when they run many countries on one schedule.
This article explains how holidays affect payroll timing in Italy and what operations teams can build to handle it.
National holidays and the working-day rule   Italy has a fixed set of national public holidays. Some fall on the same date every year. Easter Monday moves with Easter. Sundays also count as non-working days for most deadline purposes.
The practical rule is simple. If a payment or filing deadline falls on a non-working day, it normally rolls to the next working day. That is the general principle. Your team should still confirm each case against the official source for the specific obligation, because the rule is applied through the rules of each authority and not through one universal switch.
For payroll, three things are affected:
Salary payment dates. Employees expect to be paid by a set day. If that day is a holiday, the bank will not settle the transfer. Funds must leave earlier. Social contribution and tax payments. These follow their own due dates. A holiday can push them forward, but only when the rule says so. Reporting and filings. Submissions to authorities follow the same working-day logic, with some exceptions. Why the bank calendar matters more than the legal one   A deadline can be legally valid on a given day and still be impossible to meet. Banks process transfers only on banking days. Italy has its own set of banking closures, and they follow the national holiday calendar. Cross-border transfers add the calendar of the sending country and the intermediary bank.
This is where most missed payments come from. The team sees a legal due date. The bank sees a closed day. The money arrives late.
The fix is to work backwards. Start from the date the employee must have the funds. Subtract the settlement time. Then subtract your internal approval and funding steps. Check every day in that chain against the relevant holiday calendars.
Local holidays   National dates are only part of the picture. Many Italian cities celebrate the feast day of their patron saint. In those cities, local offices, and sometimes local branches of banks and public bodies, close for the day.
The effect on payroll depends on who is local. An employee’s workplace may sit in a city with a local holiday. The bank branch may be elsewhere. The authority receiving the filing may be national. Each of these may have a different calendar.
Local holidays also matter for time-sensitive employee requests. Questions about payslips, certificates or document delivery take longer when a local office is closed. Support teams should know which cities in their employee base have a local holiday in a given week.
Collective agreements add another layer   Italian employment is shaped by national collective agreements. Many of them say how holidays that fall on a Sunday or a rest day are paid, and how work on a holiday is compensated. They can also set rules for holidays that coincide with a day the employee would not normally work.
This does not change the deadline calendar. It changes the amount. A holiday in the pay period can alter the pay calculation, depending on the agreement that applies to the employee. Payroll engines should hold the holiday treatment as data tied to the agreement, not as a fixed rule in code.
Bridge days and company closures   When a holiday falls next to a weekend, many employers and public bodies see extra absences. Employees take leave to create a long break. Offices run with fewer staff. Approvals slow down.
This is not a legal change to the deadline. It is a real change to how fast things get done. Build slack into the days around these periods. Ask clients early about planned closures so payroll inputs arrive before the break and not after it.
What platforms should build   A reliable holiday approach has a few parts.
A single calendar source per jurisdiction. Keep national, banking and local calendars as structured data, each with its source and the date it was last checked. Do not rely on a spreadsheet that one person updates.
Deadline rules as data. Store each obligation with its own rule for what happens on a non-working day. Some roll forward. Some do not. Do not assume.
Backward scheduling. Compute the funding date from the employee pay date, not from the payroll run date. Show the result to the operations team so they can see why a cut-off moved.
Alerts before the holiday, not on it. Warn clients and internal teams well ahead when a cut-off will shift. Late warnings turn a calendar fact into an incident.
Local overrides. Let the schedule account for the employee’s work location. A patron saint day in one city should not move payments for employees in another.
An audit trail. When a payment goes out early because of a holiday, record the reason. Finance and client teams will ask.
Common mistakes   The errors repeat across providers:
Treating the legal due date as the date to start the transfer. Using one holiday calendar for all countries. Ignoring local holidays because they are not national. Hard-coding the Easter-related dates instead of computing them. Applying one deadline-roll rule to every filing. Each of these is cheap to avoid once the calendar is treated as data and reviewed on a schedule.
Summary   Holidays in Italy shift payroll in three ways: they move legal deadlines, they close banks, and they change pay calculations through collective agreements. Local holidays add differences by city. The way to manage this is to keep calendars and rules as sourced data, schedule backwards from the employee pay date, and warn early.
Partnership teams that want to share holiday and deadline data with us in a structured way can request the data-exchange specification.

## Quarter-end compliance checklist for Italian payroll
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/quarter-end-compliance-checklist-italian-payroll.html
Summary: A recurring quarter-end checklist for Italian payroll: contracts, contributions, collective agreements, leave balances and reconciliations for EOR teams.
Quarter-end is when small payroll errors in Italy become visible. A wrong contribution code, a missed collective agreement update or an unreconciled benefit can sit unnoticed for months. Then it shows up in an audit or in an employee complaint.
This checklist is for operations and payroll managers at global EOR and payroll platforms. It is built for repetition. Run it every quarter, in the same order, with the same owners.
Before you start   Freeze the data. Take a snapshot of the employee master data, contract terms and payroll results for the period. Every check below runs against that snapshot, so findings do not shift while you work.
Name an owner for each section. If the platform runs on local partners, name the partner contact too. Unowned checks do not get done.
Contracts and employee records   Confirm that every active employee has a signed contract on file and that the contract type matches the payroll setup. Check start dates, end dates and probation status for each new hire or leaver in the period. Verify that fixed-term contracts approaching their end are flagged, with a decision recorded: renew, convert or close. Check job title, level and working hours against the contract. Level drives pay minimums, so a mismatch has a direct cost. Confirm tax code, address and bank details are complete. Missing fields cause rejected payments and failed filings. Collective agreement alignment   Italian pay is shaped by the national collective agreement that applies to each role. Quarter-end is the right time to confirm the mapping is still correct.
Check that each employee is assigned to the right agreement and level. Look for agreement renewals or pay table updates published during the period. Apply them from the correct effective date, including any back pay. Check statutory extras that depend on the agreement, such as additional monthly payments and notice terms. Record the source and the date of every rate or rule you apply. If you cannot cite it, do not rely on it. Contributions and withholding   Reconcile the contribution base used in payroll against gross pay for each employee. Confirm the correct contribution categories are applied, including any that depend on company size or sector. Reconcile withholding tax and regional or municipal surtaxes against the period’s payslips. Match the totals due to the amounts actually paid. Investigate every difference, even small ones. Check that corrections from earlier periods were applied once and only once. Leave, overtime and accruals   Review leave balances for each employee. Check that accrual matches contract and agreement rules. Check overtime and allowances against approved timesheets. Confirm that accruals for deferred pay and end-of-service entitlements are posted and consistent with the ledger. Flag employees with unusually high leave balances. They are a liability and sometimes a compliance issue. Benefits, expenses and in-kind items   Reconcile benefits provided in the period against the amounts included in payroll. Check that taxable and non-taxable treatment is applied consistently, and that the supporting documents exist. Review expense reimbursements and allowances for the same treatment. Filings and payments   List every filing and payment that fell in the period. Mark each as submitted, accepted or pending. Keep proof of submission and proof of payment together, indexed by employee and period. Check for rejected or queried filings. Resolve them now, not at the next cycle. Confirm the year-to-date totals in the payroll system agree with the totals reported to the authorities. Changes and exceptions   Review all retroactive changes made during the period. Each needs an approver and a reason. Check terminations: final pay, accrued entitlements, notice and the closing paperwork. Review every manual override. If one repeats each quarter, fix the underlying rule. Log open questions for the local advisor, with an owner and a due date. Sign-off and handover   Close the quarter with a short written summary. Include what was checked, what was found, what was corrected and what remains open. Store it with the snapshot.
For platforms with several partners, use the same template in every country and entity. A consistent format makes it easy to compare results and spot patterns. It also makes onboarding a new reviewer much faster.
Make it routine   The checklist only works if it is boring. Schedule it before the period closes. Assign backups for each owner. Track recurring findings and treat them as process defects, not one-off mistakes.
The goal is simple. By the time the quarter closes, you can show that every employee was paid correctly, every contribution was calculated on the right base, and every filing has proof.
Partnership teams that want to automate these checks can request the data-exchange specification.

## Reconciling a funding invoice against the payroll register
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/reconciling-funding-invoice-payroll-register.html
Summary: A month where the funding invoice and the payroll register disagree, and how a platform operations team can trace the gap line by line.
A funding invoice and a payroll register describe the same month. They should agree. Some months they do not. This article walks through one such month and shows how to trace the gap.
No figures are used here. The method matters more than the amounts.
The setup   A global EOR platform sends a funding request to its local partner. The request covers net pay, employer contributions, taxes withheld and the partner’s fee. The partner runs payroll, files the returns and produces a payroll register.
At month end, the finance contact on the platform side compares the two documents. The invoice is higher than the register total. Nobody has made an obvious error. The task is to find where the difference sits.
Start with the shape of the gap   Before opening any line, ask what kind of gap it is.
Is the invoice higher or lower than the register? Does the gap sit in one cost category or across all of them? Does it affect one employee, a group, or the whole population? A gap in a single category points to a rule or a rate. A gap spread across all categories points to a headcount or timing issue. A gap tied to one person points to a data change for that person.
In this scenario the gap sits mostly in employer contributions. Net pay lines match. That narrows the search at once.
Check the basis of each document   The invoice and the register are often built on different cut-off points. Confirm these before looking at individual lines.
Period covered. Does the invoice cover the same pay period as the register? Cut-off for changes. Joiners, leavers and salary changes entered late may sit in one document and not the other. Currency and rate. If the platform funds in one currency and the partner pays in another, the conversion date matters. Inclusions. Some registers show the fee. Some do not. Some invoices bundle one-off items. Here, the period and currency match. The cut-off for changes does not. The invoice was prepared from the platform’s headcount file. The register was produced after a late correction.
Match employee by employee   Export both documents with a stable employee identifier. Do not match on names. Names are spelled differently across systems.
Then build a simple comparison with these columns:
employee identifier amount on the invoice amount on the register difference reason code Sort by the absolute difference. The largest items usually explain most of the gap. Work down the list until the remaining items are too small to matter, then group them.
In this scenario a small number of employees account for nearly all of the difference. The rest are rounding.
Common causes   When funding and actuals diverge, the cause is usually one of these.
A mid-period change. A salary increase or a change in contract terms was applied in the register after the invoice was raised. The invoice reflects the older figure.
A leaver or joiner. An employee left or started part way through the period. The invoice treats a full period. The register prorates.
A contribution rule. A rate, a ceiling or an exemption applies to some employees. The invoice used a general assumption. The register used the individual rule.
An adjustment from a prior period. A correction from an earlier run lands in this month’s register. It has no matching line on the invoice.
A timing difference on benefits. An allowance is paid in one run but accrued in another.
In this scenario the cause is a prior-period correction and a late salary change. Both are real. Neither is an error. They are timing differences.
Document the result   A reconciliation is only useful if the next person can read it. Record the following for each difference.
the employee identifier the cause the document that is correct whether a credit note, a supplementary invoice or no action is needed who approved the treatment Then decide how the gap is settled. A timing difference usually reverses in the next period. A genuine overcharge needs a credit. Agree this with the partner in writing.
Prevent the same gap next month   Most gaps repeat. The fix is upstream.
Share one cut-off date for changes and keep to it. Send changes as structured data, not as emails or spreadsheets. Include the reason code in the data, so that the invoice and the register carry the same label. Return the register in a format that can be matched to the invoice without manual work. When both sides use the same identifiers and the same fields, the comparison takes minutes. The team spends its time on the few items that need judgment.
What good looks like   A clean funding process has few surprises. Differences are explained before the invoice is paid. The register is available when the invoice arrives. Corrections are visible as corrections, not hidden in totals.
This is a data problem more than a finance problem. Better structure removes most of the work.
Partnership teams that want to see how this data can be exchanged between a platform and a local payroll partner can request the data-exchange specification.

## Response times for employee queries in Italy: how to set realistic expectations
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/employee-query-response-times-italy-benchmarks.html
Summary: How to define first response and resolution for Italian HR tickets, which query types differ, and how partners can agree service levels that hold up.
Global EOR and payroll platforms often set a single service level for employee queries across all countries. In Italy that approach breaks down fast. The reason is not slow people. It is the mix of query types, the role of third parties, and the local calendar.
This article explains how to separate first response from resolution, which query types need different targets, and what a partnership team should agree before launch.
First response and resolution are different promises   First response means a human has read the ticket and told the employee what happens next. Resolution means the issue is closed and the employee has what they asked for.
Most disputes about service levels come from mixing the two. A platform promises fast resolution and gets a fast acknowledgement. The employee feels ignored. Or the local team resolves a hard case well, but nobody confirmed receipt, so the employee wrote three more times.
Set both targets separately. Measure both separately. Report both separately.
First response is a function of staffing and language   First response is the part you can control. It depends on coverage hours, ticket routing and language.
Italian employees expect to write in Italian. A ticket that arrives in English from a platform queue, then gets translated, then answered, loses time at every step. A local team that reads the original message answers faster and makes fewer mistakes.
Time zones matter too. If your platform support sits in another region, an Italian employee may write in the morning and receive nothing until the afternoon. Agree which hours count toward the target. Business hours in Italy are the sensible default.
A realistic first-response target is one that a small local team can meet on a normal day and on a busy payroll day. If it only holds on quiet days, it is the wrong target.
Resolution depends on the query type   Not all tickets are equal. Group them before you set any target.
Simple information requests. Payslip explanations, leave balances, document copies, contract clarifications. These sit with the local team and can usually be closed in the same conversation. Resolution should be close to first response.
Payroll corrections. An employee spots an error in a payslip. The fix may need a recalculation, a review of inputs from the client, and sometimes a corrective entry in the next cycle. Resolution here follows the payroll calendar, not the clock. Tell the employee which cycle the fix will land in.
Requests that need the client. Leave approvals, role changes, expense queries. The EOR cannot close these alone. Resolution time includes the client’s response time. Show that waiting time separately in reporting, or the EOR will be blamed for delays it does not own.
Requests that depend on public bodies. Social security records, tax certificates, benefit claims. The local team can submit and follow up, but the authority sets the pace. Promise a status update rhythm, not a closing date.
Immigration and relocation questions. These often run on external appointments and document checks. Treat them as cases with milestones, not as tickets with a deadline.
The Italian calendar affects everything   Payroll cut-offs create predictable peaks. Query volume rises when payslips are released. Staff capacity should follow that rhythm.
Holiday periods also matter. Italy has long summer closures in many sectors, and public offices and client contacts may be slow to respond. Plan for it. Tell employees in advance when responses from third parties will take longer.
Collective agreements add another layer. The same question can have a different answer depending on the sector contract that applies. The local team needs time to check the right source. A fast wrong answer costs more than a slightly slower correct one.
What to put in the partnership agreement   Keep the service terms short and testable.
Define first response and resolution in plain words. Name the query categories and the target logic for each. State which hours and which calendar count. Say who owns each status, including waiting for the client and waiting for an authority. Agree an escalation path for tickets that stall. Agree how misrouted tickets are counted. Decide how often you review the numbers together. The last point matters most. Benchmarks are only useful when both sides look at the same data. Start with a pilot period, collect real ticket data by category, and then fix the targets. Targets set before you have data tend to be either too loose to matter or too tight to meet.
What employees actually notice   Employees rarely compare your numbers with a benchmark. They notice three things. Did someone answer quickly in their language? Did they know what would happen next? Did the promised update arrive?
A fast acknowledgement with a clear next step and a reliable follow-up beats a rushed answer that needs correcting. Build the process around that.
Reporting that keeps both sides honest   Share a simple report each cycle. Show first response and resolution by category. Show how long tickets waited on the client, on an authority, or on the employee. Show the tickets that reopened. Reopened tickets reveal weak first answers faster than any satisfaction score.
Keep the report small. A long dashboard nobody reads does not improve service.
Partnership teams that want to align ticket categories, status codes and reporting fields with our Italian operations can request the data-exchange specification.

## REST API vs SFTP file exchange for Italian payroll: what suits a mid-size EOR platform
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/rest-api-vs-sftp-italian-payroll-data-exchange.html
Summary: REST API or SFTP for Italian payroll data exchange? A practical comparison of reliability, auditability and effort for mid-size EOR platforms.
Your platform needs to send Italian payroll inputs to a local provider and get results back. The question is how. REST API or SFTP file exchange. Both work. They fail in different ways and cost different things to run.
This article compares them on reliability, auditability and effort. The focus is a mid-size EOR platform with a real engineering team but not an unlimited one.
What actually moves between you and Italy   Before choosing a transport, list the flows. Most platforms need the same set:
New hire and contract data going out. Monthly variable inputs going out: hours, absences, bonuses, expense reimbursements. Payslip data and cost reports coming back. Corrections, cancellations and late changes in both directions. Status confirmations for statutory filings. Some of these are batch by nature. Monthly inputs close on a cut-off and are processed together. Others are event driven. A new hire or a termination should not wait for a nightly job.
This split matters. It is why many platforms end up with both transports, not one.
Reliability   SFTP is simple and old. A file is either on the server or it is not. There is no half-processed request. If your system is down when the provider delivers a file, the file waits. That is a real strength for batch work.
The weak points are quieter. A file can be partly written when the other side picks it up. A file can arrive with the wrong encoding or a changed column order. Nobody notices until payroll is wrong. You need naming rules, a completion marker, checksums and a clear rule for what happens to a rejected file.
REST API gives you immediate feedback. Each request returns a status. Validation errors come back in seconds, not after the next batch run. You can reject a bad record and accept the rest.
The weak points here are network failures and retries. If a request times out, did the provider receive it? Without idempotency keys, a retry can create a duplicate hire or a double bonus. This is solvable, but you must design for it from day one.
In short: SFTP is forgiving about timing and unforgiving about content. REST is strict about content and demanding about timing.
Auditability   Payroll data gets questioned. By employees, by auditors, by your own finance team. You need to show what was sent, when, by whom, and what came back.
Files are natural audit objects. You can archive each one unchanged, hash it and attach it to a payroll run. When someone asks what you sent for a given month, you open the file. That is hard to argue with.
API calls leave a trail only if you build one. Log the full request and response, the caller identity, a correlation ID and a timestamp. Store them in a form that cannot be quietly edited. Done well, this is more granular than files, because you see each record’s individual history. Done badly, you have application logs that rotate away.
Whichever you pick, one rule holds. Every record needs a stable identifier shared by both sides. Without it, reconciliation turns into guesswork.
Effort   SFTP is cheaper to start. Most payroll providers in Italy already support it. Your team writes an exporter, an importer and some monitoring. The hard part is the file specification and the error handling around it.
A REST integration costs more upfront. You need authentication, versioning, retry logic, rate handling and a sandbox for testing. The provider must also offer a stable API, and many local providers do not. If they do not, you will build the API yourself on top of their files, and then you carry both costs.
Ongoing effort differs too. File formats drift slowly and break loudly. APIs drift through version changes and break in subtle ways. Plan for a named owner on each side either way.
A practical recommendation   For a mid-size platform, a hybrid is usually right.
Use SFTP, or a file-style batch, for monthly payroll inputs and payslip returns. The cut-off model fits, and the archive doubles as your audit record. Use REST for event data: hires, terminations, status checks and confirmations. Fast feedback saves manual follow-up. Put one canonical data model behind both. The transport should be a detail, not a design. Require idempotency, record identifiers and a rejection report in both channels. If your team is small and volume is modest, start with SFTP alone. Add REST for the flows where waiting hurts most. Do not start with a full API program unless the provider can support it properly.
Questions to ask any provider   How do you signal a rejected record, and how fast? What happens to a file delivered twice? Can you show the audit trail for a single employee change? How do you handle corrections after a payroll run is closed? Who owns the specification, and how are changes announced? The answers tell you more than the transport label does.
Partnership teams that want to see how this works in practice can request the data-exchange specification.

## Service credits in ICP contracts: how they are triggered and calculated
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/service-credits-icp-contracts-faq.html
Summary: A plain FAQ for partnership and payroll teams on how service credits are triggered, measured and calculated in in-country partner (ICP) contracts.
Service credits are the usual remedy when an in-country partner (ICP) misses an agreed service level. They are simple in principle. They go wrong in the details. This FAQ covers how credits are triggered and how they are calculated, so your team can write clauses that work in practice.
This article does not quote rates or thresholds. Those belong in your own contract and depend on your volumes and risk.
What is a service credit?   A service credit is a reduction in the fees you pay the ICP. It applies when the ICP fails to meet a defined service level. It is not a penalty and it is not damages. It is a pre-agreed price adjustment for a known type of failure.
Most contracts say credits are the sole remedy for the specific service level breach. Check this wording. If credits are the sole remedy, you cannot also claim damages for the same event. If they are not, say so clearly.
What triggers a credit?   A credit is triggered when a measured service level falls below its target in a defined period. Three things must be clear in the contract:
The metric. For example, payroll inputs processed by the cut-off, statutory filings submitted on time, or queries answered within the response window. The target. The level the ICP promises to meet. The measurement period. The window in which performance is counted, such as a payroll cycle or a calendar month. If any of these is vague, the trigger is vague. Disputes follow.
Who measures performance?   The contract should name the source of truth. Good options are timestamps in a shared system, submission receipts from the authority, or a log both parties can read. Weak options are one party’s internal report that the other cannot check.
Agree the data fields up front. Agree how each event is time-stamped and in which time zone. Many credit disputes are really data disputes.
Does the ICP have to report breaches?   It should. A good clause requires the ICP to report any miss within a set time after the period closes. It also requires a short root-cause note. Do not rely on the client to find every miss.
Also decide what happens if the ICP does not report. A common answer is that the credit applies automatically once the platform shows the miss in the shared data.
What are the usual exclusions?   Credits normally do not apply when the miss is caused by something outside the ICP’s control. Typical exclusions are:
Late or incorrect inputs from the platform or the client. Missing documents from the employee. Outages at an authority or a bank. Changes requested by the platform after the cut-off. Keep the list short and specific. A long, loose list lets the ICP excuse almost any miss. Also require the ICP to show that the exclusion caused the failure.
How is a credit calculated?   There are three common models.
Percentage of fees. The credit is a percentage of the fees for the affected period or service. It is easy to compute. It scales with the size of the account.
Fixed amount per event. Each miss costs the ICP a set sum. This works for discrete failures, such as one missed filing.
Tiered credits. The credit grows as performance gets worse. A small shortfall gives a small credit. A severe shortfall gives a larger one.
Whatever model you pick, write the formula in the contract with a worked example. State the base the percentage applies to. Is it the monthly fee, the fee for the affected service line, or the fee for the affected employees only? The base changes the result a lot.
Is there a cap?   Most contracts cap total credits in a period. The cap is usually a share of the fees for that period. A cap protects the ICP. It also tells you the maximum value of the remedy.
If the cap is low, credits will not change behaviour. Pair credits with a right to terminate for repeated or severe failures. Credits alone rarely fix a weak partner.
How are credits applied?   Two methods are common. The credit is deducted from the next invoice, or the ICP pays it out as a refund. Deduction is faster and avoids a separate payment flow. State a deadline for applying the credit. State what happens at contract end if credits are still owed.
What about repeated misses?   Single misses are manageable. Patterns are the real risk. Add a clause that treats repeated misses of the same metric as a material issue. It should trigger a remediation plan, a review meeting and, if needed, an exit right.
How do you dispute a credit?   Give each side a short window to raise a dispute. Name the evidence that counts. Set an escalation path with named roles. Keep the process light. A heavy process means nobody uses it.
A practical checklist   Each metric has a clear definition, target and period. The source of truth is shared and both sides can read it. Exclusions are few and specific. The formula is written out with an example. The cap and the sole-remedy wording are explicit. Reporting duties and deadlines are set. Repeated failure leads to a defined escalation. Credits work when both sides can see the same data and agree what it means. That is a data-exchange question as much as a legal one.
Partnership teams can request the data-exchange specification.

## Sick leave in Italy: employee support FAQ
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/sick-leave-italy-employee-support-faq.html
Summary: Plain answers for EOR and payroll support teams on Italian sick leave: medical certificates, pay during sickness and the checks employers can request.
Sick leave questions reach support teams fast. Employees want to know what to send, who pays and what happens if someone checks. This FAQ gives short answers you can adapt for your own help centre. It stays at the level of process. Exact amounts and durations depend on the national collective agreement (CCNL) that applies to the employee, so your data should come from the contract, not from a general rule.
Certificates   Does the employee send a paper certificate? No. In Italy the doctor issues the medical certificate electronically and sends it to the national social security body, INPS. The employee does not carry a paper copy to the employer in the normal case.
How does the employer get the certificate? The employer reads it through the INPS channel, using the protocol number of the certificate. The employee should give that protocol number if the employer asks for it. Your platform can store the protocol number against the absence record.
What must the employee do on the day of illness? Tell the employer without delay, using the channel the company has set. Many contracts and company rules say how and by when. The employee should also ask the doctor for the certificate right away and keep the protocol number.
What if the employee forgets to notify the employer? The absence can be treated as unjustified. That can lead to disciplinary steps. Support teams should say clearly that notice to the employer and the certificate are two separate duties.
Can a certificate be corrected or extended? Yes. If the illness continues, the doctor issues a continuation certificate. If there is an error, the doctor can cancel or correct it. The employee should ask the doctor, not the employer, to fix it.
What about hospital stays or work accidents? These follow separate rules and separate channels. Work accidents and occupational illness are handled differently from ordinary sickness. Route these cases to a specialist rather than answering from this FAQ.
Pay during sickness   Who pays the employee? Two sources can be involved. INPS pays a sickness allowance for many categories of employees. The employer then pays an integration or the full amount, depending on the CCNL. In practice the employer often advances the payment through payroll and recovers the INPS part.
Is the first part of the absence paid? Often there is a short waiting period where INPS does not pay. In that period the CCNL decides whether the employer pays anything. Do not give one answer for all employees. Look up the contract.
Does the amount depend on the contract? Yes. The CCNL sets the percentage of pay, the length of the paid period and any rules on integration. Seniority and category can also change the result. Keep these values in a verified table per CCNL, with the source and the date you checked it.
Is there a limit to how long the job is protected? Yes. The CCNL sets a protected period for illness, often called the comporto. During it the employer cannot dismiss the employee for the illness. After it ends, the employer has more options, and the employee may ask for unpaid leave if the contract allows it. Support should escalate any case near the end of this period.
Does sickness affect holidays and other pay items? It can. Some items depend on attendance, such as certain allowances. The CCNL and company rules decide. Payroll should flag these items in the payslip notes so the employee is not surprised.
Checks   Can the employer ask for a check? Yes. The employer can request a medical check, called a visita fiscale, through INPS. A doctor then visits the employee at home during set hours of availability.
What does the employee need to do? Be at the address on the certificate during the availability hours. If the address is different from the home address, the doctor must write it on the certificate. If the employee has to leave for a medical visit, tests or another serious reason, they should be able to prove it afterwards.
What if the employee is not at home? An absent employee without a valid reason can lose part of the allowance and face disciplinary action. A missed visit is recorded and the employee is usually asked to give a justification. Rules on exemptions exist for some conditions, so support should not promise either outcome.
Can the employer check on its own? Not freely. Italian law limits how an employer may monitor sick employees. The official medical check is the normal route. Support should discourage managers from calling the employee repeatedly or using investigators without legal advice.
What a good support answer looks like   State the duty: notify the employer, get the certificate, keep the protocol number. State who pays, and say the split depends on the CCNL. State the check rules and the availability duty. Give a clear escalation path for long absences, accidents and disputes. Cite the contract source, never a guess. A clear process lowers ticket volume and avoids payroll errors. It also protects the employee, who often writes in when unwell and needs a short, correct answer.
Partnership teams that want to connect absence data to their own platforms can request the data-exchange specification.

## Tax wedge measures in the payroll engine: how the non-taxable sum and extra deduction work month by month
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/tax-wedge-payroll-engine-monthly-application.html
Summary: How a payroll engine should apply the Italian non-taxable sum and the extra deduction each month, with income bands, rates and a data checklist.
Italy’s tax wedge measures change net pay for employees in specific income ranges. For a payroll platform, the hard part is not the rule. It is applying the rule month by month while the annual income is still an estimate.
This article explains the two measures, how they are built, and what your engine needs to handle them.
The two measures   There are two separate mechanisms. They work differently and they apply to different income ranges.
The non-taxable sum. This is a share of employment income that is not taxed. The share depends on the income band:
Up to 8,500 EUR: 7.1% of employment income. From 8,500 to 15,000 EUR: 5.3% of employment income. From 15,000 to 20,000 EUR: 4.8% of employment income. The extra deduction. This is a tax deduction on top of the ordinary ones. It is 1,000 EUR per year for income from 20,000 to 32,000 EUR. Between 32,000 and 40,000 EUR it decreases until it reaches zero.
The two do not overlap in the bands above. An employee sits in the non-taxable sum range or in the extra deduction range, depending on annual employment income.
Why the monthly run is the problem   Both measures depend on annual employment income. Your engine runs every month. So the engine must answer one question each period: what is this employee’s expected annual income?
The answer drives everything. It picks the band. It sets the rate or the deduction amount. A raise, a bonus, a new contract or an unpaid leave can move the employee into a different band during the year.
A practical approach:
Project annual employment income from the contract and the payments already made. Select the band from that projection. Compute the annual benefit. Spread it across the pay periods, net of what was already given. Recompute when the projection changes. The key point is step four. Each month the engine should apply the benefit due to date, not a fixed slice. This keeps the cumulative figure right when the projection moves.
Handling band changes   Three cases cause most errors.
Mid-year hires. The employee has no earlier payslips with you. The projection must come from the contract. If they worked elsewhere earlier in the year, you need that data, or the benefit may be applied twice or not at all.
Variable pay. A bonus can push annual income over a threshold. For the non-taxable sum, a higher band means a different rate. For the extra deduction, crossing the upper range means the amount shrinks. Your engine should show the employee what changed and why.
Employees near the edges. Someone close to a threshold may switch band after a single payment. Flag these cases in the run, so a reviewer sees them before payslips go out.
Year-end adjustment   Projections are never exact. The year-end adjustment closes the gap. If the engine gave too much, it recovers the difference. If it gave too little, it pays the rest.
Good engines make this adjustment small by recomputing early and often. They also keep a record of each projection used. That record lets support teams explain a payslip without rebuilding the calculation by hand.
What to store for each employee   To run these measures reliably, keep these fields per employee:
Projected annual employment income and the date of each revision. The band selected and the rule version used. Benefit given to date and benefit due to date. Income from earlier employers in the same year, when available. A source reference and a verification date for each rate and threshold. The last item matters. The figures in this article come from a secondary source. Before you configure production rules, check them against the official text and record the date you did so. Rules for these measures are set year by year, so version them and never overwrite old ones.
What to ask your provider   If you use a local partner for Italy, ask direct questions:
How do you project annual income, and how often do you revise it? How do you treat mid-year hires with earlier income? Can you send the band, the projection and the benefit to date with every payroll file? How do you version the rules and show the source for each figure? A partner who answers these clearly will save your support team many tickets.
Partnership teams can request the data-exchange specification to see the exact fields we send for each payroll run.

## The extra 1% employee contribution above the threshold: when it triggers and how it is reconciled
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/italy-extra-1-percent-employee-contribution-threshold.html
Summary: How the extra 1% employee pension contribution in Italy triggers above the pay threshold, and how payroll teams reconcile it at year end.
Italian payroll has a small rule that causes a large share of reconciliation questions. Above a pay threshold, the employee owes an extra 1% social security contribution. It is easy to miss in a platform that was built around flat rates.
This article explains when it triggers, who bears it, and how to reconcile it at year end.
What the rule is   The employee already pays a standard pension contribution on gross pay. Above a set threshold, an additional 1% applies to the part of pay that exceeds it. It is charged to the employee. It does not change the employer’s contribution.
The extra 1% applies only to the excess. It is not a new rate on the whole salary. A common error is to apply it to total pay once the threshold is crossed.
The threshold   The figures we use come from a secondary source, so confirm them against the official INPS circular before you hard-code them.
Annual threshold: 56,224 EUR Monthly threshold: 4,685 EUR The monthly figure is the practical trigger for payroll. Each payslip is tested against it. The annual figure is the reference for the year-end check.
When it triggers   The trigger is the contribution base for the period, not net pay and not the headline salary in the contract. Check these points:
Use the right base. The base is the pay subject to social security. It includes recurring and one-off items that are contributory. Items that are exempt from contributions do not count. Test every period. A month that includes a bonus, an overtime peak or a payout of accrued items may cross the monthly threshold even when base salary sits below it. Do not assume a steady state. An employee on a salary close to the monthly threshold can cross it in some months and not in others. Your engine must evaluate each pay run on its own. Watch part-year employment. Joiners and leavers have a shorter year. Decide how your platform treats the threshold for a partial period, and document that choice for the local payroll provider. If your platform stores a single annual salary and divides it by twelve or more, you will miss the months where variable pay pushes the base over the line.
How it shows on the payslip   The extra 1% should appear as part of the employee’s social security deduction for that month. In practice, it adds to the withheld amount only in months where the base is above the monthly threshold.
For platform teams, this means the deduction line cannot be a fixed percentage of gross. It needs a conditional component that depends on the base and the threshold.
A clear display helps the employee. A separate line, or at least a visible breakdown in the payslip detail, reduces support tickets from employees who see a deduction that changes from month to month.
Year-end reconciliation   Monthly testing is an approximation of an annual rule. At year end, the total extra contribution withheld should match what is due on the annual base above the annual threshold. The two can differ for several reasons.
Timing of variable pay. A bonus paid in one month is tested against that month’s threshold. Spread over the year, the same pay might not have crossed the annual figure at all, or might have crossed it by a different amount. Late adjustments. Retroactive pay, corrections and back-dated changes can shift the contribution base into a different period. Partial years. Joiners, leavers and unpaid leave change both the base and how the thresholds apply. Multiple payers. If the employee had income from another employer in the same year, the picture is incomplete from your side. Your reconciliation can only cover the pay you processed. A workable year-end routine looks like this:
Sum the contribution base for each employee across all pay runs in the year. Compute the amount above the annual threshold. Compute the extra 1% on that amount. Compare it with the total extra contribution actually withheld. Flag every employee where the two differ, and pass the differences to the local payroll provider with the supporting pay run data. The provider decides how to settle the difference in the final pay run of the year or in the first pay run after the closing. Your platform should not settle it silently. Record the difference, the reason and the period it relates to.
Controls worth building   A rule test that checks the deduction in a month just below, at and just above the monthly threshold. A year-end report listing each employee’s annual base, the annual threshold, the expected extra amount and the withheld amount. An alert for employees whose base is near the threshold, so payroll operations can review before a large one-off payment. A stored source and date for the threshold values. Thresholds are updated, and your records should show which values applied to which pay run. What partnership teams should agree with their provider   Which base is used for the test, and how exempt items are excluded. Whether the monthly test and the annual check are both run, and by whom. How differences are communicated: format, timing and who approves the correction. How partial-year employees are handled. Who owns the threshold update when the official figures change. Put these answers in writing. Most disputes about this contribution come from two parties that each assumed the other one handled the annual check.
Summary   The extra 1% is small per employee but systematic. It depends on the contribution base, it is tested monthly, and it is checked against the annual threshold at year end. Build the conditional deduction, keep the audit trail, and run the annual comparison for every employee.

## The Italian payroll compliance calendar for 2026: filings that affect platforms
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/italian-payroll-compliance-calendar-2026.html
Summary: A month-by-month view of the 2026 Italian payroll filings that matter to EOR and payroll platforms: CU in March, April and October, and the 770 in November.
Italian payroll does not run on a single deadline. It runs on a set of filings, and some of them depend on data your platform holds or feeds to a local partner. This guide covers the year-end certification and annual declaration dates that we have verified for 2026. It is written for partnership, operations and payroll managers at global EOR and payroll platforms.
A note on sources first. The dates below come from a secondary source, not from the tax authority itself. Treat them as a planning baseline and confirm them against official notices before you commit customers to a date.
What the filings are   The Certificazione Unica, or CU, is the annual certificate of income paid and tax withheld. The employer issues it to each worker and also reports it to the Agenzia delle Entrate, the Italian tax authority. The Modello 770 is the annual withholding tax return. It summarises what the withholding agent paid and withheld during the year.
Both documents are built from payroll data over the whole year. If a worker moved between entities, changed contract type or left mid-year, the quality of that history decides how clean the filing is.
The calendar, month by month   January and February   There is no verified filing date for these months in our data set. Use them for preparation. Close out the prior year, check worker records and reconcile payroll runs against what will appear on each certificate.
March 2026   This is the busiest month for platforms.
16 March 2026: deadline to deliver the CU to employees. 16 March 2026: deadline to send the CU to the Agenzia delle Entrate for the same population. Both dates fall on the same day. That leaves no gap between delivering certificates to workers and reporting them to the authority. Any correction found after delivery means a reissued certificate and a corrected submission.
For a platform, the practical point is data readiness. Your local payroll provider needs final figures before this date. A late correction from your side is the most common reason a CU has to be redone.
April 2026   30 April 2026: deadline to send the CU to the Agenzia delle Entrate for self-employed workers. This matters if your platform also supports contractors alongside employees in Italy. Self-employed income follows a separate track from employee income. Keep the two populations apart in your data exports, so each one lands in the right filing.
May to September   No verified filing date for these months is in our data set. Use this window to fix issues found during the spring filings and to prepare the second half of the year.
October 2026   31 October 2026: deadline to send the CU to the Agenzia delle Entrate for the exempt category. This is a later, narrower deadline. It covers income that is exempt, and it sits well after the main March date. It is easy to miss because it falls outside the main year-end rush. Check whether any of your Italian workers fall into this category and assign an owner for the filing.
The same date, 31 October, is also the nominal deadline for the Modello 770. In 2026 it falls on a Saturday.
November 2026   2 November 2026: the Modello 770 deadline, moved from Saturday 31 October to the next working day. The 770 is a summary return. It depends on the same withholding data that fed the CU. If the CU data was right, the 770 is mostly a matter of assembly. If the CU needed late corrections, check that the 770 reflects them.
December 2026   No verified filing date for this month is in our data set. Plan the handover of final-year data and start the next cycle.
What this means for platform operations   Three habits reduce risk.
Work backwards from 16 March 2026. Your internal data freeze has to come before it, with time for review. Separate populations. Employees, self-employed workers and exempt income each have their own date. Tag workers by category from the start. Treat the weekend rule as real. When a deadline falls on a Saturday, it moves to the next working day. In 2026 that is how the 770 lands on 2 November. Do not build your calendar on the nominal date. What we have not covered   This calendar lists only the dates we have verified. Other recurring obligations exist across the year, such as monthly payroll and contribution payments. We have not included them here, because we have no verified dates for them in this data set. We will add them once each one is confirmed with its source.
