## The monthly evidence pack your Italian in-country partner should send you
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/monthly-evidence-pack-italian-icp.html
Summary: What a global EOR or payroll platform should receive from its Italian in-country partner each month, and why a fixed evidence pack protects your operations.
Your platform promises clients a compliant payroll in Italy. You do not run that payroll yourself. Your in-country partner (ICP) does. So the question for partnership and operations teams is simple: what proof do you get each month that the work was done correctly?
A good ICP does not wait to be asked. It sends the same evidence pack every month, in the same structure, on a fixed schedule. This article lists what that pack should contain and why each item matters.
Why a fixed pack matters   Without a defined pack, evidence arrives by email, in different formats, when someone remembers. Your finance team chases. Your support team cannot answer client questions. Your auditors ask for documents that nobody can find.
A fixed pack changes this. Everything is predictable. Anyone on your team can open the folder for a given month and see what happened.
The documents   Payroll calculation file   This is the base of the pack. It shows, for each worker, gross pay, deductions, employer cost and net pay. It should match the figures in your own ledger line by line. If it does not, you want to know before the client does.
Ask for it in a machine-readable format as well as a readable one. Your team should be able to reconcile it without retyping anything.
Payslips   Every worker needs a payslip. The pack should include a copy of each one issued, or a clear link to where they are stored. Your platform should be able to confirm that every active worker received one.
Check that the payslip shows the right collective agreement and job level. Errors here are common and they cause disputes later.
Proof of tax and social contribution payments   Payroll is not finished when the calculation is done. The employer must pay withholding tax and social contributions to the authorities. The pack should include proof that these payments were made, and the matching filings.
This is the item that matters most for risk. A late or missing payment creates liability that can come back to your client and to you. Ask for the payment receipts, not a statement that payment was made.
Net pay confirmation   The pack should show that net salaries were actually paid to workers. A bank confirmation or payment batch report is enough. It closes the loop between the calculation and the money.
Variance report   Show what changed against the previous month. New hires, leavers, salary changes, unpaid leave, overtime, bonuses and corrections. This is where your operations team spends its time, because most questions from clients are about changes.
A short note from the ICP on each material change saves many emails.
Headcount and status list   A current list of workers, with start dates, contract type and status. It lets you check that your own records and the ICP’s records agree. Mismatches in headcount are a quiet source of billing errors.
Open items and exceptions log   Every month has loose ends. A missing document from a worker. A pending authority reply. A correction waiting for approval. The ICP should list them, name an owner and give a target date for each. An empty log is fine. A missing log is not.
Document and authority correspondence   Copies of notices received from Italian authorities or institutions about your workers or your client entities. These need fast attention. They should reach you in the pack at the latest, and sooner if urgent.
How to ask for it   Put the pack into your service agreement. Define the list of documents, the format, the delivery deadline and who receives it. Add what happens if it is late.
Agree on naming and folder rules. Agree on how corrections are labelled so you can tell a revised file from the original.
Treat personal data with care. The pack contains pay data for named people. Use a secure transfer channel, not plain email attachments, and limit who can open the files.
What you do with it   Once the pack arrives, run the same checks each month. Reconcile totals to your ledger. Confirm payslip count against headcount. Match payment proofs to the calculation. Review the variance report and the open items log.
Keep the packs. They are your audit trail. If a client, an auditor or an authority asks what happened in a given month, you can answer in minutes.
A sign of a mature partner   A mature ICP treats the pack as part of the service, not as an extra. It delivers on time, flags problems before you find them and does not need reminders. If your partner resists a fixed pack, that tells you something about how the rest of the work is run.
Partnership teams that want to see how this pack can be exchanged as structured data are welcome to request the data-exchange specification.

## Trattamento integrativo: when Italian payroll adds it
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/trattamento-integrativo-italian-payroll-eligibility-monthly-application.html
Summary: How Italian payroll applies the trattamento integrativo: who may get it, what operators must check each month, and what to pass between platforms.
The trattamento integrativo is a small payment that Italian payroll can add to an employee’s net pay. It is easy to miss. It is also easy to apply when it should not apply. For a global EOR or payroll platform, both errors reach the employee and the employer. This article looks at it from the operator’s side: who qualifies, how the monthly run handles it, and what your platform needs to hand over.
What it is   The trattamento integrativo is a benefit for employees with low income. The reference figure we use is up to 1,200 EUR per year, for employees with income up to 15,000 EUR, and subject to conditions. That is the whole headline. The details sit in the conditions.
The source for these figures is a secondary one. Treat the figures as a guide for planning and confirm them against the current official rules before you build logic around them.
Why the operator cares   The payment is not a request from the employee. Payroll is expected to look at the position and apply it when the conditions are met. If payroll skips it, the employee loses money during the year. If payroll applies it and the conditions were not met, the amount may have to be recovered later. Neither outcome is good for a service whose value is that payroll just works.
For a foreign company hiring in Italy, this is a typical surprise. Their home payroll has no equivalent. The employee earns a modest salary, sees an extra line on the payslip, and the client asks what it is.
Eligibility from the operator’s view   The test is about the employee’s income level and their tax position. Three things matter in practice.
Expected annual income. The ceiling is 15,000 EUR. Payroll has to estimate income for the year, not just look at one month. A part-time contract, an unpaid leave period or a mid-year start all change that estimate.
Tax position. The payment is linked to the employee’s income tax situation. An employee with no tax due in the year is treated differently from one with tax due. Your payroll provider’s rules decide how this is read. You should not guess it from the gross salary alone.
Other income. An employee may have more than one employer, or other income, during the year. Payroll sees only its own employment unless told otherwise. This is the main source of wrong results.
Because the figure is conditional, a simple salary threshold is not enough. Do not build a rule in your platform that says: salary below the ceiling, so the benefit applies. Let the Italian payroll engine decide, and make sure it has the facts it needs.
Monthly application   The benefit is applied through the monthly payroll run. The yearly maximum is the cap. The monthly amount is a share of what the employee is expected to receive over the year, adjusted as the year goes on.
What this means for your process:
Each run should recalculate the position, not copy the previous month. A change in contract hours, pay or start date can change the monthly amount. At year end, payroll compares what was paid with what was due. A difference can show up as an adjustment. Operators should expect the line to appear, disappear and change size during the year. That is normal behaviour, not an error. The error is when nobody can explain why.
What can go wrong   Mid-year hires. The employee joins and payroll has no income history. The estimate rests on the new contract alone. If the employee had income earlier in the year, the estimate is too low.
Unreported second jobs. Payroll applies the benefit. The employee’s total income is above the ceiling. The mismatch appears later.
Variable pay. Bonuses and overtime push income up. A benefit applied in earlier months may no longer fit. Payroll must be told about expected variable pay as early as possible.
Gross-to-net quotes. If you quote net salary to a client or candidate, state clearly whether the quote includes the benefit. A quote that includes it can be wrong later if the conditions stop being met.
What to pass between platforms   If your platform sits in front of Italian payroll, the data you send decides the outcome. At minimum, send:
contract start date and end date working hours and gross pay expected variable pay a declaration from the employee about other employment or income in the year any change to these items, with its effective date Also agree on what comes back. Payroll should return whether the benefit was applied, the amount for the period, and the amount to date. That lets your support team answer questions without opening a ticket with the payroll provider.
A practical checklist   Do not hard-code the 1,200 EUR figure or the 15,000 EUR ceiling. Keep them as data with a source and a review date. Show the line on the payslip preview, with a short plain explanation for the client. Flag employees near the income ceiling. These are the cases most likely to change during the year. Ask new hires about other income at onboarding, and again when pay changes. Keep an audit trail of what was told to payroll and when. The trattamento integrativo is small compared with other payroll items. It still generates many questions, because it is conditional and because it moves during the year. A clean data flow removes most of them.
Partnership teams that want to align on this can request our data-exchange specification.

## Validating the Italian codice fiscale before onboarding
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/validating-italian-codice-fiscale-before-onboarding.html
Summary: How the Italian codice fiscale is built and how its check character works, so your platform can reject bad IDs before a worker is onboarded.
A wrong codice fiscale causes trouble late. Payroll fails, a registration is rejected, a contract has to be reissued. Most of these errors can be caught at the first form field. The code has a fixed structure and a check character. Both can be tested in your own system before anything is sent on.
This article explains what to test and in what order.
What the code contains   The codice fiscale is a string of letters and digits. It is built from personal data, not issued at random. Each block has a defined role.
Surname block: consonants taken from the surname, then vowels if there are too few. Padding is used for very short surnames. Given name block: consonants from the given name, with a special rule when there are many consonants. Vowels fill the gap if there are too few. Birth year: the last two digits of the year. Birth month: a single letter that maps to a month. The mapping is a fixed table. Birth day and sex: the day of birth, with a fixed amount added for women. A day value above the normal range of a month therefore signals a female holder. Place code: a letter followed by digits. It identifies the Italian municipality of birth, or the foreign state for people born abroad. Check character: a final letter computed from everything before it. This means you can compare the code against the data you already collect. If the form says the worker is male and the day block says female, one of them is wrong.
Step one: shape check   Start with a pattern test. It is cheap and removes most typos.
Normalise the input. Remove spaces and convert to upper case. Check the length against the expected fixed length. Check that each position holds a letter or a digit as the structure requires. Check that the month letter belongs to the allowed set. Check that the day block falls in a valid range for either sex. A failed shape check should return a specific message. “The month letter is not valid” helps the user more than “Invalid ID”.
Step two: the check character   The last character is a checksum. It protects against single-character errors and most swaps.
The method is simple. Take the leading characters. Split them by position into two groups: odd positions and even positions, counting from the start. Each character is converted to a number, but the conversion table differs by group. Digits and letters both have entries in each table. For the even group the value is mostly the position of the character in its own set. For the odd group the values come from a fixed lookup table that looks scrambled. You need the official table, so copy it carefully and test it.
Add all the converted values. Divide the total by the size of the alphabet and keep the remainder. Map that remainder to a letter, where zero is the first letter of the alphabet. That letter must equal the final character of the submitted code.
If it does not match, reject the input. Do not try to correct it.
Step three: cross-check with form data   A code can pass the checksum and still belong to someone else. Use the data you hold to catch that.
Rebuild the surname and given name blocks from the submitted names and compare. Compare the year, month and day blocks with the date of birth. Compare the sex implied by the day block with the declared sex. Check the place code against your list of municipalities and states. Treat a mismatch as a warning for review, not always as a hard stop. Names with accents, double surnames and transliterated names from other alphabets can produce legitimate differences. Let a human confirm and log the decision.
Shared codes and substituted digits   Two people can produce the same base code. Italy resolves this by replacing some digits with letters from a fixed substitution table. The result is still valid and the check character still applies. A strict digit-only pattern will wrongly reject these codes. Your shape test must allow the substituted letters in the numeric positions, and your cross-checks must reverse the substitution before comparing.
This is the most common bug in home-built validators. Test with such a case before release.
Foreign nationals   Workers who come to Italy from abroad often have a code too. It is built the same way, with a state code in place of a municipality code. It may be issued before the person arrives. Do not assume a holder was born in Italy. Do not require a municipality from the Italian list when the place block points to a foreign state.
What a valid code does not prove   A code that passes every test is well formed. It is not proof that the code is registered, or that it belongs to the person in front of you. Validation at source reduces bad data. It does not replace identity checks. Keep the two steps separate in your onboarding flow, and record which one failed.
Practical rules for your platform   Validate on entry, not at export. Store the normalised value only. Return a precise reason for each failure. Keep the lookup tables in versioned configuration, with a test suite that covers odd cases. Log the validation result with the input data version. Small checks at the form save large corrections later. A clean code on day one means fewer rejected filings and fewer payroll corrections.
Partnership teams that want to align field formats and validation rules with ours can request the data-exchange specification.

## Volume tiers in ICP contracts: how headcount discounts are usually set
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/volume-tiers-icp-contracts-faq.html
Summary: How headcount-based discounts are usually structured in in-country partner contracts, and which terms global EOR and payroll platforms should settle early.
Global EOR and payroll platforms often ask us how volume discounts work in contracts with an in-country partner (ICP). There is no universal formula. There are common patterns, though. This FAQ covers the ones we see most and the points that cause disputes later.
What is a volume tier?   A volume tier is a price band tied to the number of employees the platform places with the ICP in a country. As headcount rises, the fee per employee falls. The aim is to reward the platform for scale and to give the ICP predictable revenue.
How are tiers usually set?   Most contracts follow the same logic.
The ICP sets a base fee per employee per month for the lowest band. Each higher band has a lower fee per employee. Band edges are tied to round headcount numbers that both sides can track easily. The discount is steeper at the start and flatter later, because the ICP’s fixed costs are covered early. The ICP’s cost structure drives this. Onboarding, payroll runs, statutory filings and support all have a fixed part and a variable part. The fixed part is spread across more people as the count grows. The variable part does not shrink much. So the discount has a floor, and a good partner will tell you where it is.
Marginal or whole-book pricing?   This is the most important choice in the contract.
In marginal pricing, each band applies only to the employees inside it. The first block of employees is charged at the top rate. The next block is charged at the next rate, and so on. It is simple to audit and cheap for the ICP, so the discounts are usually smaller.
In whole-book pricing, once you cross a threshold, the lower rate applies to every employee. It is generous to the platform. ICPs usually offer it with a higher base fee or a longer commitment to offset the cost.
Ask which model is used before you compare quotes. Two offers with the same headline rates can differ a lot in what you pay.
What counts as headcount?   Agree on the definition in writing. Common options:
Active employees on payroll at month end. Average active employees during the month. Employees paid at any point in the month. Edge cases matter. Leavers mid-month, employees on unpaid leave, and people in a notice period can all move a count over a threshold. Contractors or secondees, where the ICP supports them, may be counted differently or priced separately. State how each case is treated.
Which period decides the tier?   There are three typical approaches.
Monthly: the tier follows the current month’s headcount. Fair, but the rate can move back and forth. Rolling average: the tier follows an average over a set window. This smooths seasonal swings. Annual commitment: the platform commits to a volume and gets a fixed tier for the year, with a true-up at the end. Platforms with steady growth tend to prefer rolling averages. Platforms with a pipeline they can forecast may prefer a commitment, since it locks in a lower rate from the start.
What happens if headcount drops?   Discounts are easy to give and hard to take back. Contracts should say what happens when volume falls below a band. Typical answers: the rate steps up at the next review, the platform has a grace period, or a minimum monthly fee applies. A minimum fee protects the ICP but can hurt a platform entering a new country with few employees. Negotiate the grace period and the review dates early.
Per country or across the whole relationship?   Some ICPs operate in several countries or have a single master agreement. Platforms then ask whether headcount can be pooled. Pooling helps the platform reach better tiers. ICPs often resist it when costs and local rules differ a lot by country. A middle path is a shared tier for the commercial relationship with country-specific base fees.
What else belongs in the tier schedule?   Which services the per-employee fee covers, and which are charged on top. How and when tier changes take effect. Who reports headcount, in what format, and how disputes are resolved. Audit rights over the headcount data. Currency and indexation of fees. The reporting point deserves attention. Tiers only work if both sides see the same numbers. A shared data format and a monthly reconciliation remove most arguments before they start.
A practical way to approach the talk   Bring your growth forecast, your expected mix of countries, and your preferred counting rule. Ask the ICP for the base fee, the band edges and the pricing model in a single table. Test the table against a low case and a high case for your headcount. If the result is not stable, adjust the bands before signing.
Partnership teams that want to see how headcount and service data can be exchanged with us, request the data-exchange specification.

## What a Meaningful SLA for an Italian ICP Looks Like
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/meaningful-sla-italian-icp-payroll.html
Summary: Payroll accuracy is not an SLA. Here are the measurable service levels a global EOR or payroll platform should ask of its Italian in-country partner.
Most payroll SLAs say the same thing. The partner will process payroll accurately. That sentence cannot be measured, cannot be audited and cannot be enforced.
If you run partnerships or operations at a global EOR or payroll platform, you need more than that from your Italian in-country provider (ICP). Accuracy is an outcome. An SLA should describe the behaviours that produce it, and the points where it fails.
This article sets out what to measure, and why each item matters in Italy.
Why accuracy alone fails   Accuracy is usually reported after the fact. It is a lagging figure. By the time you see it, an employee has been underpaid or a contribution has been filed wrongly.
It is also hard to define. Is a payslip accurate if the net pay is right but the contribution breakdown is wrong? Is it accurate if the figures are right but they arrive after the pay date? A single accuracy number hides these differences.
Italy adds complexity. Pay depends on the national collective agreement (CCNL) that applies to the employee. Contributions follow social security rules that change. Local and sector rules affect what goes on the payslip. A provider can be accurate on average and still wrong where it counts for your client.
The SLA components that matter   1. Input cut-off and confirmation   Define the date by which your platform sends changes. Then define how fast the ICP confirms that it received and validated them.
Measure the time from submission to confirmation. Measure how many input files are rejected and why. A partner that accepts bad data silently is worse than one that rejects it loudly.
2. Pre-payroll review delivery   The ICP should send a draft payroll for review before the final run. The SLA should state when it arrives and what it contains: gross to net, employer cost, and a list of changes against the previous period.
Measure on-time delivery of the draft. Measure how many items were flagged by the ICP before you found them yourself. That second measure shows whether the partner is actually checking.
3. Final file and payslip delivery   This is the date that employees feel. Define the deadline for the final payroll file, the payslips and the payment instructions, all in the format you agreed.
Track misses as a count and as a pattern. One late delivery is an incident. A repeated late delivery on the same step is a process fault.
4. Statutory filing and payment timeliness   Italian employers owe social contributions and tax withholdings on set deadlines. A late filing creates penalties and exposure for your client, even if the employee was paid correctly.
The SLA should require proof of each filing and payment, delivered on a stated schedule. Ask for the receipt, not a statement that it was done.
5. Error classification and correction time   Split errors by type: calculation, data, rule interpretation, filing. Each type has a different cause and a different fix.
Set a correction time for each severity level. An error that affects net pay needs a faster response than a cosmetic issue on a report. Measure time to acknowledge, time to correct and time to confirm the fix with evidence.
Also measure repeat errors. The same fault twice should trigger a root cause review, not another correction.
6. Rule change notification   CCNL renewals and contribution changes alter payroll. Your platform needs advance notice, not a surprise in the draft.
Define how early the ICP warns you of a change, in what form, and what the impact is on the affected employees. Measure whether notice arrived before the change took effect.
7. Reconciliation and reporting   The ICP should deliver a reconciliation between payroll, the general ledger input and the filings. Define the format and the deadline.
Measure unreconciled items at close and how long they stay open.
8. Support responsiveness   Define response and resolution targets for queries from your team and from employees. Separate urgent pay-date issues from routine questions. Measure both, and report them on a regular schedule.
9. Audit access   You need to see how a number was produced. The SLA should guarantee access to calculation logic, source documents and change history for any pay element on request, within a defined time.
Make it measurable on both sides   An SLA that only binds the ICP will fail. Your platform controls the inputs. Late or incomplete data from your side causes many payroll problems.
Write the obligations of both parties. Define what counts as a valid input. Define what happens to service levels when your data arrives late. This protects the partnership and removes arguments at review time.
Define consequences and review   A service level without a consequence is a wish. Decide in advance what follows a miss: a corrective plan, a service credit, an escalation path. Keep the structure simple so it gets used.
Review the figures on a fixed cadence. Look at trends, not just breaches. A metric that is slowly getting worse is the early warning you want.
The point   Accuracy is what you want. These components are how you get it and how you prove it. Ask for the data behind each one, in a structured form you can load into your own reporting.
Partnership teams that want to see how this data can be exchanged between platform and ICP can request the data-exchange specification.

## What a payroll audit of an Italian ICP should cover
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/payroll-audit-italian-icp-scope.html
Summary: A scope for platform internal audit and SOC teams reviewing an Italian in-country partner: data flows, calculations, payments, filings, access and evidence.
A global EOR or payroll platform that relies on an in-country partner (ICP) in Italy carries the operational risk of that partner. Your customers see your brand. Your auditors will ask what you checked.
This note sets out a scope for internal audit or SOC teams. It is a checklist of areas, not a legal opinion. Adapt the depth to your own control framework.
Start with the data flow   Map how data moves before you test anything. Draw the path from your platform to the ICP and back.
Which system is the source of truth for employee master data? How do changes arrive: file, API, manual entry? Who approves a change before it reaches payroll? Where is the evidence stored, and for how long? Manual re-keying is the main risk to find here. Each re-key is a point where an amount, a tax code or a contract type can change without a trace.
Contract and collective agreement mapping   Italian payroll depends heavily on the national collective agreement (CCNL) that applies to the employee. It drives minimum pay, extra monthly payments, leave, notice and many allowances.
Audit questions:
How does the ICP assign a CCNL to each employee, and who signs off? Is the assignment recorded with a source and a date? What happens when an agreement is renewed and rates change? Are the job level and the pay components in the contract consistent with the agreement? Sample a set of employees and trace each one from contract to payslip. Check that the agreement on file is the one actually applied.
Gross-to-net calculation   Test the calculation, not just the output. Ask the ICP for the rule set behind it.
Employer and employee social security contributions. Income tax withholding and regional and municipal surcharges. Deductions and family-related tax elements. Year-end adjustments and tax settlement on the final payslip of the period. Severance accrual, which is specific to Italy and often missed by foreign teams. Re-perform a sample of calculations independently. Where the ICP uses payroll software, ask for the version history and the change log for rate tables. Rate updates should be traceable to an official source.
Payments and cash control   Payroll in Italy involves several payment streams. Net salaries go to employees. Withholdings and contributions go to the tax and social security bodies, usually through a consolidated payment form.
Audit questions:
Is there segregation between the person who prepares payments and the person who releases them? Do funds for taxes and contributions sit in a segregated account, or are they mixed with the ICP’s own money? How are payment files checked against the approved payroll? What is the reconciliation process, and who reviews it? How are rejected or returned payments handled? Funding is where platform risk concentrates. If you pre-fund the ICP, you need to know how that cash is held and when it is paid out.
Filings and reporting   The ICP files periodic declarations with the tax and social security authorities. It also handles monthly and annual reporting for each employee.
Check that:
A filing calendar exists and is owned by a named person. Each filing has a submission receipt stored with the payroll run it belongs to. Corrections and late filings are logged with a cause. The employee’s annual tax certificate is issued and matches the payslips. Ask for the receipts, not a statement that filings are done.
Starters, leavers and changes   Most errors cluster around events. Test them separately from the regular run.
Starter notifications and the timing of registration. Leaver calculations: unused leave, notice, severance, final tax. Mid-month changes in pay, hours or contract. Long absences and the split between employer and social security payments. Trace each event from the request on your platform to the effect on the payslip.
Access, security and data protection   This is the SOC part of the scope.
User access review for payroll systems and bank portals. Multi-factor authentication on every system that can change pay or release payments. Joiner, mover and leaver process for the ICP’s own staff. Encryption of files in transit and at rest. Sub-processors, and where employee data is stored and processed. Incident response: how fast you are told, and what you receive. Backup and recovery tests, with evidence. Italian employee data includes sensitive items such as health-related absence information. Confirm that access to it is limited by role.
Evidence and audit trail   A control that cannot be shown does not exist for audit purposes. Agree up front what evidence the ICP will hand over and in what format.
Useful evidence sets:
Approved payroll input for each run. Calculation reports and variance analysis against the previous run. Payment files and bank confirmations. Filing receipts. Reconciliation sign-offs. Change logs for rate tables and employee data. Variance analysis deserves attention. A good ICP explains every material movement between runs without being asked.
Service levels and governance   Finally, check how the relationship is managed.
Are service levels defined for input cut-off, payslip delivery and error correction? Who reports breaches, and how often? Is there a documented escalation path? How are the ICP’s own audits and certifications shared with you? Is there an exit plan that returns your data in a usable format? How to run it   Keep the first review narrow. Pick a small sample of employees across different agreements and event types. Trace each one end to end. Findings from a sample show you where to widen the scope.
Agree a remediation owner and a due date for every finding. Review progress on a fixed rhythm, not only at the next audit.
A structured data exchange makes all of this easier. When inputs, calculation results, payments and filings arrive in a consistent format, your team can test controls on the full population instead of a sample.
Partnership teams that want to see how that exchange can be structured can request the data-exchange specification.

## What an Italian in-country partner does each payroll month
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/italian-in-country-partner-monthly-payroll-tasks.html
Summary: The monthly task list of an Italian in-country payroll partner, from input cut-off to payment of contributions and taxes, seen from the partner's desk.
Global EOR and payroll platforms often see Italian payroll as a black box. Data goes in. Payslips and a payment confirmation come out. This article opens the box and walks through the month as the in-country partner lives it.
Input cut-off   The month starts with a hard line. After the cut-off, new inputs wait for the next cycle. Without that line, nothing downstream can be trusted.
Before the cut-off, the partner chases the inputs it does not yet have:
New hires and terminations, with the dates that drive pro-rata pay. Absences, sick leave and unpaid leave. Overtime and variable pay. Changes to bank details and family tax situation. Benefits and expense reimbursements that carry tax or contribution effects. Most late inputs are not late because someone forgot. They are late because the platform and the local entity use different names for the same event. A good partner keeps a short glossary and applies it every month.
Validation of the input file   The partner does not simply load the file. It reads it first.
Checks run against the applicable national collective agreement, the employee’s level and the contract terms. A missing level, an unusual allowance or a start date that conflicts with the contract all get a query back to the platform. These queries are short and specific. They name the employee, the field and the question.
This step is where most errors are caught. A wrong figure found now costs a message. The same figure found after payment costs a correction run and an awkward conversation with the employee.
Calculation   Italian payroll is rule-heavy. Contributions, withholding tax, regional and municipal surcharges, tax credits and conguaglio effects all interact. Collective agreements add their own rules on pay elements, notice and leave.
The partner runs the calculation, then runs it again from a different angle. Net pay is compared with the previous month. Every movement above a sensible threshold needs an explanation. If a net figure moves and nobody can say why, the run does not go out.
Review and approval   The partner sends a pre-payroll report to the platform. It lists gross-to-net by employee, employer cost, and the exceptions found during validation. The platform’s operations team reviews it and approves, or sends changes back.
Two habits keep this step short. First, the report format never changes without notice. Second, exceptions are listed at the top, not buried in the tables.
Payslips and payment instructions   Once approved, the partner issues the payslips and the net pay file. Payslips must be clear to the employee. Italian employees read them closely, and queries about a single line are normal.
The partner also tells the platform how much cash is needed for net salaries and for the contributions and taxes. Treasury teams need these figures early. A late funding request is one of the most common causes of delay.
Contributions and tax filings   After the run, the partner prepares the monthly social security declaration and the data for tax withholding. These are separate obligations with separate recipients and separate rules. Each needs its own check.
The partner also handles the other social insurance positions that sit alongside the main contributions. These are easy to forget on a platform dashboard. They are never forgotten in the filing.
Payment through the unified payment form   The last task of the cycle is paying contributions and taxes through the unified payment form. The partner builds the form with the correct codes for each obligation, period and office. A wrong code does not always cause an immediate rejection. It can cause a mismatch that surfaces months later.
The partner then keeps proof of payment and reconciles it to the payroll run. That reconciliation is the control that lets the platform sign off the month with confidence.
After the payment   The work does not stop at payment. The partner:
Answers employee queries on payslips. Records corrections that must be applied in a later run. Updates the file for each employee, including changes in tax and family data. Keeps the audit trail: inputs, approvals, calculations, filings and payments. Then the next cycle opens, and the cut-off comes again.
What this means for platforms   Three practical points follow from the partner’s desk.
Send inputs in a fixed, structured format. Free-text emails create manual work and manual errors. Agree event definitions once. Hire, change and termination should mean the same thing on both sides. Plan treasury early. Payment deadlines are fixed by law, so late funding is a platform problem, not a partner problem. A stable monthly rhythm between platform and partner is worth more than any single feature. It makes errors rare and visible.
Partnership teams can request the data-exchange specification to see the exact fields, formats and cut-off rules we use.

## What Italian employees ask their employer most
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/what-italian-employees-ask-their-employer-most.html
Summary: The main categories of questions Italian employees raise with their employer, and how an Italy-based representative handles them for global EOR platforms.
Global EOR and payroll platforms hire people in Italy through a local entity. The employee still has questions that the platform’s support team cannot answer from a global playbook. Italian employment rules have their own vocabulary, and employees expect answers in that vocabulary.
This article groups the questions by category. It shows what an Italy-based representative (ICP) handles on behalf of a platform, and where the platform’s own team stays in the loop.
Payslip questions   This is the largest category. The Italian payslip is dense. It lists contributions, withholdings, regional and municipal taxes, and several items that do not exist in other countries.
Typical questions:
Why is my net pay different from last month? What is this deduction? Why did my overtime or allowance change? Where do I see my accrued leave and permits? Most of these are not errors. They come from the collective agreement, a change in tax situation, or a variable item. The ICP reads the payslip against the agreement and the payroll inputs, then explains the line in plain terms. If there is an error, the case goes back to payroll with the exact line and the reason.
Collective agreement questions   Italian employment is shaped by the national collective agreement that applies to the role. It sets minimum pay levels, job grading, notice, leave and many other terms.
Employees ask:
Which agreement applies to me? Is my grade correct? What does the agreement say about sick pay, overtime or shift work? Am I owed an allowance listed in the agreement? These questions need a source. A good answer names the agreement, the clause and the version in force. Platforms should not improvise here. The ICP keeps the verified reference data and answers from it.
Leave, permits and absence   Employees want to know how much leave they have, how to request it, and what happens in special cases. These include sickness, family events, parental leave and study leave.
The practical questions are about process. Who approves? Which certificate is needed? Who notifies the social security institute? Sickness in particular has a defined certificate flow, and employees often do not know it. The ICP explains the steps and makes sure the notification reaches the right place.
Additional pay and end-of-service pay   Italian employees expect certain payments that foreign platforms may not model by default. They ask when additional monthly payments arrive, how they are calculated, and what the end-of-service entitlement is.
The end-of-service entitlement causes the most confusion. Employees want to know how it builds up, where it is held, and when they can ask for an advance. Platform teams often cannot answer this because it has no direct equivalent in their home market.
Contract changes   After the first months, employees ask about changes:
A raise or a change of grade. A change of working hours or location. Remote work arrangements. A move to another country, or arrival from abroad. Each change has formal steps and notifications. The ICP checks what the contract and the agreement allow, prepares the documents, and handles the filings with the competent bodies.
Termination and notice   Questions about leaving come from both sides. The employee asks how much notice is needed and what they will receive. The platform’s client asks what it can and cannot do. The ICP gives the Italian process and the documents required. It escalates anything with dispute risk to qualified counsel.
Visas, residence and relocation   For employees who move to Italy, the questions go beyond employment. They ask about work authorisation, residence registration, tax code, health coverage and bank accounts. These are not payroll topics, but the employee asks the employer first. A representative who knows the local steps removes a lot of friction.
Social security and tax status   Employees ask how they are covered, what they contribute, and what happens if they worked in another country before or will later. Cross-border situations need extra care. The ICP explains the Italian side and coordinates with the platform on the rest.
What this means for platforms   Three patterns repeat.
First, most questions are repeatable. They fit a small set of categories, and the answers depend on verified data, not opinion.
Second, the employee wants an answer in Italian terms, from someone who knows the system. A generic reply from a foreign support desk creates a second question.
Third, a clean split of work helps. The platform keeps the contract, billing and relationship. The ICP answers local questions, prepares local filings and returns structured data to the platform. Tickets close faster and fewer cases bounce between teams.
The result is a lower support load on your side and a better experience for the employee in Italy.
Partnership teams can request the data-exchange specification to see how questions, answers and filings are passed between your platform and ours.

## Why Italian payroll runs on a thirteenth and sometimes fourteenth month
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/italian-payroll-thirteenth-fourteenth-month.html
Summary: How Italian additional monthly payments work, why they are an accrual and not a bonus, and what platforms must model so pricing matches real payroll cost.
Many global payroll platforms quote Italy as a simple monthly salary. Then the first year closes and the real cost does not match the quote. The reason is the additional monthly payments, known in Italy as the thirteenth and, in many sectors, the fourteenth month.
This article explains how they work, so your pricing and accruals can reflect them from the first payslip.
What they are   The thirteenth and fourteenth month are not bonuses. They are part of the annual pay of the employee. Italian pay is often described as annual compensation split into more installments than calendar months. A gross annual figure agreed with a candidate is therefore not divided by the number of months in a year. It is divided by the number of installments the contract and the collective agreement provide.
This is the first point where platforms go wrong. If the offer letter says annual gross, the monthly figure on the payslip is lower than a simple monthly split would suggest. If the offer says monthly gross, the annual cost is higher than a simple multiplication would suggest. Both are valid. They must not be mixed.
Where the rules come from   The thirteenth month is established by law and by national collective agreements. The fourteenth month is different. It does not apply to every employee. It comes from the national collective agreement (CCNL) that covers the employee’s sector and, in some cases, from company-level agreements or individual contracts.
So you cannot answer the question “does this employee get a fourteenth month” at country level. You answer it per agreement, per job level, and sometimes per employer. Your data model needs the applicable agreement as an input, not as a note.
How the installments accrue   Each additional payment accrues month by month during the reference period. The employee earns a share of it for each month worked. The payment itself is made later, at the time the agreement sets.
This has three consequences for finance and operations teams.
Cost is incurred monthly, cash leaves later. If you book the cost only when the payment is made, your monthly margin looks better than it is, and the payment month looks worse. Accrue monthly. Partial periods are pro rata. An employee who joins or leaves part way through the reference period earns only the accrued share. Your engine needs a clear rule for part months. Termination settles the balance. When employment ends, any accrued but unpaid share is paid out in the final settlement. A client who offboards an employee early still owes it. Contributions follow the payment   The additional installments are part of taxable and contributory pay. Employer social contributions apply to them, as they do to ordinary salary. When you price the employer cost of an Italian hire, the contribution base includes all installments, not only the twelve ordinary monthly payments.
A quote that applies the employer contribution rate to twelve payments, and then adds the extra installments without contributions, understates cost. Apply the contribution base to the full annual pay.
Absence, leave and unpaid periods   Periods of absence can reduce or change the accrual, depending on the type of absence and the agreement. Some absences are covered by social security or by the employer for accrual purposes. Others reduce the share earned. Do not assume one treatment for all. Map absence types to accrual effect per agreement, and keep the mapping versioned.
What platforms should model   A practical data model for Italy needs the following fields.
The applicable national collective agreement and the job level. The number of installments per year under that agreement. The payment timing of each additional installment. The accrual rule for partial periods and for absences. The contribution base, which includes all installments. A clear flag on whether the client’s offer is stated as annual or as monthly gross. With these fields, the quote, the payslip, the accrual ledger and the final settlement all use the same logic. Without them, each system makes its own assumption and the differences surface at year end.
Common mismatches we see   Quote built on a monthly split, payroll run on the contractual installments. Accrual booked at payment instead of monthly. Fourteenth month assumed for everyone, or for no one. Employer contributions calculated on ordinary pay only. Final settlement missing the accrued share. Each of these is easy to fix once the agreement and installment count are captured as data. None is easy to fix after clients have signed on a wrong number.
The practical point   Italian payroll is not complicated because of one rule. It is complicated because the rule depends on the agreement. Treat the agreement as a primary key, accrue monthly, apply contributions to the full annual pay, and your Italian pricing will match what payroll actually costs.
Partnership teams that want to align their models with ours can request the data-exchange specification.

## Worked margin on a small Italian client: partner rate against platform price
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/margin-small-italian-client-partner-rate-platform-price.html
Summary: How a global EOR or payroll platform builds margin on a small Italian client, using the partner rate, the platform price and the cost lines between them.
A small Italian client looks simple on a pricing sheet. The margin only shows once you lay out every line between what the client pays you and what your Italian partner charges you.
This article walks through that structure in words. It uses no figures on purpose. The exact amounts depend on contracts, contribution classes and collective agreements, and they change. Use your own numbers in the model below.
The scenario   A foreign company signs with your platform. It wants a small team employed in Italy. You do not hold a local entity. You work with a local partner that runs the employment side: contracts, payroll, social security filings and the employer-side obligations.
Two prices matter.
The platform price is what your client pays you. The partner rate is what the Italian partner charges you. Your margin is the gap between them, minus the costs you carry yourself.
Step one: separate the pass-through lines   Some lines move through your books without being yours. Gross salary, employer contributions and statutory accruals belong here. Your client owes them, the partner pays them out, and you only relay them.
Keep these lines apart from your fee. If you blend them into one monthly figure, you will misread your margin. Salary changes, an overtime month or a contribution rate update will look like a margin swing when nothing about your fee changed.
So the first rule is simple. Margin is calculated on fees only. Pass-through lines are shown, reconciled and excluded.
Step two: define the fee layer   The fee layer is what is left after pass-through. It has two sides.
On the client side, your platform price is usually a per-employee monthly fee. It may include onboarding, offboarding, and support tiers.
On the partner side, the partner rate is usually also per employee per month. It may add separate charges for hiring, for terminations, for visa work, or for extra filings.
For a small client, the per-employee fees dominate. One-off charges matter less than the recurring gap. But a single early exit can still move the result, because the partner may charge a one-off fee that your platform price does not recover.
Step three: the margin formula   Write it down so everyone on the partnership and finance teams uses the same one.
Gross fee margin equals platform price minus partner rate, per employee, per month, summed across the team.
Then subtract the costs that sit with you:
Payment and foreign exchange costs on the client invoice. Support time spent on this client. Tooling and integration cost per active employee. Credit risk, meaning the cost of carrying the partner’s invoice before your client pays yours. What remains is net margin. For a small client it is often thin, and it is very sensitive to the support line.
Step four: what moves the result   Four things change the outcome more than the headline price.
Mix of one-off work. A client that hires fast and loses people fast pays your platform price for each event, but the partner may price those events differently. Check that every partner charge has a matching line on your side.
Payment timing. If the partner is paid before the client pays you, you finance the float. On a small client the float is small, but across many small clients it adds up.
Support load. A small client often asks as many questions as a large one. If your support cost is flat per client rather than per employee, small clients lose the most.
Rate changes. Contribution rules and collective agreements change over time. Pass-through lines move on their own. Your partner rate should not move with them unless the contract says so. Read that clause.
Step five: set a floor   Before you sign a small Italian client, set a floor for net margin per employee per month. If the platform price minus the partner rate, minus your own cost lines, falls under the floor, either change the price or add a minimum monthly fee for the account.
A minimum fee is the cleaner fix. It protects the margin without hiding the per-employee price from the client.
What to ask your partner for   A clean margin model needs clean data. Ask for:
A monthly statement that splits pass-through lines from fee lines. Event-level detail for hires, exits and changes, with a reference your system can match. Advance notice of any change that affects the fee layer. A stable identifier for each employee across both systems. Without these, reconciliation becomes a manual task. Manual reconciliation is where small-client margin disappears.
Summary   Treat salary and statutory costs as pass-through. Calculate margin on fees only. Subtract your own cost lines. Set a floor. Use a minimum fee when the account is small.
Partnership teams that want to model this against real data can request the data-exchange specification.

## Working hours, overtime and night work in Italy: an FAQ for platform ops teams
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/italy-working-hours-overtime-night-work-faq.html
Summary: Answers to the working time, overtime and night work questions that EOR and payroll platform ops teams forward from clients hiring in Italy.
Clients of global EOR and payroll platforms ask the same working time questions again and again when they hire in Italy. This FAQ collects them. It gives the structure of the answer and tells you which input your platform needs to capture. It does not give figures, because the figures depend on the contract and the collective agreement that applies. Those must come from a verified source for each case.
Who sets the rules on working hours?   Three layers apply. National legislation sets the framework. The national collective agreement (CCNL) for the employee’s sector fills in most of the detail. The individual contract can add terms, but only in the employee’s favour.
The practical point: the same role can have different overtime rules depending on the sector. A software engineer and a warehouse operator hired by the same foreign company may fall under different agreements. Your platform should record the CCNL for each hire before it answers any hours question.
Can the client set any schedule it wants?   No. The contract states the normal working time. The client can organise the schedule within that, and the CCNL may require notice or agreement for changes. Remote and hybrid arrangements do not remove these limits. Time spent working counts, wherever the employee sits.
Ops teams should ask clients for the intended schedule at onboarding, not after the first payroll run.
What counts as overtime?   Overtime is work beyond the normal contractual hours. The CCNL defines the threshold, the maximum allowed, and the premium. Some agreements treat overtime as voluntary, others allow the employer to require it within limits. The premium is usually a percentage uplift on the hourly rate, and it often differs for weekday, night and holiday overtime.
Two questions come up constantly:
Can overtime be paid as a flat sum? Not as a way to avoid the statutory or CCNL premium. A flat arrangement only works if it clearly covers at least what the rules would give. Can overtime be replaced by time off? Some agreements allow a time bank. It needs a written basis. Your platform should not assume it. Who is a night worker?   Night work is defined by a time window and by regularity. An employee who regularly works a set share of their hours inside the night window can qualify as a night worker. That status triggers extra obligations, including health checks and limits on the length of the night shift. It also affects pay, since the CCNL usually sets a night premium.
If a client asks whether an occasional late call makes someone a night worker, the answer is usually no. A scheduled rota that regularly includes night hours is different. Capture the rota, not just the contract.
Are there employees who are exempt from these rules?   Some senior roles with real autonomy over their own time can fall outside parts of the working time rules. This is narrow. A job title does not decide it. The actual autonomy and the CCNL classification do. Do not let clients mark an employee as exempt on their own. Route it to review.
What about rest and breaks?   Employees are entitled to daily rest, a weekly rest day and breaks during long working days. These are protected rights. A client cannot waive them in the contract. When a client’s home-country practice differs, for example on being reachable out of hours, the Italian rules still apply to the Italian employee.
How are hours recorded?   The employer must be able to show hours actually worked, especially where overtime or night work exists. Payroll needs a reliable feed. Typical gaps we see on platforms:
No hours data for salaried staff, so overtime is never detected. Overtime approved by email but never sent to payroll. Shift changes agreed locally and not logged. Holiday and leave mixed into worked hours. The fix is a simple monthly data exchange between the client system, your platform and the local payroll provider.
What should the platform ask at onboarding?   Use a short checklist:
Applicable CCNL and employee level. Contractual normal hours and schedule. Whether overtime is expected, and who approves it. Whether any shifts fall in the night window. Whether the role is claimed to be autonomous in its working time. How hours will be reported each month. With these six answers, most client questions can be answered without escalation.
When should a case be escalated?   Escalate when the CCNL is unclear, when a client wants to change the schedule mid-contract, when night work is proposed for an existing employee, or when an exemption is requested. These are the cases where a wrong default creates back-pay exposure.
Why this matters for partners   Working time errors rarely appear at hire. They appear months later as a payroll correction or a dispute. A clear intake and a clean hours feed prevent most of them. That protects your margin and your client relationship.
Partnership teams can request our data-exchange specification to see how hours, overtime and night work data flow between your platform and ours.

## Workplace safety onboarding for remote Italian employees: training and documents for home workers
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/workplace-safety-onboarding-remote-italian-employees.html
Summary: How EOR and payroll platforms can build a safety onboarding flow for remote workers in Italy: what to train, what to document, and what to store.
A remote hire in Italy is still covered by workplace safety rules. The desk is at home, but the employer’s duties do not disappear. For EOR and payroll platforms, this is an onboarding task that is easy to skip and hard to fix later.
This article covers what a safety onboarding flow for home workers should contain, who owns each step, and what records to keep.
Why it belongs in onboarding   Safety duties start on day one of employment. If the platform collects contracts, tax data and bank details but nothing on safety, the file is incomplete. A gap shows up when there is an accident claim, an inspection or a client audit.
The foreign client often assumes the EOR handles this. The EOR often assumes the worker’s home is the worker’s business. Neither is correct. The flow needs a named owner.
What the training should cover   Keep it short and practical. A long generic course is rarely read. A focused module for home workers should cover:
Setting up a workstation: chair, screen height, lighting, keyboard and mouse position. Breaks and posture during long screen sessions. Electrical basics: sockets, extension leads, cable routing, overloaded multi-plugs. Fire and emergency basics at home: exits, smoke detection, who to call. Choosing a work location in the home that is suitable, not a sofa or a bed. How to report an accident or a near miss, and how fast. Stress, isolation and working-time limits, including the right to disconnect. The module should be in the worker’s language. Italian is the default. Offer English if the worker asks for it, but keep the Italian version as the reference.
Written information on risks   Italian practice expects the employer to give remote workers written information about the risks tied to working outside company premises. This is separate from the training. It is a document the worker receives, reads and acknowledges.
A good version is plain and specific to home work. It should not be a copy of an office safety manual. Include the risks above, the worker’s own duty to cooperate, and the duty to use equipment safely.
Your platform should record three things:
The version of the document sent. The date it was delivered. The worker’s acknowledgement. If the document changes, send the new version and record it again.
Equipment and the home workspace   If the client supplies a laptop, monitor or chair, the platform should log what was issued. Equipment that comes from the employer must be safe and suitable. Equipment that belongs to the worker raises harder questions, so decide a policy early and write it down.
A self-assessment checklist helps. The worker confirms the workstation setup with a few yes or no answers and optional photos. This is not an inspection. It is a record that the employer asked, and that the worker answered.
Accident insurance and the INAIL premium   Employees in Italy are covered by the national workplace accident insurance, INAIL. Remote workers are included. Accidents linked to the work can be covered, even at home, subject to the usual conditions.
The premium is calculated with INAIL rates. According to a secondary source, the rates set in 2019 remain in force. The way they are applied was changed in 2026. Because the source is secondary, check the current position on the INAIL site before you quote any premium to a client or build it into a pricing model.
For your platform, the practical point is simple. Classify each remote role correctly, keep the data used for the premium up to date, and make sure the client understands that accident cover is part of the employment cost.
Who does what   A clear split avoids gaps.
Client company: describes the real tasks, tools and working pattern of the role. EOR: sends the information, delivers the training, collects acknowledgements and stores the records. Worker: completes the module, returns the checklist and reports incidents. Payroll team: keeps the insurance classification current. Put these roles in the service agreement, not only in an internal guide.
What to store   Store the minimum that proves the process happened:
Training completion with date. Risk information document, version and acknowledgement. Workstation checklist and date. Equipment issued, if any. Incident reports and follow-up. Treat all of it as employee personal data. Limit access, set a retention rule and be able to export a worker’s full safety file on request.
Build it once   This flow is the same for every Italian remote hire. It should be automatic. Trigger it when the contract is signed, send reminders if steps are open, and block the first payroll cycle sign-off if the file is incomplete. Your support team then answers fewer questions, and your clients see a complete record.
Partnership teams: request the data-exchange specification to receive safety onboarding status for each Italian hire directly in your platform.

## Year-End Readiness Checklist for Italian ICP Operations
URL: https://italyincountry.com/articles/year-end-readiness-checklist-italian-icp-operations.html
Summary: A practical checklist for EOR and payroll platforms running Italian ICP operations through year-end payroll, the extra monthly salary and new-year recalculations.
Year-end in Italy is not a normal payroll cycle. The extra monthly salary, final adjustments and new-year recalculations all land close together. Platforms that treat it as routine tend to find the gaps late.
This checklist is for partnership, operations and payroll managers who rely on an Italian ICP to run local payroll for their workers. It covers what to confirm before the year closes and what to expect once the new year starts.
Agree the calendar early   Ask your Italian partner for a written year-end calendar. It should show the cut-off for employee data changes, the date payroll inputs are frozen, the payment run and the point where reports are released to you.
Your own systems also have cut-offs. Match them to the partner’s calendar. If your platform sends changes after the freeze, they will fall into the next cycle. Make sure your support teams know this, so they can tell customers and workers what to expect.
Confirm who owns each input   Most year-end errors come from unclear ownership. Write down who supplies each of these and in what format:
New hires, leavers and contract changes Salary changes and bonuses Unpaid leave, sickness and other absences Benefits and expense reimbursements Tax and social security data that changed during the year If your platform is the source of truth for some of these, say so. If the ICP is, say that too. A field with two owners will produce two different values.
Check the extra monthly salary   Italian employees usually receive an additional monthly salary at the end of the year, commonly called the tredicesima. Some contracts and collective agreements add further extra payments. Your platform should not assume one pattern fits every worker.
Before the payment run, confirm these points with your partner:
Which workers are entitled to it under their contract and applicable collective agreement How it is calculated for part-year employees, part-time staff and people with unpaid absences How it appears on the payslip and in your reports What it adds to employer cost, so your invoices reflect the true figure Finance teams are often surprised here. The payment affects employer contributions as well as net pay. Show your customers the expected cost before the run, not after it.
Review the year-end payroll run   The final payroll of the year carries more weight than usual. Ask for a pre-run preview and review it against your own records.
Look for headcount differences, unexpected zero payments, workers missing from the run and large swings in cost compared with the previous month. Check that leavers are handled correctly, including any final entitlements that must be paid out.
Agree a clear sign-off step. Someone on your side should approve the preview, and the partner should record that approval. If a problem appears after payment, you will want a trail showing what was reviewed and when.
Plan for recalculations after year-end   The new year often brings adjustments. Some come from late information about the old year. Others come from rule changes that apply from the start of the new period, such as updated contribution parameters or tax settings.
Ask your partner how they handle three cases:
A late change that affects a payslip already issued A correction that crosses the year boundary Updated parameters applied to the first payroll of the new year For each case, find out whether the correction is paid in the next run, issued as a separate payment or handled through a later adjustment. Then check that your platform can display it clearly. Workers who see an unexplained difference will contact support, and your teams need a ready answer.
Align reporting and data exchange   Year-end creates a surge in reports, certificates and data requests. Confirm in advance which documents your partner will issue, who receives them and how they reach the worker.
Also test your data exchange. If you use an API or file transfer, run a trial with realistic year-end data before the busy period. Check field mappings for the extra payment, adjustments and corrections. A mapping that works for a normal month can fail on a retroactive item.
Prepare your support teams   Workers ask the same questions every year. Why is the payment larger than usual? Why is a deduction different? When will the certificate arrive? Prepare short, accurate answers with your partner and keep them in your knowledge base.
Set an escalation path with named contacts on both sides, including response expectations over the holiday period. Italian offices often run with reduced staff at year-end, so do not assume normal turnaround.
A short summary list   Get the partner’s year-end calendar in writing Assign an owner to every payroll input Confirm entitlement and calculation rules for the extra monthly salary Review a payroll preview and record the sign-off Agree how late and cross-year corrections are handled Test data exchange with realistic year-end items Brief support teams and name escalation contacts None of this is complicated. It only needs to be done before the pressure starts. Platforms that agree the process early spend the busy weeks resolving real exceptions rather than basic misunderstandings.
Partnership teams are invited to request the data-exchange specification.

## Partner Onboarding

## Partner Pricing
URL: https://italyincountry.com/pricing.html
Summary: Wholesale in-country employer of record pricing for platforms: from €100 per employee per month, employment cost on actuals.
 Partner pricing Wholesale, per active employee from €100 per employee per month
Final rate depends on volume, sectors and how much of the process runs through the API. You set your own price to the client.
Partner feeFlat monthly fee per active employee. Includes contract, onboarding, monthly payroll, F24 payments, payslips, outputs and ops support.
Employment costGross salary, employer contributions, INAIL, TFR accrual and other statutory costs are passed through monthly on actuals, line by line.
DepositOne month of employment cost per employee, held as a deposit and returned or offset when employment ends.
BillingInvoiced monthly in advance, based on the approved payroll register. Payment before the pay date.
Retail list prices for Italy, for reference: our end-client brands sell at €250 all inclusive.
The lowest all-inclusive Employer of Record price for Italy ItalyInCountry: €250 per employee per month, all included: Italian employment contract and CCNL selection, monthly payroll, payslips and filings, onboarding and offboarding, HR documents and amendments, invoicing in your currency at the EUR reference rate, no FX spread, no setup fee.

## Partner Program
URL: https://italyincountry.com/partner-program.html
Summary: Partner program for payroll bureaus, global mobility advisors, HR consultants and law firms that serve EOR platforms and multinational clients in Italy.
 Advisor partners For the professionals behind global employers Payroll bureaus, global mobility consultants, HR advisors, law and accounting firms, trade agencies and resellers that support EOR platforms or multinational clients: route their Italian headcount to ItalyInCountry, the Employer of Record (EOR) built to run on someone else's process.
Start a partner enquiryRead our SLAs Where you fit Global clients rarely want an Italian legal entity for a handful of people, and many EOR platforms lack a dependable local employer. You already advise both. Bring us in and Italy is covered: employment contracts, payroll, contributions and data delivered in the format your client or platform uses. €250 per employee per month for direct clients, everything included.
Benefits by partner type Payroll, mobility and legal advisorsAn advisor desk with a named counterpart for the cases you send.Referral compensation per activated client, or a client discount if that suits your engagement better.Training for your consultants on Italian employment rules.A white-labelled cost model to show clients the full Italian cost.A clean handover when a client moves from EOR to its own Italian company, with no exit penalty.Regular notes on CCNL renewals, contribution changes, visa rules and filing dates. Trade agencies and chambersUp to 20% off the list price for the companies you introduce, by volume.Live-translated support for employers and employees.Co-authored guides, shared webinars and speaking slots at your events.Priority lanes for onboarding and permits.Links to Italian regional agencies, incentives, recruiters and relocation providers. Platforms and white-label resellersYour brand on the service and on payslips, at a dedicated reseller rate.A partner manager on fixed response times.A portal for protected lead registration, client status and monthly reporting. The process Partner agreementTerms, data protection and your choice between referral compensation and client discount. Lead registrationRegister the platform or company in the portal; attribution is locked to you. Client onboardingWe agree the payroll calendar and data format, then hire to our service levels. Reporting and payoutsA monthly statement of active employees, SLA results and amounts due. Partner FAQ Whose client is it?Yours, or your platform client's. We never approach a referred company outside the agreed channel.
Will you advise my clients?No. We provide employment and payroll in Italy. Tax, legal and mobility advice stays with you, and we refer those questions back.
What about confidential data?Data is exchanged under a data processing agreement and kept in the EU. See our data exchange page.
Which languages do you work in?English and Italian by default, with real-time translation for other languages.
How quickly can we go live?A quote in one business day; employees with complete documents can start within days, non-EU staff once the permit allows.
When does a client outgrow the EOR?When it wants an Italian presence that trades and contracts locally. We move the staff over and the incorporation work goes to you.
Start a partner enquiry

## Service Levels
URL: https://italyincountry.com/service-levels.html
Summary: Onboarding times, payroll cut-off and response times for platforms using ItalyInCountry as their Italian partner.
 Service levels Times we commit to in writing These are the default targets. We can move payroll dates to match your global calendar during onboarding. Business days and hours are Italian (CET/CEST).
AreaItemTarget OnboardingStart date for non-EU hiresDepends on visa; timeline given with the quote Fixed Italian deadlines are not movable: taxes withheld and social contributions are paid through the F24 form by the 16th of the month after payment. Our calendar always leaves room for them.
